[[4:22|till thou know|Donec scias]] by experience of due chastisement: know, I say, firmly and perfectly, [[4:22|that the most High ruleth|quod dominetur Excelsus]], that is, God most high, in comparison with whom all things are low, [[4:22|over the kingdom of men|super regnum hominum]], that is, that he presides over all kingdoms as the supreme, first and almighty ruler: according to that of the Psalm, [[Ps 94:4|in his hand are all the ends of the earth|In manu ejus sunt omnes fines terræ]]; [[4:22|and giveth it to whomsoever he will|et cuicumque voluerit, det illud]], justly putting down one and raising up another at his pleasure.

paras.t: Quod autem vigil et sanctus præcepit, ut germen radicum ejus, id est arboris, relinqueretur : sic enim superius dixit, Attamen germen radicum ejus in terra dimittite : id (inquam) significat, quod regnum tuum tibi manebit, id est, te exspectabit, et illud recipies, postquam cognoveris, vexatione tibi intellectum præstante, et corde tuo per humilitatem ac supernam illuminationem disposito, potestatem esse cœlestem, id est, esse unam summam ac primam virtutem increatam et independentem, in cœlis regnantem, et terrestria moderantem, providentiam universorum habentem. Itaque per germen radicum arboris, designatur possibilitas redeundi ad regnum.
paras.en: [[4:23|But whereas|Quod autem]] the watcher and holy one [[4:23|he commanded|præcepit]], [[4:23|that the stump of the roots thereof, that is, of the tree, should be left|ut germen radicum ejus, id est arboris, relinqueretur]] (for so he said above, [[4:20|but leave the stump of the roots thereof in the earth|Attamen germen radicum ejus in terra dimittite]] [the margin gives v. 12, which says the same; the words are those of v. 20]): that, I say, signifies that [[4:23|thy kingdom shall remain to thee|regnum tuum tibi manebit]], that is, shall await thee, and thou shalt receive it again, [[4:23|after thou shalt have known|postquam cognoveris]], affliction giving thee understanding, and thy heart being made ready by humility and heavenly enlightenment, [[4:23|that power is from heaven|potestatem esse cœlestem]], that is, that there is one supreme and first power, uncreated and independent, reigning in heaven and governing earthly things, having providence over all. So by the stump of the roots of the tree is signified the possibility of returning to the kingdom.

paras.t: Nunc exponenda sunt quædam superius transilita. Succidite arborem, et præcidite ramos ejus, id est, regem Nabuchodonosor de regno propellite, et dilatationem sui imperii tollite. Et excutite folia ejus, id est, verba ejus magnifica et ornatum, ostendite vana, et dispergite fructus ejus, id est, opes ipsius auferte ab eo. Aliqui etiam dicunt, quod divitiæ regni Babylonici, durante regis insania, a pluribus rapiebantur. Et fugiant bestiæ quæ subter eam sunt, id est, subditi, inferiores, rusticani et simplices, de regis jugo recedant ; et volucres, id est divites, potentes, et in dignitatibus constituti, de ramis ejus, scilicet Nabuchodonosor, abeant, sub latitudine suæ potestatis non amplius se tuendo. Cor ejus ab humano commutetur, id est, mens seu ratio ejus ab aliorum mente varietur, ita quod in amentiam transferatur. Ratione enim a brutis secernimur : dum ergo usu rationis privamur, brutales efficimur. Et cor feræ detur ei, videlicet judicio rationis nudato.
paras.en: Now some things passed over above are to be explained. [[4:11|Cut down the tree, and chop off the branches thereof|Succidite arborem, et præcidite ramos ejus]], that is, drive King Nabuchodonosor out of his kingdom, and take away the breadth of his empire. [[4:11|shake off its leaves|Et excutite folia ejus]], that is, show his grand words and his adornment to be vain, [[4:11|and scatter its fruits|et dispergite fructus ejus]], that is, take his wealth away from him. Some also say that the riches of the Babylonian kingdom, while the king's madness lasted, were plundered by many. [[4:11|let the beasts fly away that are under it|Et fugiant bestiæ quæ subter eam sunt]], that is, let the subjects, the lower sort, the country folk and the simple, withdraw from the king's yoke; [[4:11|and the birds|et volucres]], that is, the rich, the powerful and those set in dignities, [[4:11|from its branches|de ramis ejus]], that is, of Nabuchodonosor, let them go away, no longer sheltering under the breadth of his power. [[4:13|Let his heart be changed from man's|Cor ejus ab humano commutetur]], that is, let his mind or reason be made different from the mind of others, so that it is turned into madness. For by reason we are set apart from the brutes: when therefore we are deprived of the use of reason, we become brutish. [[4:13|and let a beast's heart be given him|Et cor feræ detur ei]], that is, once it is stripped of the judgement of reason.

paras.t: In sententia vigilum, id est per sententiam promulgatam per angelos, decretum est, id est, divinitus ordinatum est sic fieri : ita quod institutio seu ordinatio Dei per sententiam angelorum, innotuit mundo de regis hujus punitione præfata. Et licet unus vigil seu angelus verba inducta clamaverit, alii tamen consenserunt, aut executioni sententiæ cooperati sunt. Porro qui die ac nocte, quantum natura permittit, sanctis instant vigiliis, Dei laudibus aut actibus virtuosis vacando, cœlestium vigilum agilitatem sectantur. Hinc ait Hieronymus : Nos quoque crebris pernoctationibus imitamur officia angelorum. Et Christus in Evangelio : Beatus, inquit, servus ille, quem, quum venerit dominus ejus, et pulsaverit januam ejus, invenerit vigilantem ; et rursus, Vigilate itaque, quia nescitis qua hora Dominus vester venturus sit.
paras.en: [[4:14|by the sentence of the watchers|In sententia vigilum]], that is, by the sentence promulgated by the angels, [[4:14|This is the decree|decretum est]], that is, it has been divinely ordained that it be so: so that the institution or ordinance of God concerning the punishment of this king, foretold above, was made known to the world through the sentence of the angels. And though one watcher or angel cried out the words given, the others nevertheless agreed, or worked together in carrying out the sentence. Further, those who by day and by night, as far as nature allows, keep holy vigils, giving themselves to the praises of God or to virtuous acts, follow the alertness of the heavenly watchers. Hence Jerome says: We too, by frequent night watches, imitate the offices of the angels. And Christ in the Gospel: Blessed, he says, is that servant whom his lord, when he shall come and knock at his door, shall find watching[[Luke 12:37||]] [Denis's wording joins Luke 12:36–37, in the singular as in Matt 24:46]; and again, [[Matt 24:42|Watch ye therefore, because you know not what hour your Lord will come|Vigilate itaque, quia nescitis qua hora Dominus vester venturus sit]].

paras.t: Et sermo sanctorum : id est, eorum qui divinæ æquitati consentiunt in supernis, sermo et verbum est ut taliter fiat ; et petitio eorumdem. Sancti namque expostulant ultionem contra malignos, et Dei omnipotentiam in impiorum justa dejectione declarari precantur, juxta illud Apocalypsis : Usquequo, Domine (sanctus et verus), non judicas, et non vindicas sanguinem nostrum de his qui sunt in terra ?
paras.en: [[4:14|and the word|Et sermo]] [[4:14|of the holy ones|sanctorum]]: that is, of those on high who agree with the divine justice, it is the saying and the word that it be done so; [[4:14|and demand|et petitio]] of the same. For the saints demand vengeance against the wicked, and pray that God's almighty power be shown in the just casting down of the ungodly, according to that of the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 6:10|How long, O Lord (Holy and True), dost thou not judge and revenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?|Usquequo, Domine (sanctus et verus), non judicas, et non vindicas sanguinem nostrum de his qui sunt in terra]]

paras.t: Donec cognoscant viventes in terra, quod dominetur Excelsus, id est Deus sublimis, in regno hominum, id est, cuncta regna ejus potestati subdantur : sicut plenius dictum est super illud, Ipse transfert regna atque constituit. Et cuicumque voluerit, dabit illud. Subest enim ei, quum voluerit, posse. Ideo secundum Dei voluntatem quisque ad præsidentiam est vocandus, ut ait Gregorius ; nec debet se quisquam ingerere, neque vulpinis uti cautelis, sed rem dispositioni divinæ committere, quum ad Hebræos dicat Apostolus : Nemo sumit sibi honorem, sed qui vocatur a Deo tanquam Aaron. Et humillimum hominem constituet super eum, id est super regni principatum. Quidam per humillimum hominem intelligunt Christum, qui protestatur, Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra ; alii, regem Nabuchodonosor, qui post suam amentiam profundissime humiliavit se Deo. Generalius tamen exponi potest indeterminate, quod Deus quemcumque hominem sibi placentem ad promovendum, promoveat ad regnandum, si ita decrevit, quantumcumque ille sit vilis atque abjectus. Juxta quod dicitur primo Regum libro : Suscitat de pulvere egenum, et de stercore elevat pauperem, ut sedeat cum principibus, et solium gloriæ teneat.
paras.en: [[4:14|till the living know|Donec cognoscant viventes]] on earth, [[4:14|that the most High ruleth|quod dominetur Excelsus]], that is, God on high, [[4:14|in the kingdom of men|in regno hominum]], that is, that all kingdoms are subject to his power: as was said more fully on the words, He [[Dan 2:21|taketh away kingdoms, and establisheth them|transfert regna atque constituit]]. [[4:14|and he will give it to whomsoever it shall please him|Et cuicumque voluerit, dabit illud]]. For his power is at hand when he will[[Wis 12:18||]]. Therefore each man is to be called to high office according to God's will, as Gregory says; and no one ought to thrust himself forward, nor use the wiles of the fox, but commit the matter to the divine disposition, since the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 5:4|Neither doth any man take the honour to himself, but he that is called by God, as Aaron was|Nemo sumit sibi honorem, sed qui vocatur a Deo tanquam Aaron]]. [[4:14|and he will appoint the basest man over it|Et humillimum hominem constituet super eum]], that is, over the rule of the kingdom. Some understand by *the basest man* [that is, *humillimus*, the lowliest] Christ, who declares, [[Matt 28:18|All power is given to me in heaven and in earth|Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra]]; others, King Nabuchodonosor, who after his madness humbled himself most deeply before God. But it can be explained more generally and without restriction: that God raises to reign any man whom it pleases him to raise, if he has so decreed, however mean and abject that man may be. According to what is said in the first book of Kings: [[1 Kings 2:8|He raiseth up the needy from the dust, and lifteth up the poor from the dunghill: that he may sit with princes, and hold the throne of glory|Suscitat de pulvere egenum, et de stercore elevat pauperem, ut sedeat cum principibus, et solium gloriæ teneat]].

paras.t: Nunc visio tota exposita est ; subjungiturque consilium sancti Prophetæ, qui nil melius vidit pro rege, quam ad divinam confugere misericordissimam pietatem. Quamobrem, rex, consilium meum tibi placeat. Consilium etenim sapientium, præsertim in arduis, est quærendum atque servandum, ut in Tobia habetur : Consilium semper a sapiente perquire ; et in Proverbiis, Qui cuncta agunt consilio reguntur sapientia. Et peccata tua eleemosynis redime, ne debitor pœnæ permaneas, neque peccatis obnoxius, et iniquitates tuas misericordiis pauperum. Contraria enim curantur contrariis. Ideo decet, ut qui pauperes oppressisti, eis subvenias. Et ad impetrandum misericordiam Dei maxime confert, misericordiam pauperibus, imo et cunctis, impendere. Propter quod ait Salvator : Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur. Et iterum ait Scriptura : Sicut aqua exstinguit ignem, ita eleemosyna exstinguit peccatum ; et in Proverbiis, Per misericordiam et fidem purgantur peccata. Sed et in Tobia inde notabiliter scriptum est : Noli avertere faciem tuam ab ullo paupere : ita enim fiet, ut nec a te avertatur facies Domini. Eleemosyna ab omni peccato liberat, et non patietur animam ire in tenebras.
paras.en: Now the whole vision has been explained; and there follows the counsel of the holy Prophet, who saw nothing better for the king than to take refuge in the most merciful divine goodness. [[4:24|Wherefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to thee|Quamobrem, rex, consilium meum tibi placeat]]. For the counsel of the wise, especially in hard matters, is to be sought and kept, as is said in Tobias: [[Tob 4:19|Seek counsel always of a wise man|Consilium semper a sapiente perquire]]; and in Proverbs, [[Prov 13:10|they that do all things with counsel, are ruled by wisdom|Qui cuncta agunt consilio reguntur sapientia]]. [[4:24|and redeem thou thy sins with alms|Et peccata tua eleemosynis redime]], lest thou remain a debtor to punishment and liable for thy sins, [[4:24|and thy iniquities with works of mercy to the poor|et iniquitates tuas misericordiis pauperum]]. For contraries are cured by contraries [a maxim of the physicians, applied to the healing of the soul]. Therefore it is fitting that thou who hast oppressed the poor shouldst help them. And to obtain God's mercy it avails most to show mercy to the poor, nay, to all. Wherefore the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:7|Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy|Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur]]. And again Scripture says: As water quencheth fire, so alms quencheth sin[[Ecclus 3:33||]] [the margin notes "according to the old version", that is, an older Latin rendering; the Vulgate reads: Water quencheth a flaming fire, and alms resisteth sins]; and in Proverbs, [[Prov 15:27|By mercy and faith sins are purged away|Per misericordiam et fidem purgantur peccata]]. And in Tobias too it is notably written on this: [[Tob 4:7|turn not away thy face from any poor person: for so it shall come to pass that the face of the Lord shall not be turned from thee|Noli avertere faciem tuam ab ullo paupere : ita enim fiet, ut nec a te avertatur facies Domini]]. [[Tob 4:11|alms deliver from all sin|Eleemosyna ab omni peccato liberat]], [[Tob 4:11|and will not suffer the soul to go into darkness|et non patietur animam ire in tenebras]].

paras.t: Forsitan ignoscet Deus delictis tuis. Quum per Ezechielem Dominus dicat, Si impius egerit pœnitentiam, omnium iniquitatum ejus non recordabor amplius : cur Daniel dubitative locutus est, Forsitan ignoscet Deus delictis tuis ? Et respondendum, quod non dubitavit quin culpam Deus regi dimitteret, si veraciter pœniteret ; sed certus non fuit an pœnam in præsenti comminatam dimitteret. Pœnitenti enim dimittitur culpa, non protinus pœna : nisi forte fervor caritatis et dolor contritionis esset tam vehemens, quod etiam ad pœnæ deletionem sufficeret.
paras.en: [[4:24|perhaps he will forgive thy offences|Forsitan ignoscet Deus delictis tuis]]. Since the Lord says by Ezechiel: [[Ezech 18:21|if the wicked do penance|Si impius egerit pœnitentiam]], [[Ezech 18:22|I will not remember all his iniquities|omnium iniquitatum ejus non recordabor amplius]] any more: why did Daniel speak doubtfully, [[4:24|perhaps he will forgive thy offences|Forsitan ignoscet Deus delictis tuis]]? The answer is that he did not doubt that God would forgive the king his guilt, if he truly repented; but he was not certain whether He would remit the punishment threatened in this present life. For to the penitent the guilt is forgiven, but not at once the punishment [that is, the guilt (*culpa*) of sin and the temporal punishment (*pœna*) due to it are distinct], unless perhaps the fervour of charity and the sorrow of contrition were so vehement as to suffice for wiping out the punishment as well.

paras.t: Rursus, Propheta tam sobrie loquitur, ne quis alteri temerarie veniam repromittat. Nam et facilitas veniæ præstat peccandi audaciam. Nec quicumque dolor aut gemitus ad veritatem pœnitentiæ sufficit, sed oportet (secundum Hieronymum) ut dolor pœnitentialis sit adæquatus peccato, quatenus quo major est culpa, eo major dolor sit : quem etiam provenire oportet non ex solo servili timore, sed ex zelo justitiæ ac divino amore, si meritorius erit atque idoneus. Hinc Glossa hic dicit, et sunt quasi verba Hieronymi : Daniel præscius futurorum, de Dei sententia dubitat : in quo apparet eorum intolerabilis temeritas, qui audacter peccatoribus veniam pollicentur ; nemini tamen desperandum, quia et Nabuchodonosor regi, si bona fecerit, indulgentia promittitur. Et hoc est quod ait Hieronymus : Sciendum quod si Nabuchodonosor bona opera facienti venia repromittitur, quanto magis aliis qui minus peccaverunt ? Ideo quoque ait, Forsitan, secundum Albertum, quia in voluntate et gratia Dei est, secundum illud Joelis : Quis scit si ignoscat Deus ?
paras.en: Again, the Prophet speaks so soberly lest anyone should rashly promise pardon to another. For easiness of pardon gives boldness to sin. Nor does just any sorrow or groaning suffice for true penance; but (according to Jerome) penitential sorrow must be proportioned to the sin, so that the greater the guilt, the greater the sorrow; and it must also spring not from servile fear alone [that is, fear of punishment only], but from zeal for justice and from the love of God, if it is to be meritorious and fitting. Hence the Gloss says here, and they are almost the words of Jerome: Daniel, who foreknew things to come, is in doubt about God's sentence; in which appears the intolerable rashness of those who boldly promise pardon to sinners; yet no one must despair, since even to king Nabuchodonosor indulgence is promised, if he does good. And this is what Jerome says: Be it known that if pardon is promised to Nabuchodonosor if he does good works, how much more to others who have sinned less? He says *perhaps* also, according to Albert, because it lies in the will and grace of God, according to that saying of Joel: [[Joel 2:14|Who knoweth but he will return, and forgive|Quis scit si ignoscat Deus]]?

paras.t: Denique circa prædicta S. Hieronymus et alii movent hanc quæstionem : Quum Daniel prædixerit Dei sententiam, quæ non potest cassari et immutari, quomodo hortatur regem ad eleemosynas, ut Dei sententia commutetur ? Et respondetur, quod prophetia seu prænunciatio prædestinationis semper impletur, quia in ea aliquid dicitur secundum quod est in providentia Dei ; non autem prophetia aut prænuntiatio comminationis, cujus impletio ex meritis nostris dependet frequenter. Daniel autem non scivit, ut dicitur, an prænuntiatio sua prophetica, esset comminationis dumtaxat. Comminationes vero propheticæ intelliguntur sub conditione, utpote nisi illi contra quos dicitur, se emendent, aut precibus suis seu aliorum suffragio procurent oppositum, ut patet in Ninivitis et Ezechia. Propterea per Jeremiam Dominus profitetur : Repente loquar adversum gentem et regnum, ut eradicem et destruam illud. Si pœnitentiam egerit gens illa, agam et ego pœnitentiam super malo quod cogitavi ut facerem ei.
paras.en: Lastly, concerning what has been said, St Jerome and others raise this question: since Daniel foretold God's sentence, which cannot be annulled or changed, how does he exhort the king to almsgiving so that God's sentence may be changed? The answer is that a prophecy or foretelling of predestination is always fulfilled, because in it something is said as it stands in the providence of God; but not so a prophecy or foretelling of threatening [that is, one that foretells what will befall unless men amend], whose fulfilment often depends on our merits. Now Daniel did not know, as is said, whether his prophetic foretelling was one of threatening only. And prophetic threats are understood under a condition: namely, unless those against whom they are spoken amend, or by their own prayers or the intercession of others obtain the opposite, as is plain in the Ninivites[[Jon 3:4||]] and in Ezechias[[Is 38:1||]]. Therefore the Lord declares by Jeremias: [[Jer 18:7|I will suddenly speak against a nation, and against a kingdom, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy it|Repente loquar adversum gentem et regnum, ut eradicem et destruam illud]]. [[Jer 18:8|If that nation against which I have spoken, shall repent|Si pœnitentiam egerit gens illa]], [[Jer 18:8|I also will repent of the evil that I have thought to do to them|agam et ego pœnitentiam super malo quod cogitavi ut facerem ei]].

paras.t: Omnia hæc mala pœnalia prænunciata, venerunt super Nabuchodonosor regem, per modum qui subditur. Post finem mensium duodecim, uno scilicet anno completo a prænuntiatione jam habita, quo ad pœnitentiam exspectabatur a Deo : de quo in libro Sapientiæ fertur, Misereris omnium, et dissimulas peccata hominum propter pœnitentiam; in aula Babylonis deambulabat, id est in suo palatio, plenus superbia. Ait quippe Hieronymus : Fecit Nabuchodonosor juxta Danielis consilium misericordias in pauperes : idcirco usque ad mensem duodecimum in eum est dilata sententia. Postea vero intumuit, putans non esse implendum quod a Daniele audivit.
paras.en: [[4:25|All these things|Omnia hæc]], namely the penal evils foretold, [[4:25|came upon king Nabuchodonosor|venerunt super Nabuchodonosor regem]], in the manner that follows. [[4:26|At the end of twelve months|Post finem mensium duodecim]], that is, when one year was complete from the foretelling already made, during which God waited for him to repent; of which it is said in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 11:24|thou hast mercy upon all|Misereris omnium]], [[Wis 11:24|and overlookest the sins of men for the sake of repentance|et dissimulas peccata hominum propter pœnitentiam]]; [[4:26|he was walking in the palace of Babylon|in aula Babylonis deambulabat]], that is, in his own palace, full of pride. For Jerome says: Nabuchodonosor, following Daniel's counsel, showed mercy to the poor: therefore the sentence against him was deferred until the twelfth month. But afterwards he swelled with pride, thinking that what he had heard from Daniel was not to be fulfilled.

paras.t: Responditque rex, et ait. An solus deambulavit vel cum aliis, et utrum aliquis eum alloquebatur, cui responderet, in textu non scribitur. Et multi expositores testantur, quod non alicui se affanti, sed proprii cordis elationi respondit. Et quidam imaginantur, quod tunc cogitavit de abjectione sibi a Daniele prædicta, quam falsam putavit, quia jam transiit annus, et ipse tantæ potentiæ se præsumpsit, quod nullus posset eum dejicere. Ideo dixit : Nonne hæc est Babylon civitas magna ? De cujus dispositione et magnitudine infra, Domino concedente, dicetur. Quam ego ædificavi, id est, auxi, melioravi et roboravi. Nam et ante eum fuit constructa; siquidem in Genesi scriptum est, quod principium regni Nemrod fuit Babylon, et Arach, et Achad, et Chalanne. In domum regni, id est, ut in ea personaliter residerem, palatiumque haberem. Sicque (ut dicitur) fecit eam regni ac monarchiæ suæ metropolim. In robore fortitudinis meæ, id est propria potestate et exsecutione subditorum meorum. Sicque totum sibi, nil Deo, attribuit: quem superbi et præsumptuosi sequuntur, ita de Dei donis gloriantes, quasi a se ipsis ea haberent. Et in gloria decoris mei, id est in gaudio prosperitatis et ornatus ac excellentiæ meæ, vel ad ostentationem propriæ majestatis.
paras.en: [[4:27|And the king answered, and said|Responditque rex, et ait]]. Whether he was walking alone or with others, and whether anyone was speaking to him to whom he replied, is not written in the text. And many expositors testify that he replied not to anyone addressing him, but to the pride of his own heart. And some imagine that he was then thinking of the casting down foretold him by Daniel, which he thought false, because a year had now gone by, and he presumed himself of such great power that no one could cast him down. Therefore he said: [[4:27|Is not this the great Babylon|Nonne hæc est Babylon civitas magna]]? Of its layout and size more will be said below, the Lord granting [see Art. VI, towards the end]. [[4:27|which I have built|Quam ego ædificavi]], that is, enlarged, improved and strengthened. For it had been built before him too; for it is written in Genesis of Nemrod: [[Gen 10:10|the beginning of his kingdom was Babylon, and Arach, and Achad, and Chalanne|principium regni Nemrod fuit Babylon, et Arach, et Achad, et Chalanne]]. [[4:27|to be the seat of the kingdom|In domum regni]], that is, that I might reside in it in person and have my palace there. And so (as is said) he made it the metropolis of his kingdom and monarchy. [[4:27|by the strength of my power|In robore fortitudinis meæ]], that is, by my own power and the labour of my subjects. And so he attributed all to himself, nothing to God: and in this the proud and presumptuous follow him, glorying in God's gifts as though they had them of themselves. [[4:27|and in the glory of my excellence|Et in gloria decoris mei]], that is, in the joy of my prosperity, adornment and excellence, or for the display of my own majesty.

paras.t: Quum adhuc sermo esset in ore regis, vox de cœlo ruit, formata per angelum, Deo jubente, et forte per illum quem Nabuchodonosor ante vocavit sanctum et vigilem, arboremque præcepit in visione succidi. Sermo enim obscurus non ibit in vacuum, ut dicit Sapiens. Et Sallustius dicit: Frangit Deus omne superbum. Ferturque vox de cœlo ruisse, quia de aere sonuit, et prolator ejus de cœlo descendit. An vero solus rex eam audivit, an etiam alii, certum non est: quamvis aliqui dicunt, quod multitudo obsequentium adfuit, vocemque audivit, ut Dei vindicta intelligeretur a populo, quæ idcirco regi inflicta est, ut Dei potentia monstraretur. Tibi dicitur, Nabuchodonosor rex: Regnum transiit a te, id est, tibi nunc auferetur. Unde, ad innuendum quod in proximo fiet hoc, dictum est: Transiit.
paras.en: [[4:28|And while the word was yet in the king's mouth, a voice came down from heaven|Quum adhuc sermo esset in ore regis, vox de cœlo ruit]], formed by an angel at God's command, and perhaps by him whom Nabuchodonosor earlier called a holy one and a watcher, who in the vision commanded the tree to be cut down. [[Wis 1:11|for an obscure speech shall not go for nought|Sermo enim obscurus non ibit in vacuum]], as the Wise Man says. And Sallust says [the editor notes that this line is Sedulius's, not Sallust's]: God breaks everything proud. And the voice is said to have *rushed* from heaven [*ruit*, where the Douay-Rheims has "came down"] because it sounded from the air, and he who uttered it came down from heaven. Whether only the king heard it, or others too, is not certain; although some say that a crowd of attendants was present and heard the voice, so that God's vengeance might be understood by the people; for it was inflicted on the king precisely so that God's power might be shown. [[4:28|To thee, O king Nabuchodonosor, it is said|Tibi dicitur, Nabuchodonosor rex]]: [[4:28|Thy kingdom shall pass from thee|Regnum transiit a te]] [Denis reads *transiit*, "hath passed", for the Vulgate's *transibit*, "shall pass"], that is, shall now be taken from thee. Hence, to suggest that this will happen very soon, it was said: *hath passed*.

paras.t: Et ab hominibus ejicient te, etc. Ista exposita sunt. Fœnum quasi bos comedes. Quod quidam exponunt: Comedes radices herbarum et fructus silvestres, sicut bos comedit fœnum. Vel per fœnum omnia hæc intelliguntur.
paras.en: [[4:29|And they shall cast thee out from among men|Et ab hominibus ejicient te]], etc. These things have been expounded. [[4:29|thou shalt eat grass like an ox|Fœnum quasi bos comedes]]. Which some expound: thou shalt eat the roots of herbs and wild fruits, as an ox eats grass. Or by *grass* all these things are understood.

paras.t: Eadem hora sermo completus est super Nabuchodonosor, et ex hominibus abjectus est. Mox enim furere cœpit, et tanquam insanus, pulsus est regno a suis. Et fœnum ut bos comedit, et rore cœli corpus ejus infectum est, id est tinctum ac madefactum, quoniam nudum fuit, donec capilli ejus in similitudinem aquilarum crescerent. Crines enim ipsius, intonsi incultique manserant, secundum multitudinem alarum aquilinarum crescentes, ut pilis esset opertus, sicut aquila plumis. Et ungues ejus quasi ungues avium: quia nemo eas a digitis manuum aut pedum abscidit. Aquilæ autem propter suam rapacitatem comparatur. Unde in Ezechiele de ipso habetur: Aquila grandis magnarum alarum, plena varietate et plumis, venit ad Libanum.
paras.en: [[4:30|The same hour the word was fulfilled upon Nabuchodonosor, and he was driven away from among men|Eadem hora sermo completus est super Nabuchodonosor, et ex hominibus abjectus est]]. For he at once began to rage, and as one insane was driven from the kingdom by his own people. [[4:30|and did eat grass, like an ox, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven|Et fœnum ut bos comedit, et rore cœli corpus ejus infectum est]], that is, stained and soaked [*infectum*, properly "dyed" or "steeped"], because it was naked, [[4:30|till his hairs grew like the feathers of eagles|donec capilli ejus in similitudinem aquilarum crescerent]]. For his locks, remaining uncut and untended, grew after the manner of the many feathers of an eagle's wings, so that he was covered with hair as an eagle is with feathers. [[4:30|and his nails like birds' claws|Et ungues ejus quasi ungues avium]]: because no one cut them from the fingers of his hands or his feet. And he is compared to an eagle because of his rapacity. Hence it is said of him in Ezechiel: [[Ezech 17:3|A large eagle with great wings|Aquila grandis magnarum alarum]], [[Ezech 17:3|full of feathers, and of variety, came to Libanus|plena varietate et plumis, venit ad Libanum]].

paras.t: Igitur post finem dierum castigationis meæ, septem scilicet annis expletis, ego Nabuchodonosor oculos meos mentis et corporis ad cœlum levavi, ut cœlum intuens, ejus Creatorem considerarem ac venerarer; et sensus, id est intellectus ususque rationis, meus redditus est mihi a clementissimo Deo, qui peccatis meis punitis, mentem meam illuminare dignatus est. Simili modo accipitur sensus in prima Joannis epistola, ubi legitur: Scimus quoniam Filius Dei venit, et dedit nobis sensum. Prius tamen redditus est ei sensus, quam oculos ad Deum erexit. Et Altissimo benedixi, gratias referendo, quod me paternaliter flagellavit et illustravit: sequens Tobiam qui ait: Benedico te, Domine Deus Israel, quoniam tu castigasti me, et tu sanasti me. Itemque Psalmista: Lætati sumus pro diebus quibus nos humiliasti, annis quibus vidimus mala. Propterea et nos adversitatem et disciplinam perpessi, non indignemur, sed gratias proferamus, scientes quod Deo ordinante aut saltem permittente, talia nobis ad nostrum contingant profectum. Et Viventem in sempiternum laudavi: qui solus absolute æternus est, et actualissime, deliciosissime, ac simplicissime vivens vita intellectuali; cujus essentia est superperfectissima ac superbeatissima, superessentialisque vita, fons omnis vitæ; et glorificavi, id est, gloriosum monstravi verbo et facto; quia potestas ejus, potestas sempiterna, et regnum ejus in generatione et generationem. Hoc in fine præcedentis capituli, quantum ad sensum, scriptum est atque expositum. Quoniam ergo talis ac tantus est Deus, dignus et superdignus est omni benedictione, glorificatione ac laude.
paras.en: [[4:31|Now at the end of the days|Igitur post finem dierum]] of my chastisement, namely when seven years were fulfilled, [[4:31|I, Nabuchodonosor, lifted up my eyes|ego Nabuchodonosor oculos meos]] of mind and of body [[4:31|to heaven|ad cœlum levavi]], so that, looking upon heaven, I might consider and worship its Creator; [[4:31|and my sense|et sensus]], that is, the understanding and the use of reason, [[4:31|was restored to me|meus redditus est mihi]] by the most merciful God, who, having punished my sins, deigned to enlighten my mind. *Sense* is taken in the same way in the first epistle of John, where we read: [[1 John 5:20|we know that the Son of God is come|Scimus quoniam Filius Dei venit]]. [[1 John 5:20|And he hath given us understanding|et dedit nobis sensum]] [*sensum*, the same word as *sense* here]. Yet his sense was restored to him before he raised his eyes to God. [[4:31|and I blessed the most High|Et Altissimo benedixi]], giving thanks that He had scourged me as a father and enlightened me: following Tobias, who says: [[Tob 11:17|I bless thee, O Lord God of Israel, because thou hast chastised me, and thou hast saved me|Benedico te, Domine Deus Israel, quoniam tu castigasti me, et tu sanasti me]] [Denis reads *sanasti*, "thou hast healed me"]. And likewise the Psalmist: [[Ps 89:15|We have rejoiced for the days in which thou hast humbled us: for the years in which we have seen evils.|Lætati sumus pro diebus quibus nos humiliasti, annis quibus vidimus mala]]. Therefore let us too, when we suffer adversity and correction, not be indignant, but give thanks, knowing that by God's ordering, or at least by His permission, such things befall us for our profit. [[4:31|and I praised|laudavi]] [[4:31|him that liveth for ever|Et Viventem in sempiternum]]: who alone is absolutely eternal, living most actually, most delightfully and most simply the life of the intellect; whose essence is most superperfect and most superblessed, a superessential life, the fount of all life; [[4:31|and glorified|et glorificavi]], that is, I showed Him to be glorious by word and deed; [[4:31|for his power is an everlasting power, and his kingdom is to all generations|quia potestas ejus, potestas sempiterna, et regnum ejus in generatione et generationem]]. This was written, as to the sense, at the end of the preceding chapter[[Dan 3:100||]], and expounded there. Since, then, God is such and so great, He is worthy and more than worthy of all blessing, glorification and praise.

paras.t: Et omnes habitatores terræ apud ipsum in nihilum reputati sunt. Simile est illud Isaiæ : Omnes gentes quasi non sint, sic sunt coram eo, et quasi nihilum et inane reputatæ sunt ei. Scit enim Deus omnipotens et immensus, universa creata, comparatione ipsius, nullius esse momenti, et fragile esse genus humanum, miseriis atque defectibus animæ et corporis plenum; et item quod omnis creatura ex se nihil est, atque ex nihilo, et laberetur in nihilum, nisi conservaretur ab ipso : præsertim autem homines, in quantum sunt peccatores, terrena, non Deum, amantes : qui proprie habitatores terræ censentur, quorum videlicet conversatio non est in cœlis, contemptibilesque sunt coram Deo, et pro nihilo reputantur ab ipso. Hinc fertur in Psalmo : Homo vanitati similis factus est; et item, Verumtamen universa vanitas omnis homo vivens. Attamen homo, ut est ad Dei imaginem factus, beatitudinis susceptivus, atque ad eam plasmatus, præsertim ut a Christo redemptus, et caritate ac gratia decoratus, non reputatur a Deo pro nihilo absolute, neque ab ipso despicitur : imo sic ait Psalmista, Minuisti eum paulo minus ab angelis, gloria et honore coronasti eum, et constituisti eum super opera manuum tuarum; et rursum, Numquid enim vane constituisti omnes filios hominum? Imo sic ipsemet Deus ait in libro Proverbiorum, Deliciæ meæ, esse cum filiis hominum; et alibi, Eritis mihi in filios et filias; in Apocalypse quoque, Ecce tabernaculum Dei cum hominibus, et habitabit cum eis. Itaque vilipendamus nos ipsos in nobis, sed in Deo curemus nos, perpendentes ad quid conditi simus; et transitoria atque carnalia detestemur, Deum jugiter totis viribus, omni affectu et toto conatu quærentes, nec labori, difficultati aut tentationi cedentes.
paras.en: [[4:32|And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing before him|Et omnes habitatores terræ apud ipsum in nihilum reputati sunt]]. Like it is that saying of Isaias: [[Is 40:17|All nations are before him as if they had no being at all, and are counted to him as nothing, and vanity.|Omnes gentes quasi non sint, sic sunt coram eo, et quasi nihilum et inane reputatæ sunt ei]]. For the omnipotent and immeasurable God knows that all created things, compared with Him, are of no weight, and that the human race is frail, full of miseries and defects of soul and body; and also that every creature is of itself nothing, and from nothing, and would slip back into nothing unless it were preserved by Him: but above all men in so far as they are sinners, loving earthly things, not God; who are properly reckoned the inhabitants of the earth, those, namely, whose conversation is not in heaven; and they are contemptible before God and are reputed as nothing by Him. Hence it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 143:4|Man is like to vanity|Homo vanitati similis factus est]]; and again: [[Ps 38:6|and indeed all things are vanity: every man living|Verumtamen universa vanitas omnis homo vivens]]. Yet man, as he is made to the image of God, capable of beatitude and fashioned for it, and above all as redeemed by Christ and adorned with charity and grace, is not reputed by God as nothing absolutely, nor is he despised by Him: nay, so says the Psalmist: [[Ps 8:6|Thou hast made him a little less than the angels, thou hast crowned him with glory and honour|Minuisti eum paulo minus ab angelis, gloria et honore coronasti eum]], [[Ps 8:7|and hast set him over the works of thy hands|et constituisti eum super opera manuum tuarum]]; and again: [[Ps 88:48|for hast thou made all the children of men in vain?|Numquid enim vane constituisti omnes filios hominum?]] Nay, God Himself says thus in the book of Proverbs: [[Prov 8:31|my delights were to be with the children of men|Deliciæ meæ, esse cum filiis hominum]]; and elsewhere: [[2 Cor 6:18|you shall be my sons and daughters|Eritis mihi in filios et filias]]; and in the Apocalypse too: [[Apoc 21:3|Behold the tabernacle of God with men: and he will dwell with them|Ecce tabernaculum Dei cum hominibus, et habitabit cum eis]]. Let us therefore hold ourselves cheap in ourselves, but care for ourselves in God, weighing for what end we were made; and let us detest things passing and carnal, seeking God continually with all our strength, all our affection and all our endeavour, yielding neither to toil, nor difficulty, nor temptation.

paras.t: Juxta voluntatem enim suam facit tam in virtutibus cœli, id est angelicis spiritibus, seu virtutibus cœlestium corporum, eis a principio suæ creationis inditis, per quas influunt inferioribus, secundum quod ait Philosophus : Oportet hunc mundum esse contiguum lationibus superiorum, ut tota ejus virtus inde gubernetur. Omnes itaque virtutes istæ ei obediunt. Quam in habitatoribus terræ. Propter quod ait per Isaiam : Consilium meum stabit, et omnis voluntas mea fiet.
paras.en: [[4:32|for he doth according to his will, as well with the powers of heaven|Juxta voluntatem enim suam facit tam in virtutibus cœli]], that is, with the angelic spirits, or with the powers of the heavenly bodies, given them from the beginning of their creation, by which they flow into lower things, according to what the Philosopher says: This world must be contiguous with the motions of the higher bodies, so that all its power may be governed from there. All these powers, then, obey Him. [[4:32|as among the inhabitants of the earth|Quam in habitatoribus terræ]]. Because of this He says through Isaias: [[Is 46:10|My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be done|Consilium meum stabit, et omnis voluntas mea fiet]].

paras.t: Et non est qui resistat, id est, resistere vel impedimentum ponere possit, manui, id est omnipotentiæ ejus, ita quod ei prævaleat, vel ejus beneplacitum ab effectu impediat. Nec obstat quod de impiis scriptum est in Job, Ipsi fuerunt rebelles lumini. Vitiosi equidem, quantum in ipsis est, Deo resistunt, Spiritui Sancto obicem ponunt; et dæmones salutem quam Deus facit in suis, impedire conantur. Verumtamen Deus, quum voluerit voluntate beneplaciti, quæ est ipsemet Deus volens, ad nutum prævalet cunctis adversariis suis : imo rebelles voluntates inclinat in omne quod complacet sibi, eas ad libitum immutando, et quocumque voluerit, has vertendo. Ideo ait ad Job : Quis resistere potest vultui meo? Omnia quæ sub cœlo sunt, mea sunt. Per Jeremiam quoque : Quis similis mei? et quis sustinebit me? Et quis est iste pastor qui resistat vultui meo?
paras.en: [[4:32|and there is none that can resist|Et non est qui resistat]], that is, who can resist or put a hindrance in the way of, [[4:32|his hand|manui]], that is, his omnipotence, so as to prevail over Him or keep His good pleasure from taking effect. Nor is it against this that it is written of the wicked in Job: [[Job 24:13|They have been rebellious to the light|Ipsi fuerunt rebelles lumini]]. The vicious indeed, as far as in them lies, resist God and set an obstacle to the Holy Spirit; and the demons strive to hinder the salvation that God works in His own. Yet God, when He wills with the will of good pleasure [that is, His will properly so called, as distinct from the "will of sign": His precepts, prohibitions and the like], which is God Himself willing, prevails at a nod over all His adversaries: nay, He inclines rebellious wills to whatever pleases Him, changing them at His pleasure and turning them whithersoever He will. Therefore He says to Job: [[Job 41:1|who can resist my countenance?|Quis resistere potest vultui meo?]] [[Job 41:2|All things that are under heaven are mine|Omnia quæ sub cœlo sunt, mea sunt]]. By Jeremias too: [[Jer 49:19|who is like to me? and who shall abide me? and who is that shepherd that can withstand my countenance?|Quis similis mei? et quis sustinebit me? Et quis est iste pastor qui resistat vultui meo?]]

paras.t: Et dicat ei, Quare sic fecisti? Nullus enim sapientior, nullus justior, nullus potentior eo; sed ipse universis et singulis in infinitum sapientior, potentior, justiorque consistit. Et quamvis secundum voluntatem suam in omnibus agat, non tamen tyrannice agit, quamvis voluntas secundum se comparetur tyranno : quoniam in supersimplici ac supersanctissimo Deo realiter idem sunt, sapientia, justitia atque potentia. Ipseque Deus sublimis et benedictus, est omnium prima regula, prima virtus, et totius veritatis, æquitatis et sanctitatis fontalis ac summa mensura. Idcirco errare, falli, reprehendi non potest. Propter quod etiam in libro de Causis habetur : Omnes virtutes quibus est finis, pendentes sunt per primum infinitum, quod est virtus virtutum. Et Augustinus octavo de Civitate Dei : Celebriores, inquit, philosophi aliquid tale de Deo senserunt, ut in illo inveniatur et causa subsistendi, et ratio intelligendi, et ordo vivendi. Denique imperscrutabilia sunt judicia Dei. Propter quod ait Apostolus ad Romanos : O homo, tu quis es qui respondeas Deo? Et in Job libro Eliu loquitur : Quis poterit scrutari vias ejus? Aut quis ei dicere potest, Operatus es iniquitatem? Sed et Isaias dicit : Væ qui contradicit factori suo. Numquid dicit lutum figulo suo, Quid facis?
paras.en: [[4:32|and say to him: Why hast thou done it?|Et dicat ei, Quare sic fecisti?]] For none is wiser, none juster, none mightier than He; but He is infinitely wiser, mightier and juster than all and each. And although He does all things according to His will, yet He does not act tyrannically, even though will, taken by itself, may be likened to a tyrant: for in the supersimple and most holy God, wisdom, justice and power are really the same. And God Himself, sublime and blessed, is the first rule of all things, the first power, and the fontal and supreme measure of all truth, equity and holiness. Therefore He cannot err, be deceived or be reproved. Wherefore it is also said in the book *On Causes*: All powers that have an end hang upon the first infinite, which is the power of powers. And Augustine, in the eighth book of *The City of God*: The more celebrated philosophers, he says, thought some such thing of God, that in Him is found both the cause of subsisting, and the reason of understanding, and the order of living. In short, the judgments of God are unsearchable[[Rom 11:33||]]. Wherefore the Apostle says to the Romans: [[Rom 9:20|O man, who art thou that repliest against God?|O homo, tu quis es qui respondeas Deo?]] And in the book of Job Eliu says: [[Job 36:23|Who can search out his ways? or who can say to him: Thou hast wrought iniquity?|Quis poterit scrutari vias ejus? Aut quis ei dicere potest, Operatus es iniquitatem?]] And Isaias too says: [[Is 45:9|Woe to him that gainsayeth his maker|Væ qui contradicit factori suo]]. [[Is 45:9|shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it: What art thou making|Numquid dicit lutum figulo suo, Quid facis?]]?

paras.t: In ipso tempore sensus meus reversus est ad me. Hoc, modo expositum est. Et ad honorem regni mei decoremque perveni. Secundum Hieronymum, Nabuchodonosor eleemosynis suis regni sui recuperationem promeruit.
paras.en: [[4:33|At the same time my sense returned to me|In ipso tempore sensus meus reversus est ad me]]. This has just been expounded. [[4:33|and I came to the honour and glory of my kingdom|Et ad honorem regni mei decoremque perveni]]. According to Jerome, Nabuchodonosor by his almsgiving merited the recovery of his kingdom.

paras.t: Et figura mea reversa est ad me. Occasione hujus verbi perhibuit Josephus, Nabuchodonosor regem non solum in amentiam versum, sed et in bovem mutatum, ita quod exteriorem figuram amiserit, indueritque bovinam. Quemadmodum etiam dixit, quod Adam in statu innocentiæ de nuditate sua non erubuit, quia bestiali vixit simplicitate : quod dici non potest, quia sic ex peccato melioratus fuisset primorum status parentum, per peccatum usu rationis adepto. Epiphanius vero et doctores catholici communiter tenent oppositum. Nam superius dictum est : Cor ejus ab humano commutetur; et, Fœnum quasi bos comedes. Non dicit, quod factus bos comedit fœnum. Albertus ergo ita exponit, ut intelligatur ratio figuræ consona, ut ad humanam rationem figuret opera sua. Quidam enim figurantur ad canes, quidam ad porcos. Verba hæc intricata videntur : quorum sensus apparet, ut per figuram designetur figuratio vitæ secundum rationem. Nam et Petrus in prima sua ait Canonica : Non configurati prioribus ignorantiæ vestræ tenebris. Alii clarius dicunt, quod figura accipitur hic pro exteriori compositione, quia post furiam fuit vestitus et tonsus, sicque in figura suo modo mutatus.
paras.en: [[4:33|and my shape returned to me|Et figura mea reversa est ad me]]. On the occasion of this word Josephus asserted that king Nabuchodonosor was not only turned to madness, but also changed into an ox, so that he lost his outward shape and put on that of an ox. Just as he also said that Adam in the state of innocence was not ashamed of his nakedness[[Gen 2:25||]] because he lived in a beastlike simplicity: which cannot be said, for then the state of our first parents would have been bettered by sin, the use of reason having been gained through sin. But Epiphanius and the Catholic doctors commonly hold the opposite. For it was said above: [[4:13|Let his heart be changed from man's|Cor ejus ab humano commutetur]]; and: [[4:29|thou shalt eat grass like an ox|Fœnum quasi bos comedes]]. It does not say that, made an ox, he ate grass. Albert therefore expounds it so that *shape* is understood as a likeness fitted to reason, so that he shaped his works to human reason. For some are shaped after dogs, some after swine. These words seem tangled; their sense appears to be that by *shape* is meant the shaping of life according to reason. For Peter too says in his first Canonical epistle: [[1 Pet 1:14|not fashioned according to the former desires of your ignorance|Non configurati prioribus ignorantiæ vestræ tenebris]] [Denis reads *tenebris*, "darkness", for *desideriis*, "desires"; *configurati*, "fashioned", comes from the same root as *figura*, "shape"]. Others say more clearly that *shape* is taken here for his outward bearing, because after his frenzy he was clothed and shorn, and so changed in his shape after a fashion.

paras.t: Verumtamen reor, quod et de exteriori figura quodammodo accipi possit, non quod illam quoad lineamenta amiserit, sed quantum ad multiplicem deordinationem, incurvationem et deformitatem. Herbarum enim radices rodendo, in terra cum bobus, feris, bestiisque jacendo, et varias amentias exercendo, notabilem incurrit immutationem figuræ, quantum ad plurimas corporis partes. Vel, figura reversa est ad eum, quantum ad manifestationem. Pilis enim opertus, in terram prostratus, et bestiis se conformans, non videbatur figuram habere humanam.
paras.en: Yet I think that it can also be taken in a way of his outward shape: not that he had lost it as to its features, but as to its manifold disorder, stooping and deformity. For by gnawing the roots of herbs, lying on the ground with oxen, wild animals and beasts, and doing all sorts of mad things, he underwent a notable change of shape in very many parts of the body. Or, his shape returned to him as to its appearance: for, covered with hair, prostrate on the ground and making himself like the beasts, he did not seem to have a human shape.

paras.t: Et optimates mei et magistratus requisierunt me ad mentem reversum, recordati quantum promoverim regnum Chaldææ; et ex Danielis eloquio agnoverunt eum de cetero rationabiliter regnaturum ; atque, ut aliqui dicunt, quia Evilmerodach filius Nabuchodonosor, regnans post eum, tantæ erat nequitiæ, quod lassi de ejus imperio, patrem ipsius requisierunt. Et in regno meo restitutus sum, et magnificentia amplior addita est mihi. Videntes enim Chaldæi mirabilem regis modestiam, mansuetudinem, prudentiam et probitatem in omnibus post suam ad mentis usum reversionem, magis quam ante venerati sunt eum. Et ipse de cetero plus profecit et crevit pietate atque consilio, quam ante crudelitate ac impetu. Quia et Seneca loquitur : Melius vincit homo consilio, quam iracundia. Et de Romanis scriptum est primo Machabæorum : Possederunt omnem locum consilio suo et patientia. Salomon quoque in Proverbiis scribit : Roboratur clementia thronus regis.
paras.en: [[4:33|and my nobles, and my magistrates, sought for me|Et optimates mei et magistratus requisierunt me]] when I had returned to my mind, remembering how much I had advanced the kingdom of Chaldea; and they knew from Daniel's word that he would reign reasonably from then on; and also, as some say, because Evilmerodach, the son of Nabuchodonosor, who reigned after him, was of such wickedness that, weary of his rule, they sought his father. [[4:33|and I was restored to my kingdom: and greater majesty was added to me|Et in regno meo restitutus sum, et magnificentia amplior addita est mihi]]. For the Chaldeans, seeing the king's wonderful moderation, gentleness, prudence and uprightness in all things after his return to the use of his mind, venerated him more than before. And he himself thereafter made more progress and grew more by piety and counsel than before by cruelty and violence. For Seneca too says: A man conquers better by counsel than by anger. And it is written of the Romans in the first book of Machabees that they [[1 Mach 8:3|had gotten possession of all the place by their counsel and patience|Possederunt omnem locum consilio suo et patientia]]. Solomon too writes in Proverbs: [[Prov 20:28|his throne is strengthened by clemency|Roboratur clementia thronus regis]] [Denis reads *regis*, "the king's throne"].

paras.t: Nunc ergo ego Nabuchodonosor laudo et magnifico et glorifico, id est, magnum et gloriosum profiteor ac ostendo, regem cœli, id est cœlestis exercitus, angelorum et orbium ac astrorum; quia omnia opera ejus vera veritate justitiæ, et omnes viæ ejus, id est processus in regimine universi, præcepta atque consilia, sunt judicia, id est, recto fiunt judicio, secundum censuram increatæ sapientiæ Dei : ita quod Deus nil agit præcipitanter, tyrannice aut injuste, sed omnia sapienter et juste. Verba ista capitulo præcedenti clarius sunt exposita. Et gradientes de malo in pejus in superbia, potest humiliare. Frequenter enim differt vindictam, non ex impotentia, sed clementia, ut impius convertatur, juxta illud Job : Nunc enim Deus non infert furorem suum, nec ulciscitur scelus valde. Porro humiliare superbos et omnem elatum posse dejicere, competit vere ac proprie Deo, qui ait ad sanctum Job : Si habes brachium sicut Deus, et voce simili tonas : disperge superbos in furore tuo, et respiciens omnem arrogantem humilia; et facies eorum demerge in foveam. In Numeris quoque scriptum est : Anima quæ per superbiam aliquid commiserit, quoniam adversum Dominum rebellis fuit, peribit de populo suo : verbum enim Domini contempsit.
paras.en: [[4:34|Therefore I, Nabuchodonosor, do now praise, and magnify, and glorify|Nunc ergo ego Nabuchodonosor laudo et magnifico et glorifico]], that is, I profess and show to be great and glorious, [[4:34|the King of heaven|regem cœli]], that is, of the heavenly host, of the angels and the spheres and the stars; [[4:34|because all his works are true|quia omnia opera ejus vera]] with the truth of justice, [[4:34|and his ways|et omnes viæ ejus]] [Denis's text has "all his ways"], that is, His proceedings in the governance of the universe, His precepts and counsels, are [[4:34|judgments|judicia]], that is, they are done by right judgment, according to the decree of the uncreated wisdom of God: so that God does nothing hastily, tyrannically or unjustly, but all things wisely and justly. These words were expounded more clearly in the preceding chapter[[Dan 3:27||]]. [[4:34|and them that walk|Et gradientes]] from bad to worse [[4:34|in pride he is able to abase|in superbia, potest humiliare]]. For He often defers vengeance, not from want of power, but from clemency, that the wicked may be converted, according to that of Job: [[Job 35:15|For he doth not now bring on his fury, neither doth he revenge wickedness exceedingly|Nunc enim Deus non infert furorem suum, nec ulciscitur scelus valde]]. Moreover, to humble the proud and to be able to cast down every one who is lifted up belongs truly and properly to God, who says to holy Job: [[Job 40:4|hast thou an arm like God, and canst thou thunder with a voice like him?|Si habes brachium sicut Deus, et voce simili tonas]] [[Job 40:6|Scatter the proud in thy indignation, and behold every arrogant man, and humble him|disperge superbos in furore tuo, et respiciens omnem arrogantem humilia]]; [[Job 40:8|and plunge their faces into the pit|et facies eorum demerge in foveam]]. In Numbers too it is written: [[Num 15:30|the soul that committeth any thing through pride|Anima quæ per superbiam aliquid commiserit]], [[Num 15:30|because he hath been rebellious against the Lord|quoniam adversum Dominum rebellis fuit]], [[Num 15:30|shall be cut off from among his people|peribit de populo suo]]: [[Num 15:31|For he hath contemned the word of the Lord|verbum enim Domini contempsit]].

paras.t: Præterea advertendum, quod de facto isto Nabuchodonosor regis, multa in Scholastica feruntur historia, utpote quod ablatus est ei usus linguæ ad loquendum, videbaturque ei quod bos esset in anterioribus, et aquila in posterioribus, secundum mysterium, id est juxta mysticam significationem proprietatum tyrannorum, qui in prima ætate cervicosi et voluptatibus dediti, jugo dæmonis subjiciuntur, in fine vero interficiunt, diripiunt, et conculcant. Multi quoque egrediebantur, et videbant eum. Solus Daniel non egrediebatur ad videndum eum, quoniam toto tempore alienationis ejus, orationi pro eo vacabat; et ad preces ejus, septem anni in septem menses versi sunt. In quibus, quadraginta diebus in insaniam vertebatur; et per alios quadraginta ad cor hominis reversus, flevit, supplicavitque Deo, in tantum quod oculi ejus ex nimiis fletibus ut caro livida facti erant; et iterum per alios quadraginta dies vertebatur in insaniam, donec septem menses complerentur. Postquam autem revocatus est, non regnavit, sed statuti sunt pro eo judices, et usque ad finem septem annorum pœnitentiam egit, panem et carnes non comedens, et vinum non bibens, sed leguminibus utebatur et herbis, juxta consilium Danielis. Et quum iterum regnasset, voluit Danielem facere coheredem filiorum suorum. Et ait Daniel : Absit a me, ut patrum relinquens hereditatem, incircumcisorum donis inhæream. Hæc in præfata Historia continentur.
paras.en: Further, it should be noted that many things are related in the *Scholastic History* [of Peter Comestor] about this happening to king Nabuchodonosor: for instance, that the use of his tongue for speaking was taken from him, and that he seemed to himself to be an ox in his fore parts and an eagle in his hind parts, according to a mystery, that is, according to a mystical signification of the properties of tyrants, who in the first part of life are stiff-necked and given to pleasures and are subjected to the yoke of the devil, but at the end kill, plunder and trample down. Many also went out and saw him. Daniel alone did not go out to see him, because throughout the whole time of his madness he was given to prayer for him; and at his prayers the seven years were turned into seven months. During these, for forty days he was turned to madness; and for another forty, returned to a man's heart, he wept and besought God, so much that his eyes from excessive weeping had become like livid flesh; and again for another forty days he was turned to madness, until seven months were completed. But after he was recalled he did not reign, but judges were appointed in his stead, and until the end of seven years he did penance, not eating bread and meat and not drinking wine, but living on pulse and herbs, according to Daniel's counsel. And when he reigned again, he wished to make Daniel co-heir with his sons. And Daniel said: Far be it from me to forsake the inheritance of my fathers and cleave to the gifts of the uncircumcised. These things are contained in the aforesaid *History*.

paras.t: Quæ non sunt adeo certa : imo Glossa super illud, Septem tempora mutentur super eum, dicit quod mentiuntur qui dicunt septem annos oratione Danielis mutatos in septem menses. Hieronymus quoque, Albertus, ceterique communiter dicunt quod insania ejus septem annis duravit. Unde insufficienter dicere videntur volentes Glossam et Scholasticam historiam concordare, dicendo quod septem anni non sunt mutati quoad hoc, quod usque ad finem septem annorum non est reductus ad regnum. Iterum sunt mutati, quia post septem menses recuperavit sensum oratione Danielis, quem, nisi Daniel pro eo orasset, non recepisset usque ad finem septem annorum. Jam enim ex superioribus patuit, quod secundum Hieronymum, Glossam et Albertum, septem annis privatus est usu rationis. Nec videtur quod infra septem menses, capilli ejus in tantum ut dictum est, excrevissent. Glossa etiam magis consonat textui, qui sonare videtur quod non sit reversus ad mentem, nisi toto tempore furiæ consummato, et quod tunc statim ad regnum reductus sit.
paras.en: These things are not so certain: nay, the Gloss on that text, [[4:13|let seven times pass over him|Septem tempora mutentur super eum]], says that those lie who say that the seven years were changed by Daniel's prayer into seven months. Jerome too, Albert and the rest commonly say that his madness lasted seven years. Hence those seem to speak inadequately who want to reconcile the Gloss and the *Scholastic History* by saying that the seven years were not changed in this respect, that he was not brought back to the kingdom until the end of seven years; and that again they were changed, because after seven months he recovered his sense by Daniel's prayer, which he would not have recovered until the end of seven years had Daniel not prayed for him. For it is already plain from what was said above that, according to Jerome, the Gloss and Albert, he was deprived of the use of reason for seven years. Nor does it seem that within seven months his hair could have grown as much as was said. The Gloss also agrees better with the text, which seems to mean that he did not return to his mind until the whole time of his frenzy was accomplished, and that he was then at once brought back to the kingdom.

paras.t: Sed si ita dicatur, oriuntur quædam instantiæ. Impossibile enim videtur, quod Nabuchodonosor rex tam delicate nutritus, septem annis fœno vesci quivit et vivere, ac totidem annis absque corporis sui laceratione inter feras et bestias vixerit. Item, quod tam potentissimum regnum amenti homini per septem annos servatum sit, et tam diu sine rege fuit. Aut si alius ei successit in regnum, non videtur ut propter illum imperio cederet, præsertim quum Chaldæorum historiæ nil tale contineant. Rursus non videtur, quod tam diu nudus ac sub dio vivere potuisset.
paras.en: But if it is put so, certain objections arise. For it seems impossible that king Nabuchodonosor, so delicately nurtured, could feed on grass and live for seven years, and live as many years among wild animals and beasts without his body being torn. Again, that so very mighty a kingdom should have been kept for a madman for seven years, and was so long without a king. Or if another succeeded him in the kingdom, it does not seem likely that he would have given up the rule for him, especially as the histories of the Chaldeans contain nothing of the kind. Again, it does not seem that he could have lived so long naked and under the open sky.

paras.t: Propter hæc motiva quidam finxerunt, quod Daniel hic ad litteram loquatur de diabolo sub metaphora de Nabuchodonosor rege, ut refert Hieronymus, asserentes dæmonem tandem salvandum, et pristinam beatitudinem adepturum. Quod penitus falsum est atque hæreticum, ex fabulis et hæresibus Origenis contractum. Præfati etiam erroris intolerabilis falsitas, ex textu clarissime demonstratur. Quomodo enim diabolus somnium habuit, qui incorporeus nunquam dormivit? Et dato quod somniasset, quomodo a Daniele viro sancto expositionem somnii expetisset, præsertim quum ipse diabolus tantæ sit subtilitatis? Quomodo etiam Daniel cum diabolo tantam habuit amicitiam? Et quomodo nominavit eum dominum suum ac regem? Stultissimus ergo error hic exstitit. — Arguebant quoque ex hoc, quod potestas regis Babylonis non se extendit per totam terram. Sed dictum est satis, quomodo hoc hyperbolice exponatur.
paras.en: Because of these motives some have imagined that Daniel here, in the literal sense, speaks of the devil under the metaphor of king Nabuchodonosor, as Jerome relates, asserting that the demon is at length to be saved and to obtain his former beatitude. Which is wholly false and heretical, drawn from the fables and heresies of Origen. The falsity of this intolerable error is also most clearly shown from the text. For how did the devil have a dream, who, being incorporeal, never slept? And granting that he had dreamed, how would he have asked an exposition of the dream from Daniel, a holy man, especially since the devil himself is of such subtlety? How, too, did Daniel have such friendship with the devil? And how did he call him his lord and king? This was therefore a most foolish error. They also argued from this, that the power of the king of Babylon did not extend over the whole earth. But enough has been said of how this is to be expounded as hyperbole.

paras.t: Instantiæ quoque facile dissolvuntur, quia ut tangit Hieronymus, furiosis sunt quædam possibilia, quæ sanis impossibilia essent. In furiosis enim, propter passionum vehementiam, et rationis subversionem, imaginationisque tenebrosum errorem, corporalis natura totaliter deordinatur, ac bestialis efficitur, ita ut crudis delectentur, et sub dio morentur, ac bestiis familiariter copulentur : quemadmodum cernimus quod mulieres prægnantes, terra et carbonibus vesci desiderent, ex deordinatione naturæ. Rationabiliter etiam dici potest, quod divina virtute fuit a ferarum laceratione et morte inter tot incommoda præservatus. Postremo quidam affirmant, quod durante furia regis, regnum ejus per principes, et potissime per Danielem, fuerat gubernatum : quia ex Daniele sciebant regem sanandum ac reducendum. Alii dicunt, quod filius regis successit ei in regno, et postea cedere est coactus, omnibus patrem ejus quærentibus.
paras.en: The objections too are easily resolved, because, as Jerome touches on, certain things are possible to madmen that would be impossible to the sane. For in madmen, because of the vehemence of the passions, the overthrow of reason and the dark error of the imagination, the bodily nature is wholly disordered and becomes beastlike, so that they delight in raw things, stay under the open sky, and keep familiar company with beasts: just as we see that pregnant women long to eat earth and coals, from a disorder of nature. It can also reasonably be said that he was preserved by divine power from being torn by wild animals and from death amid so many hardships. Lastly, some affirm that while the king's frenzy lasted his kingdom was governed by the princes, and chiefly by Daniel: because they knew from Daniel that the king would be healed and brought back. Others say that the king's son succeeded him in the kingdom, and was afterwards forced to give way, when all were seeking his father.

paras.t: Postremo inquiritur, an Nabuchodonosor rex sit salvatus. Et ex dictis videtur quod imo, præsertim quia et Daniel secum permansit usque ad obitum ejus. Idem etiam in Decreto habetur, quod scilicet fecerit pœnitentiam salutarem. Sed in Isaia multa dicuntur quæ in contrarium sonare videntur, videlicet: Detracta est ad inferos superbia tua; Infernus conturbatus est in occursum adventus tui. Quæ omnia si de isto Nabuchodonosor exponantur ad litteram, pertinere dicuntur ad prophetiam comminationis, non prædestinationis: quamvis in præallegatis auctoribus, quidam per regem Babylonis, non istum Nabuchodonosor, sed Balthasar ejus nepotem (de quo sequenti dicetur capitulo) intelligendum exponant. De ista quæstione nunc transeo, quoniam super Isaiam eam latius pertractavi.
paras.en: Lastly, it is asked whether king Nabuchodonosor was saved. And from what has been said it seems that he was, especially as Daniel also stayed with him until his death. It is also held in the *Decretum* that he did salutary penance. But in Isaias many things are said that seem to sound the contrary, namely: [[Is 14:11|Thy pride is brought down to hell|Detracta est ad inferos superbia tua]]; [[Is 14:9|Hell below was in an uproar to meet thee at thy coming|Infernus conturbatus est in occursum adventus tui]]. All of which, if they are expounded of this Nabuchodonosor literally, are said to belong to the prophecy of threatening, not of predestination: although in the authors cited before, some expound that by the king of Babylon is to be understood not this Nabuchodonosor but Balthasar his grandson (of whom we shall speak in the next chapter). I pass over this question now, since I have treated it at greater length on Isaias [the margin gives "Ibidem", that is, Isaias 14].

paras.t: Postremo, quæ in isto capitulo de arbore, quantum ad Nabuchodonosor regem, litteraliter dicta sunt, non est difficile applicare ad principes et prælatos, juxta sensum quo dispositio arboris de Nabuchodonosor jam fuit exposita. Qui principes et prælati, si vel de temporalibus vel de spiritualibus bonis Deique donis cœperint superbire, a corpore mystico electorum succiduntur, spiritualiter moriuntur, dæmonibus sociantur, bestialiter conversantur, vestimentis virtutum privantur, aquis concupiscentiarum inficiuntur, ferreis vinculis, id est pessimis consuetudinibus, involvuntur, et a bonis subditis principatu judicantur indigni, subinde quoque spoliantur dominio. Qui tamen, si se humiliaverint, gratiam sortiuntur amissam. De hac moralitate, brevitati studens, pertranseo, et tantumdem tetigisse sufficiat.
paras.en: Lastly, what has been said literally in this chapter of the tree, as regards king Nabuchodonosor, is not hard to apply to princes and prelates, in the sense in which the arrangement of the tree has already been expounded of Nabuchodonosor. These princes and prelates, if they begin to grow proud either of temporal or of spiritual goods and the gifts of God, are cut off from the mystical body of the elect, die spiritually, are made companions of the demons, live like beasts, are stripped of the garments of the virtues, are steeped in the waters of concupiscence, are bound with iron chains, that is, with very evil habits, and are judged by their good subjects unworthy of rule, and presently are despoiled of dominion too. Yet if they humble themselves, they obtain the grace they had lost. On this moral sense, studying brevity, I pass on, and let it suffice to have touched on it so much.

6.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI SEXTI : PLACUIT DARIO, ET CONSTITUIT SUPER REGNUM SUUM SATRAPAS CENTUM VIGINTI.
6.title_en: Exposition of the sixth chapter: It seemed good to Darius, and he appointed over his kingdom a hundred and twenty governors.

paras.t: Placuit Dario, et constituit super regnum suum, id est totale imperium, satrapas centum viginti. Quid satrapæ proprie appellentur, dictum est in expositione capituli tertii. Ut essent in toto regno suo, id est, per universum ejus imperium singuli singulis præsiderent provinciis : ita quod quilibet uni provinciæ præerat, secundum Albertum, qui etiam ait, quod Darii hujus imperium continebat centum viginti septem provincias : ad quod allegat illud Esther, In diebus Assueri regis, qui regnavit ab Æthiopia usque Indiam, super centum viginti septem provincias.
paras.en: [[6:1|It seemed good to Darius, and he appointed over the kingdom|Placuit Dario, et constituit super regnum suum]], that is, over his whole empire, [[6:1|a hundred and twenty governors|satrapas centum viginti]]. What satraps properly are was said in the exposition of the third chapter[[Dan 3:2||]]. [[6:1|To be over his whole kingdom|Ut essent in toto regno suo]], that is, so that throughout his whole empire they might preside one over each province: in such a way that each was over one province, according to Albert, who also says that the empire of this Darius held a hundred and twenty-seven provinces; and for this he cites the passage of Esther: [[Esth 1:1|In the days of Assuerus|In diebus Assueri regis]], [[Esth 1:1|who reigned from India to Ethiopia over a hundred and twenty seven provinces|qui regnavit ab Æthiopia usque Indiam, super centum viginti septem provincias]] [Denis's text reads "from Ethiopia to India"].

paras.t: Sed quid allegatio ista ad Darium regem pertineat, certum non habeo, nisi forte dicatur Assuerus natus de semine Darii hujus. Quo tamen concesso, non sequeretur quod si Assuerus, de quo in Esther etiam habetur, tot provinciis præfuit, et Darius, de quo nunc sermo, totidem quoque præfuerit, præsertim quia et Assuerus iste suum auxit valde imperium, sicut in libro Esther conscribitur quod insulas maris fecit tributarias. Dicit demum Albertus, quod septem reliquæ provinciæ Darii, quæ superant præfato numero satraparum, deserviebant tribus principibus principalioribus, de quibus statim dicetur. Itaque non penitus certum apparet quod Darius iste tot provincias habuit, quod quilibet satrapum dictorum unam integram subjectam sibi habuerit. Porro Darius iste, ut refert Hieronymus, fuit (secundum Josephum) filius Astyagis : qui Astyages, ut infra legitur, dictus est Assuerus ; sed iste fuit alius ab Assuero de quo in libro Esther habetur. Præterea fuit et alius Darius rex, de quo in principio Aggæi et Zachariæ prophetarum habetur : quem multi dicunt fuisse filium Assueri regis de quo historia Esther tractat, quem aliqui dicunt illum Darium quem Alexander Magnus devicit. Sed et Assuerus de quo in Esther, ac Darius de quo in Aggæo, diu fuerunt post Astyagem et Darium de quo nunc loquitur Daniel.
paras.en: But how this citation bears on King Darius I do not know for certain, unless perhaps it be said that Assuerus was born of the seed of this Darius. Yet even granting this, it would not follow that, if Assuerus, of whom we also read in Esther, was over so many provinces, the Darius of whom we now speak was also over as many; especially since this Assuerus greatly enlarged his empire, as is written in the book of Esther, that he made the islands of the sea tributary[[Esth 10:1||]]. Lastly Albert says that the seven remaining provinces of Darius, those beyond the aforesaid number of governors, were in the service of the three chief princes, of whom we shall speak presently. So it does not appear altogether certain that this Darius had so many provinces that each of the said governors had one whole province subject to him. Further, this Darius, as Jerome relates, was (according to Josephus) the son of Astyages; and this Astyages, as we read below, was called Assuerus[[Dan 9:1||]]; but he was another than the Assuerus of whom we read in the book of Esther[[Esth 1:1||]]. There was besides yet another King Darius, of whom we read at the beginning of the prophets Aggeus and Zacharias[[Agg 1:1||]][[Zach 1:1||]], whom many say was the son of the King Assuerus with whom the history of Esther deals, and whom some say was the Darius that Alexander the Great conquered. But both the Assuerus of Esther and the Darius of Aggeus lived long after Astyages and the Darius of whom Daniel now speaks.

paras.t: Et super eos principes tres, id est, satrapis illis præfecit tres principes, ex quibus Daniel unus erat : ut satrapæ redderent rationem, id est computationem de redditibus provinciarum et expensis atque negotiis. An autem rationem reddebant omnibus tribus simul, vel eorum alicui, in textu non determinatur. Et rex non sustineret aliquam molestiam in auditu negotiorum et causarum ac computationum : præsertim quia (ut in fine præcedentis articuli dictum est) senex jam erat, idcirco quietam ducere vitam optavit. Itaque satrapæ constituti fuerunt ad discutiendum negotia, ad levandum tributa, ad disponendum partes imperii sibi commissas. De tribus autem principibus nunc repeti possent, quæ jam in præcedentibus capitulis de tribus principibus regni Babyloniæ sunt prædicta, sed in præinductis articulis hæc quæruntur. Dicit vero Albertus, quod pauciores tribus præesse non poterant, eo quod unus præfuit curiæ, alter militibus seu exercitibus, tertius negotiis sive judiciis.
paras.en: [[6:2|And three princes over them|Et super eos principes tres]], that is, he set three princes over those governors, [[6:2|of whom Daniel was one|ex quibus Daniel unus erat]]: [[6:2|that the governors might give an account|ut satrapæ redderent rationem]], that is, a reckoning of the revenues of the provinces, and of expenses and affairs. But whether they gave account to all three together, or to some one of them, the text does not determine. [[6:2|And the king might have no trouble|Et rex non sustineret aliquam molestiam]] in hearing affairs and cases and accounts; especially because (as was said at the end of the preceding article) he was already old[[Dan 5:31||]], and therefore wished to lead a quiet life. So the governors were appointed to deal with affairs, to raise the tributes, and to order the parts of the empire committed to them. Concerning the three princes, what was said in the preceding chapters about the three princes of the kingdom of Babylon could be repeated now; but it is to be sought in the articles given before. Albert says that there could not be fewer than three over them, because one was over the court, the second over the soldiers or armies, the third over affairs or judgments.

paras.t: Porro ex hac gentilis regis industria instruuntur prælati principesque fideles, ut quæ per inferiores congrue fieri queunt, officialibus suis committant, et in majoribus præsint, quatenus ab exterioribus occupationibus exonerati, Deo quietius vacent. Denique in Exodo aliquid tale inducitur. Ut enim ibi legitur, Jethro cognatus Moysis, viso quod solus Moyses sederet ad populi negotia discernenda, dixit ad eum : Non bonam rem facis; ultra vires tuas est istud negotium. Sed audi verba mea. Esto tu populo in his quæ ad Deum pertinent; et provide de omni plebe viros potentes et timentes Deum, in quibus sit veritas, et qui oderint avaritiam; et constitue ex eis tribunos et centuriones et quinquagenarios et decanos, qui judicent populum omni tempore. Quidquid autem majus fuerit, referant ad te, et ipsi minora tantummodo judicent ; leviusque tibi sit, partito onere in alios.
paras.en: Moreover, from this diligence of a heathen king faithful prelates and princes are taught to commit to their officials what can fittingly be done by inferiors, and to preside over the greater matters, so that, relieved of outward occupations, they may give themselves to God more quietly. Indeed something of the kind is set forth in Exodus. For we read there that Jethro, the kinsman of Moses, seeing that Moses sat alone to settle the people's affairs[[Ex 18:14||]], said to him: [[Ex 18:17|The thing thou dost is not good|Non bonam rem facis]]; [[Ex 18:18|the business is above thy strength|ultra vires tuas est istud negotium]]. [[Ex 18:19|But hear my words|Sed audi verba mea]]. [[Ex 18:19|Be thou to the people in those things that pertain to God|Esto tu populo in his quæ ad Deum pertinent]]; and [[Ex 18:21|provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, in whom there is truth, and that hate avarice, and appoint of them rulers of thousands, and of hundreds, and of fifties, and of tens|provide de omni plebe viros potentes et timentes Deum, in quibus sit veritas, et qui oderint avaritiam; et constitue ex eis tribunos et centuriones et quinquagenarios et decanos]], [[Ex 18:22|Who may judge the people at all times|qui judicent populum omni tempore]]: [[Ex 18:22|and when any great matter soever shall fall out, let them refer it to thee, and let them judge the lesser matters only: that so it may be lighter for thee, the burden being shared out unto others|Quidquid autem majus fuerit, referant ad te, et ipsi minora tantummodo judicent ; leviusque tibi sit, partito onere in alios]].

paras.t: Insuper, secundum Josephum et expositores communiter, Darius capta destructaque Babylone, volens reverti in Mediam, secum adduxit Danielem : quia ut refert Hieronymus, ambiguum non est quin Darius rex audivit visionem seu signum quod Balthasar regi Babylonis acciderat, expositionemque Danielis, et qualiter regnum Medorum elevandum prædixit. Idcirco in illo eum habebat honore, ad quem et Balthasar eum propter interpretationem scripturæ seu visionis promovit. Dicuntque aliqui, quod Darius reperit Danielem purpura indutum, et aurea torque circa collum ornatum : cujus decoris causam inquirens, audivit quæ de scriptura et ejus interpretatione prætacta sunt. Ideo Danielem tanquam sapientissimum virum cum omni honore assumpsit : quanquam dubium non sit, ex speciali Dei ordinatione totum hoc contigisse, ut per Danielem Deus suam majestatem gentilibus declararet, et populus Israel hinc inde dispersus, per Danielem consolaretur.
paras.en: Further, according to Josephus and the expositors generally, Darius, when Babylon had been taken and destroyed, wishing to return to Media, took Daniel with him: because, as Jerome relates, there is no doubt that King Darius had heard of the vision or sign that had befallen Baltasar king of Babylon, and of Daniel's exposition, and how he foretold that the kingdom of the Medes was to be raised up. Therefore he held him in the same honour to which Baltasar too had promoted him for interpreting the writing or vision. And some say that Darius found Daniel clothed in purple and adorned with a golden chain about his neck, and, asking the reason for this distinction, heard what has been told above of the writing and its interpretation.
