So he took Daniel to himself with all honour as a man most wise; though there is no doubt that all this came about by a special ordinance of God, that through Daniel God might make His majesty known to the gentiles, and that the people of Israel, scattered here and there, might be comforted through Daniel.

paras.t: Præterea advertendum, quod (ut in Historia scholastica fertur) quamvis visio ista sit quinta secundum ordinem libri hujus, puta secundum ordinem quo Daniel visiones istas describit, septima tamen est secundum rem gestam seu historiæ ordinem. Nam duæ sequentes visiones, duobus capitulis immediate sequentibus scriptæ, ante hanc contigerunt, scilicet tempore Balthasar regis : quo occiso, quod in isto capitulo legitur, contigit. Cur vero Daniel in processu hujus voluminis, ordinem temporis atque historiæ ac visionum non servat, causa (secundum Hieronymum) est, quia historiam historiæ copulat, ut quia in fine præcedentis capituli dictum est, quod Darius superavit Balthasar regem, descripsit quid sibi post hoc accidit. Quamvis autem in libro isto decem visiones in decem capitulis describantur, quarum prima est in primo capitulo, ultima in undecimo, quædam tamen visionum istarum præ ceteris historiales vocantur, quia plus historia eis miscetur. Ideo ait Hieronymus, hic historiam historiæ copulari; imo in isto capitulo res gesta describitur, et tamen in eo visio contineri asseritur : quia ut Lyra affirmat, hic fit mentio de angelo in lacum leonum descendente, ora leonum claudente, Danielemque liberante : in quibus Christi de morte surgentis figurabatur mysterium.
paras.en: It should be noted besides that (as the Scholastic History says) although this vision is the fifth in the order of this book, that is, in the order in which Daniel describes these visions, it is nevertheless the seventh according to the event, or the order of the history. For the two following visions, written in the two chapters immediately following, took place before this one, namely in the time of King Baltasar; whereas what is read in this chapter happened after he was slain. Why Daniel in the course of this volume does not keep the order of time, of history and of the visions, the reason (according to Jerome) is that he joins history to history: thus, since at the end of the preceding chapter it was said that Darius overcame King Baltasar, he described what befell him after this. Now although ten visions are described in this book in ten chapters, the first of which is in the first chapter and the last in the eleventh, some of these visions are nevertheless called historical above the rest, because more history is mingled with them. Hence Jerome says that here history is joined to history; indeed in this chapter an event is described, and yet a vision is said to be contained in it, because, as Lyra affirms, mention is made here of the angel coming down into the lions' den, shutting the lions' mouths and delivering Daniel: in which was figured the mystery of Christ rising from death.

paras.t: Igitur Daniel superabat omnes principes et satrapas Darii, etiam duos quibus ipse fuerat sociatus : hos superavit sapientia, providentia, honestate, justitia omnique virtute, quia spiritus Dei, id est Spiritus Sanctus, amplior, id est major seu copiosior in communicatione donorum suorum, erat in illo. Quamvis etenim Spiritus Dei sit unus et simplex in se, multiplex tamen est in donis. Rursus, quemadmodum Spiritus Sanctus dicitur dari et infundi ac esse in his, quibus sua dona præstantur; sic dicitur esse major in eis, in quibus dona ejus magis abundant. Vel hoc loco per spiritum Dei, intelligitur virtus, gratia, seu manifestatio Spiritus Dei in donis suis. Sicut ergo gratia fortior est quam sit natura, sic Daniel per dona gratiæ virtute Spiritus Sancti vicit naturalem providentiam atque virtutem satraparum ac principum.
paras.en: [[6:3|And Daniel excelled all the princes, and governors|Igitur Daniel superabat omnes principes et satrapas]] of Darius, even the two with whom he had been joined: these he surpassed in wisdom, foresight, uprightness, justice and every virtue, [[6:3|because a greater spirit of God|quia spiritus Dei]] (that is, the Holy Ghost), [[6:3|greater|amplior]], that is, larger or more abundant in the communication of His gifts, [[6:3|was in him|erat in illo]]. For although the Spirit of God is one and simple in Himself, He is nevertheless manifold in His gifts. Again, just as the Holy Ghost is said to be given and poured into, and to be in, those to whom His gifts are granted, so He is said to be greater in those in whom His gifts more abound. Or in this place by the spirit of God is understood the power, grace or manifestation of the Spirit of God in His gifts. As therefore grace is stronger than nature, so Daniel, through the gifts of grace, by the power of the Holy Ghost, overcame the natural foresight and virtue of the governors and princes.

paras.t: Porro rex Darius cogitabat cum deliberato consensu, constituere eum super omne regnum, id est toti imperio suo eum præficere, propter providentiæ suæ eminentiam, ut esset primus post regem : sicut Joseph fuit in regno Ægypti primus post Pharaonem, juxta illud Genesis, et sunt verba Pharaonis ad eum : Ad tui oris imperium cunctus populus obediet; uno tantum regni solio te præcedam. Sicque Daniel præficeretur duobus illis magnis principibus. Unde principes hi duo, et satrapæ centum viginti, seu multi eorum, quærebant inter se modum impediendi promotionem ipsius, ut invenirent occasionem accusationis Danieli ex latere regis exsistenti, id est Danieli qui erat regi collateraliter familiariterque conjunctus : quoniam rex fecit eum sibi specialissimum et quasi collegam. Vel, Ex latere regis, id est ex parte reginæ seu concubinarum regis ad ejus latus cubantium. Observabant itaque an Daniel in sermone, tactu, nutu seu internuntio indecenter se haberet ad aliquam harum. Hanc expositionem dicit Hieronymus esse Hebræorum, suspicationem addens quod propter occasionem unius verbi, longas soleant fabulas texere. Vel sic : Quærebant Danieli occasionem ex latere regis, id est, ut separarent eum a tanta amicitia regis. Nullamque causam et suspicionem reperire potuerunt contra eum, eo quod fidelis esset regi in omnibus fidelitate ad justitiam pertinente, et omnis culpa et suspicio non inveniretur in eo, id est nulla culpa contra regem, imo nec suspicio. Non tamen fuit sine omni peccato, saltem veniali. Sed de hoc non poterant eum Dario accusare.
paras.en: [[6:4|And the king thought|Porro rex Darius cogitabat]], with deliberate consent, [[6:4|to set him over all the kingdom|constituere eum super omne regnum]], that is, to place him over his whole empire, for the excellence of his foresight, so that he should be first after the king: as Joseph was first after Pharao in the kingdom of Egypt, according to that word of Genesis, which is Pharao's to him: [[Gen 41:40|at the commandment of thy mouth all the people shall obey: only in the kingly throne will I be above thee|Ad tui oris imperium cunctus populus obediet; uno tantum regni solio te præcedam]]. And so Daniel would have been set over those two great princes. [[6:4|Whereupon the princes, and the governors|Unde principes hi duo, et satrapæ]], these two princes and the hundred and twenty governors, or many of them, [[6:4|sought|quærebant]] among themselves a means of hindering his promotion, [[6:4|to find occasion|ut invenirent occasionem]] of accusation [[6:4|against Daniel, with regard to the king|Danieli ex latere regis]] [Latin *ex latere regis*, literally "from the side of the king"; Denis gives three readings of it], that is, against Daniel standing at the king's side; that is, Daniel who was joined to the king as his close companion and familiar: for the king had made him his most special friend and as it were his colleague. Or, *from the side of the king*, that is, by way of the queen or the king's concubines, who lay at his side. So they watched whether Daniel behaved unbecomingly towards any of these in word, touch or nod, or through a go-between. Jerome says this exposition is the Hebrews', adding the suspicion that on the occasion of a single word they are wont to weave long fables. Or thus: they sought occasion against Daniel *from the side of the king*, that is, so as to separate him from so great a friendship with the king. [[6:4|and they could find no cause, nor suspicion|Nullamque causam et suspicionem reperire potuerunt]] against him, [[6:4|because he was faithful|eo quod fidelis esset]] to the king in all things, with the faithfulness that belongs to justice, [[6:4|and no fault, nor suspicion was found in him|et omnis culpa et suspicio non inveniretur in eo]], that is, no fault against the king, nay, not even suspicion. Yet he was not without all sin, at least venial sin; but of this they could not accuse him to Darius.

paras.t: In his verbis commendatur maxima Danielis perfectio, quod tam irreprehensibiliter se gerebat, quod nec levis quidem suspicio contra eum inveniretur : sicut de Judith scriptum est : Quia in omnibus famosissima erat, quoniam timebat Deum valde, nec erat qui loqueretur de ea verbum malum. Sicque Daniel implevit illud Petri : Benefacientes obmutescere faciatis imprudentium hominum ignorantiam. Denique vanitatis non est, quod sanctus Daniel ista de se ipso conscribit, quoniam zelo veritatis ad Dei honorem et hominum ædificationem hoc fecit. Sic quippe sancti viri virtutes laudesque suas prodere atque conscribere consueverunt humiliter, non jactanter. Dicit quoque Albertus, quod occasio est minus quam causa per accidens. Causa enim per accidens, causat per hoc accidens quod est in ipsa. Occasio autem est, quod non per se, nec per aliquid quod in ipso est, malum est, sed est interpretatum ad malum : sicque in libro Proverbiorum sumitur, quo habetur : Occasionem quæritur, qui vult recedere ab amico ; omni tempore erit exsecrabilis. Hinc alii dicunt : Suspicio est, quando aliquis incipit dubitare de bonitate alicujus ex aliquo levi signo. Nullam ergo suspicionem, id est, nil quod alicujus posset movere suspicionem, invenerunt in Daniele : qui (secundum Josephum) super thesauros regis erat, quoniam adeo justus fuit, quod munera sprevit oblata.
paras.en: In these words the very great perfection of Daniel is commended, in that he bore himself so blamelessly that not even a slight suspicion was found against him: as it is written of Judith: [[Jdt 8:8|she was greatly renowned among all, because she feared the Lord very much, neither was there any one that spoke an ill word of her|Quia in omnibus famosissima erat, quoniam timebat Deum valde, nec erat qui loqueretur de ea verbum malum]]. And so Daniel fulfilled that word of Peter: [[1 Pet 2:15|by doing well you may put to silence the ignorance of foolish men|Benefacientes obmutescere faciatis imprudentium hominum ignorantiam]]. Nor is it vanity that holy Daniel writes these things of himself, since he did it out of zeal for the truth, for the honour of God and the edification of men. For so holy men have been wont to make known and write down their virtues and praises humbly, not boastfully. Albert also says that an occasion is less than an accidental cause [that is, a cause that brings about an effect not of its own nature but through something incidental to it]. For an accidental cause causes through the accident that is in it; but an occasion is that which is evil neither of itself nor through anything in it, but is construed as evil: and so the word is taken in the book of Proverbs, where we read: [[Prov 18:1|He that hath a mind to depart from a friend|qui vult recedere ab amico]], [[Prov 18:1|seeketh occasions|Occasionem quæritur]]: [[Prov 18:1|he shall ever be subject to reproach|omni tempore erit exsecrabilis]] [Denis reads *exsecrabilis*, "accursed", where the Vulgate has *exprobrabilis*, "subject to reproach"]. Hence others say: Suspicion is when someone begins to doubt of another's goodness from some slight sign. They found no suspicion, then, in Daniel, that is, nothing that could move anyone's suspicion: who (according to Josephus) was over the king's treasures, since he was so just that he spurned the gifts offered him.

paras.t: Dixerunt ergo viri illi ambitiosi, non ab animi veracitate seu vigore viri vocati, sed vitiis effeminati. Invidia quippe eos incessanter agitavit et torsit, eo quod virum alienum viderent sibi in cunctis præferri, seque comparatione ipsius non reputari et deprimi. Ambitiosi autem sunt invidi; et invidi occasiones quærunt contra innocentes ac virtuosos, potissime contra eos quos vident aut metuunt sibi præferri. Solentque vitia ista in magnatum curiis abundare. Non inveniemus Danieli huic aliquam occasionem deprimendi eum. Viderunt nempe quod stabilis erat in bono, nec putabant eum ab æquitate flectendum. Nisi forte in lege Dei sui, id est in observatione legis divinæ contra ordinationem quamcumque humanam. Considerabant enim, quod a cultu Dei sui nequaquam recederet. Ideo proponebant inter se aliquid ordinare, et ordinationis suæ confirmationem a rege procurare, cujus observatio esset contraria legi Dei, atque per hoc Danielem accusarent regi, tanquam inobedientem eidem. Secundum Hieronymum : Felix est conversatio in qua adversarii nullam inveniunt occasionem, nisi in legitimis Dei quæ servat, id est, quæ talis est quod in veritate reprehendi non potest, nec aliud ei objici valeat nisi quod ad veram spectat justitiam. Qui taliter vivit, dicere potest illud Apostoli ad Corinthios : Gloria nostra hæc est, testimonium conscientiæ nostræ, quod in simplicitate et sinceritate, et non in sapientia carnali, sed in gratia Dei, conversati sumus in hoc mundo.
paras.en: [[6:5|Then these men said|Dixerunt ergo viri illi]]: ambitious men, called *men* not for any truthfulness or vigour of soul but rather made effeminate by vices[[Is 3:4||]] [Latin *viri*, "men", a word Denis links with *vigor*, manly strength]. For envy ceaselessly drove and tormented them, because they saw a foreigner preferred to themselves in all things, and themselves counted for nothing and cast down by comparison with him. Now the ambitious are envious; and the envious seek occasions against the innocent and the virtuous, above all against those whom they see, or fear, preferred to themselves. And these vices are wont to abound in the courts of the great. [[6:5|We shall not find any occasion against this Daniel|Non inveniemus Danieli huic aliquam occasionem]], that is, of bringing him down. For they saw that he was steadfast in good, and did not think he could be bent from equity. [[6:5|unless perhaps concerning the law of his God|Nisi forte in lege Dei sui]], that is, in keeping the divine law against any human ordinance whatever. For they considered that he would by no means withdraw from the worship of his God. So they purposed among themselves to ordain something, and to procure the confirmation of their ordinance from the king, the keeping of which would be contrary to the law of God, and by this to accuse Daniel to the king as disobedient to him. According to Jerome: Happy is the life in which adversaries find no occasion except in the ordinances of God which it keeps; that is, a life such that it cannot in truth be blamed, nor can anything be objected to it but what pertains to true justice. Whoever lives so can say that word of the Apostle to the Corinthians: [[2 Cor 1:12|For our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience|Gloria nostra hæc est, testimonium conscientiæ nostræ]], [[2 Cor 1:12|that in simplicity|quod in simplicitate]] [[2 Cor 1:12|and sincerity|et sinceritate]], [[2 Cor 1:12|and not in carnal wisdom, but in the grace of God, we have conversed in this world|et non in sapientia carnali, sed in gratia Dei, conversati sumus in hoc mundo]].

paras.t: Tunc principes et satrapæ surripuerunt regi, id est, latenter ac deceptorie impia suggesserunt, et sic locuti sunt ei : Dari rex, in æternum vive, nunc scilicet in regia dignitate temporaliter, deinde inter deos perpetue; vel, In æternum vive, id est, quantum in nobis est, optamus te semper manere in vita atque imperio. Iste fuit modus honorandi, affandi, salutandique reges : et a blandis inchoant verbis, ut benevolentiam capiant regis, eumque facilius ad suum trahant affectum.
paras.en: [[6:6|Then the princes, and the governors, craftily suggested to the king|Tunc principes et satrapæ surripuerunt regi]] [Latin *surripuerunt*, literally "stole upon" the king], that is, secretly and deceitfully suggested wicked things, [[6:6|and spoke thus unto him|et sic locuti sunt ei]]: [[6:6|King Darius, live for ever|Dari rex, in æternum vive]]: that is, now in royal dignity in time, and afterwards among the gods for ever; or, *live for ever*, that is, as far as in us lies, we wish thee to remain always in life and in empire. This was the manner of honouring, addressing and greeting kings; and they begin with flattering words, to win the king's goodwill and draw him the more easily to their own wish.

paras.t: Consilium inierunt cuncti principes regni tui, magistratus et satrapæ (nomina ista supra exposita sunt), et senatores, qui amplioris fuerant dignitatis, et judices, ut decretum imperatorium exeat, id est, a te imperatore instituatur lex præceptoria, et edictum, id est mandatum undique ratum, et comminatione pœnarum vallatum : Ut omnis qui in tuo est regno, qui petierit aliquam petitionem a quocumque deo aut homine usque ad triginta dies, nisi a te, rex, mittatur in lacum leonum.
paras.en: [[6:7|All the princes of the kingdom|Consilium inierunt cuncti principes regni tui]], [[6:7|the magistrates, and governors|magistratus et satrapæ]] (these names were explained above), [[6:7|the senators|et senatores]], who were of greater dignity, [[6:7|and judges, have consulted together|et judices]], [[6:7|that an imperial decree|ut decretum imperatorium exeat]] go forth, that is, that a law of command be instituted by thee the emperor, [[6:7|and an edict|et edictum]], that is, a command ratified everywhere and fenced about with the threat of penalties: [[6:7|That whosoever|Ut omnis]] is in thy kingdom, and [[6:7|shall ask any petition of any god, or man, for thirty days, but of thee, O king, shall be cast into the den of the lions|qui petierit aliquam petitionem a quocumque deo aut homine usque ad triginta dies, nisi a te, rex, mittatur in lacum leonum]].

paras.t: Non immerito simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei, dum mala sub specie boni, imo et pessima sub optimorum proponunt colore. Sic isti perversi, sub specie æquitatis et zeli pro rege, quærunt ut infra tantum tempus nullus quid postulet nisi a rege : ut scilicet homines ad regis reverentiam inducerentur; rex quoque interim suam regiam liberalitatem ostenderet, et cunctis amabilior redderetur, factus jam recens monarcha. Sicque per honorem regi impendendum, moliuntur justo insidias. Mali namque, quum veritate et æquitate non queunt quod cupiunt obtinere, falsis et impiis mediis, sub aliquo boni apparatu, se armant : et istud apud reges, principes et prælatos solet potissime practicari, per eorum ministros ac familiares impia persuadentes, quasi pro honore dominorum suorum zelantes, quum tamen quæ quærunt, nociva sint illis. Propter quod scriptum est in libro Esther : Quidam aures principum simplices, et ex sua natura alios æstimantes, callida fraude decipiunt. Et iterum : Quidam in tantum vesaniæ proruperunt, ut eos qui credita sibi officia diligenter observant, et ita cuncta agunt, ut omni laude digni sint, mendaciorum cuniculis conentur subvertere. Itemque : Malis quorumdam suggestionibus regum studia depravantur. Denique triginta dierum tempus instituunt, quia infra tot dies Danielem sperabant se posse deprehendere; cogitantes quoque quod quamvis paucis forte diebus, non tamen tam multis, a Dei sui invocatione cessaret.
paras.en: Not undeservedly, [[Job 36:13|Dissemblers and crafty men prove the wrath of God|simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei]] [*prove*, that is, provoke], when they put forward evil under the appearance of good, nay, the worst things under the colour of the best. So these perverse men, under the appearance of equity and of zeal for the king, ask that within so long a time no one should ask anything except of the king: so that, namely, men might be brought to reverence the king, and the king meanwhile might show his royal liberality and be made more lovable to all, being now a new monarch. And so, by way of the honour to be paid to the king, they lay snares for the just man. For the wicked, when they cannot obtain what they desire by truth and equity, arm themselves with false and wicked means under some show of good: and this is wont to be practised above all with kings, princes and prelates, through their ministers and household, who urge wicked counsels as though zealous for the honour of their lords, when what they seek is harmful to them. Wherefore it is written in the book of Esther: Certain men [[Esth 16:6|with crafty fraud|callida fraude decipiunt]] [[Esth 16:6|deceive the ears of princes that are well meaning, and judge of others by their own nature|aures principum simplices, et ex sua natura alios æstimantes]]. And again: Certain men [[Esth 16:5|break out into so great madness, as to endeavour to undermine by lies such as observe diligently the offices committed to them, and do all things in such manner as to be worthy of all men's praise|in tantum vesaniæ proruperunt, ut eos qui credita sibi officia diligenter observant, et ita cuncta agunt, ut omni laude digni sint, mendaciorum cuniculis conentur subvertere]]. And likewise: [[Esth 16:7|the good designs of kings are depraved by the evil suggestions of certain men|Malis quorumdam suggestionibus regum studia depravantur]]. Lastly they fix a time of thirty days, because they hoped to catch Daniel within so many days; thinking also that, though he might perhaps cease from calling upon his God for a few days, he would not do so for so many.

paras.t: Nunc itaque, rex, confirma sententiam, id est sensum verborum istorum, quem nos rationabilem judicamus, et scribe decretum, id est, præfatum edictum jube in scriptis promulgari ; ut non immutetur, sed inviolabiliter observetur, quod statutum est a Medis atque Persis, id est a nobis tantis ac talibus, præ ceteris in sapientia potentiaque præclaris, ad quos monarchia devenit, nec prævaricari cuiquam subditorum tuorum liceat hoc decretum. Contra hos eisque similes scriptum est in Isaia : Væ qui condunt leges iniquas; et scribentes, injustitiam scripserunt. Ex præhabitis verbis infert Hieronymus, unum fuisse sub Dario et Cyro regnum Medorum et Persarum.
paras.en: [[6:8|Now, therefore, O king, confirm the sentence|Nunc itaque, rex, confirma sententiam]], that is, the sense of these words, which we judge reasonable, [[6:8|and sign the decree|et scribe decretum]] [Latin *scribe*, "write"], that is, order the aforesaid edict to be promulgated in writing; [[6:8|that what is decreed by the Medes and Persians|quod statutum est a Medis atque Persis]] (that is, by us, men so great and of such a kind, renowned above others in wisdom and power, to whom the monarchy has come) [[6:8|may not be altered|ut non immutetur]], but be kept inviolably, [[6:8|nor any man|nec prævaricari cuiquam]] of thy subjects [[6:8|be allowed to transgress it|liceat hoc decretum]]. Against these and their like it is written in Isaias: [[Is 10:1|Woe to them that make wicked laws: and when they write, write injustice|Væ qui condunt leges iniquas; et scribentes, injustitiam scripserunt]]. From the foregoing words Jerome infers that under Darius and Cyrus the kingdom of the Medes and Persians was one.

paras.t: Porro rex Darius calliditate pravorum deceptus, proposuit decretum, et statuit, id est, ordinavit istud observari, et in scriptis illud insinuavit.
paras.en: [[6:9|So king Darius|Porro rex Darius]], deceived by the craftiness of the wicked, [[6:9|set forth the decree, and established it|proposuit decretum, et statuit]], that is, ordered it to be kept, and made it known in writing.

paras.t: Quod quum Daniel comperisset, id est constitutam legem, id est, jussionem istam iniquam agnosceret promulgatam, ingressus est in domum suam, ut in ea oraret quietius, nec publice illud agendo, pravorum insaniam provocaret, regisque edictum inordinate videretur contemnere. Nec enim debet se quis sine causa exponere mortis periculo, vel alios ad vitium inflammare. Et fenestris apertis in cœnaculo suo contra Jerusalem, id est versus eam, tribus temporibus in die flectebat genua sua et adorabat Deum, confitebaturque confessione laudis divinæ ac culpæ suæ, vel potius populi sui Israel, seu etiam regis ac regni, coram Deo suo, immenso, ubique præsente, et omnia intuente, sicut ante facere consueverat. In quo constantia atque justitia Danielis monstratur, quod non timens eos qui corpus occidunt, maluit mortis subire periculum, quam Dei transgredi legem. Orat autem in alto loco, ut hinc inde latius circumspiciens, et Deum in suis contemplans effectibus, se ipsum ad contemplationem sublimius erigat. Nam et altior locus, videtur ad elevationem mentis conferre. Et de Petro apostolo scriptum est in Actibus, quod ascendit in superiora domus ut oraret. Porro cœnacula, secundum Hieronymum, alio nomine appellantur solaria. Et in Actibus de Apostolis eisque associatis habetur : Quum introissent in cœnaculum, ascenderunt in superiora ; et erant perseverantes unanimiter in oratione. Christus quoque in cœnaculo Pascha legitur celebrasse : in quo et Apostoli Spiritum Sanctum susceperunt. Oravit autem Daniel facie versa ad templum Jerusalem : sic enim captivis filiis Israel esse orandum, Salomon ait. Idcirco fenestras aperuit, ut versus illam terræ plagam magis libere adspectaret, sicque Dei et beneficiorum ipsius, ac Patriarcharum et Prophetarum profundius recordaretur.
paras.en: [[6:10|Now, when Daniel knew this|Quod quum Daniel comperisset]], [[6:10|that is to say, that the law was made|id est constitutam legem]], that is, when he learned that this wicked command had been promulgated, [[6:10|he went into his house|ingressus est in domum suam]], so that he might pray there more quietly, and not, by doing it in public, provoke the madness of the wicked and seem to despise the king's edict in a disorderly way. For no one ought to expose himself to the danger of death without cause, or to inflame others to vice. [[6:10|And opening the windows in his upper chamber towards Jerusalem|Et fenestris apertis in cœnaculo suo contra Jerusalem]], that is, facing it, [[6:10|he knelt down three times a day|tribus temporibus in die flectebat genua sua]] [[6:10|and adored|et adorabat]] God, [[6:10|and gave thanks|confitebaturque]] [the Latin *confitebatur* means both to give praise and to confess, and Denis takes it both ways] with the confession of the divine praise and of his own fault, or rather of his people Israel's, or even of the king's and the kingdom's, [[6:10|before his God|coram Deo suo]], who is immense, present everywhere and beholding all things, [[6:10|as he had been accustomed to do before|sicut ante facere consueverat]]. In this the constancy and justice of Daniel is shown, in that, not fearing [[Matt 10:28|them that kill the body|eos qui corpus occidunt]], he chose rather to undergo the danger of death than to transgress the law of God. And he prays in a high place, so that, looking about more widely on this side and that, and contemplating God in His effects, he may raise himself more loftily to contemplation. For a higher place too seems to help the lifting up of the mind. And of Peter the apostle it is written in the Acts that he [[Acts 10:9|went up to the higher parts of the house to pray|ascendit in superiora domus ut oraret]]. Now upper chambers, according to Jerome, are by another name called *solaria* [that is, sun-rooms, rooms open to the sun at the top of the house]. And in the Acts it is said of the Apostles and those joined with them: [[Acts 1:13|when they were come in, they went up into an upper room|Quum introissent in cœnaculum, ascenderunt in superiora]]; and they were [[Acts 1:14|persevering with one mind in prayer|perseverantes unanimiter in oratione]]. Christ too is read to have celebrated the Pasch in an upper room[[Luke 22:12||]], in which the Apostles also received the Holy Ghost[[Acts 2:4||]]. Now Daniel prayed with his face turned towards the temple of Jerusalem, for so, Solomon says, the captive children of Israel were to pray[[3 Kings 8:48||]]. For that reason he opened the windows, so that he might look more freely towards that region of the earth, and so remember more deeply God and His benefits, and the Patriarchs and Prophets.

paras.t: Circa prædicta ait Hieronymus : Tria tempora quibus Deo flectenda sunt genua, tertiam horam et sextam et nonam, evangelica traditio intelligit. Denique tertia hora descendit super Apostolos Spiritus Sanctus ; sexta, volens comedere Petrus, ascendit cœnaculum ad orandum ; nona, Petrus et Joannes pergebant ad templum. — Insuper de hac re in Scholastica historia fertur : Tribus horis orabant Judæi in die, scilicet hora tertia, sexta, nona. In tertia orabant, quia tunc datus est eis Decalogus legis in monte Sinai. In eadem hora orat Ecclesia, quia tunc datus est Spiritus Sanctus Apostolis. In sexta orabant Judæi, quia tunc erectus est serpens æneus in deserto. In eadem orat Ecclesia, quia tunc Christus suspensus fuit in ligno. In nona orabant, quia tunc petra dabat aquas in Cades. In eadem orat Ecclesia, quia tunc de Christo lanceato exivit sanguis et aqua. — Quidam vero tria hæc tempora intelligunt, mane, meridie, vesperam, juxta illud in Psalmo : Vespere et mane et meridie narrabo. Mane namque et vespere juge sacrificium offerebant ; in meridie autem peccavit Adam. Ista est expositio una Alberti. Et ad idem redit quod Lyra hic dicit : Orabat tribus temporibus in die, id est : hora matutinali, quia lotis manibus Judæi tunc Domino benedicunt ; et hora tertia vel sexta ante comestionem ; et hora vespertina, prout dicitur in Actibus, Petrus et Joannes ascenderunt in templum ad horam orationis nonam : quæ accipitur circa tempus vesperarum, ut patet in Ecclesiis majoribus, ubi tunc dicitur Nona. Hoc secundum Lyram narratum sit. — Quod autem Scholastica historia perhibet Judæos ter orasse in die, forsitan non videtur prima facie consonare ei quod scribit Nehemias, quod Judæi quater in die, et quater in nocte confitebantur et adorabant Dominum Deum suum. Et alibi legitur : Septies in die laudem dixi tibi.
paras.en: On the foregoing Jerome says: The three times at which the knees are to be bent to God the tradition of the Gospel understands as the third hour, the sixth and the ninth. Thus at the third hour the Holy Ghost came down upon the Apostles[[Acts 2:15||]]; at the sixth Peter, wishing to eat, went up to the upper room to pray[[Acts 10:9||]]; at the ninth Peter and John were going to the temple[[Acts 3:1||]]. Moreover on this matter the Scholastic History relates: The Jews prayed at three hours in the day, namely the third, sixth and ninth hours. At the third they prayed, because at that time the Decalogue of the law was given them on mount Sinai[[Ex 20:1||]] [the margin gives Exod. xx without a verse]. At the same hour the Church prays, because at that time the Holy Ghost was given to the Apostles[[Acts 2:15||]]. At the sixth the Jews prayed, because at that time the brazen serpent was set up in the desert[[Num 21:9||]]. At the same hour the Church prays, because at that time Christ was hung upon the wood[[Luke 23:33||]][[Luke 23:44||]]. At the ninth they prayed, because at that time the rock gave waters in Cades[[Num 20:11||]]. At the same hour the Church prays, because at that time from Christ, pierced with the lance, [[John 19:34|there came out blood and water|exivit sanguis et aqua]]. But some understand these three times as morning, noon and evening, according to that saying in the Psalm: [[Ps 54:18|Evening and morning, and at noon I will speak|Vespere et mane et meridie narrabo]]. For in the morning and in the evening they offered the perpetual sacrifice[[Num 28:4||]] [the margin gives Num. xxviii, 3–6], and at noon Adam sinned[[Gen 3:6||]]. This is one exposition of Albert's. And what Lyra says here comes to the same: He prayed [[6:10|three times a day|tribus temporibus in die]], that is, at the morning hour, because the Jews, having washed their hands, then bless the Lord; and at the third or sixth hour, before the meal; and at the evening hour, as it is said in the Acts: [[Acts 3:1|Peter and John went up into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer|Petrus et Joannes ascenderunt in templum ad horam orationis nonam]], which is taken to be about the time of Vespers, as is plain in the greater churches, where None is said at that time. Let this be told according to Lyra. But that the Scholastic History affirms that the Jews prayed three times in the day perhaps does not seem at first sight to agree with what Nehemias writes, that the Jews four times in the day and four times in the night [[2 Esd 9:3|confessed, and adored the Lord their God|confitebantur et adorabant Dominum Deum suum]] [in the Douay-Rheims and the Vulgate: "four times in the day, and four times they confessed"; "in the night" is Denis's]. And elsewhere we read: [[Ps 118:164|Seven times a day I have given praise to thee|Septies in die laudem dixi tibi]].

paras.t: Viri ergo illi curiosius inquirentes. In quo eorum superflua occupatio demonstratur. Curiositas quippe, secundum Tullium, est superflua investigatio rerum ad se non pertinentium. Invenerunt Danielem orantem et obsecrantem Deum suum. Forte accesserunt subito eum quasi pro negotiis regis. Oratio autem est simplex petitio ; obsecratio vero est invocatio per aliquod sacrum, per quod oratio fit exaudibilis, ut quum dicimus, Per passionem tuam libera nos, Domine. Circa prædicta ait Hieronymus : Ex hoc loco discimus, ne incaute nos offeramus periculis ; sed quantum in nobis est, declinemus insidias : unde Daniel non in foro, non in plateis, sed in abscondito fecit contra regis imperium, ut Dei omnipotentis jussa impleret.
paras.en: [[6:11|Wherefore those men carefully watching him|Viri ergo illi curiosius inquirentes]] [literally "inquiring more curiously", whence what follows on curiosity]. In this their superfluous busyness is shown. For curiosity, according to Tully, is the superfluous investigation of things that do not concern one. [[6:11|found Daniel praying and making supplication to his God|Invenerunt Danielem orantem et obsecrantem Deum suum]]. Perhaps they came upon him suddenly, as though on the king's business. Now prayer is simple petition, while supplication [*obsecratio*] is invocation by something sacred, through which the prayer becomes worthy to be heard, as when we say: By thy passion deliver us, O Lord. On the foregoing Jerome says: From this place we learn not to offer ourselves to dangers incautiously, but, as far as in us lies, to avoid snares. Hence Daniel acted against the king's command not in the market-place, not in the streets, but in secret, so as to fulfil the commands of almighty God.

paras.t: Et accedentes, locuti sunt regi super edicto, id est de præcepto non petendi aliquid nisi a Dario : Rex, numquid non constituisti ut omnis homo de subditis tuis, qui rogaret quemquam de diis et hominibus usque ad dies triginta, nisi a te, rex, mitteretur in lacum leonum ? Primo in generali inquirunt, nec Danielem in speciali accusant, quatenus rege quod jusserat confirmante, non habeat facultatem liberandi Danielem, quem sciebant regi carissimum. Ad quos respondens rex, ait : Verus est sermo quem dicitis, quod scilicet ita constitui, juxta decretum Medorum atque Persarum, quod prævaricari non licet. Quod utique falsum est, quia obedire oportet Deo magis quam hominibus. Sed tantæ æstimationis fuerunt Medi et Persæ apud se ipsos, quod verba sua putabant omnimode observanda.
paras.en: [[6:12|And they came and spoke to the king concerning the edict|Et accedentes, locuti sunt regi super edicto]], that is, about the command not to ask anything except from Darius: [[6:12|O king, hast thou not decreed, that every man|Rex, numquid non constituisti ut omnis homo]] of thy subjects [[6:12|that should make a request to any of the gods, or men, for thirty days, but to thyself, O king, should be cast into the den of the lions?|qui rogaret quemquam de diis et hominibus usque ad dies triginta, nisi a te, rex, mitteretur in lacum leonum]] They first inquire in general, and do not accuse Daniel in particular, so that, once the king had confirmed what he had commanded, he would not have the power to free Daniel, whom they knew to be most dear to the king. [[6:12|And the king answered them, saying|Ad quos respondens rex, ait]]: [[6:12|The word is true|Verus est sermo]] which you speak, namely that I so decreed, [[6:12|according to the decree of the Medes and Persians, which it is not lawful to violate|juxta decretum Medorum atque Persarum, quod prævaricari non licet]]. Which is certainly false, for [[Acts 5:29|We ought to obey God rather than men|obedire oportet Deo magis quam hominibus]]. But the Medes and Persians were of such esteem in their own eyes that they thought their words were to be kept in every way.

paras.t: Tunc dixerunt coram rege : Daniel de filiis captivitatis Judææ. De numero captivorum asserunt Danielem, ut ejus contemptus, quo regis edictum abjecit, intolerabilior videatur, secundum Hieronymum. Non curavit de lege tua, et de edicto quod constituisti. Lex et edictum hic realiter idem designant, puta præceptum, seu ordinationem quæ in quantum verbis seu scriptis promulgatur, edictum vocatur.
paras.en: Then they [[6:13|said before the king|dixerunt coram rege]]: [[6:13|Daniel, who is of the children of the captivity of Juda|Daniel de filiis captivitatis Judææ]]. They declare Daniel to be of the number of the captives, so that his contempt, by which he cast aside the king's edict, may seem the more intolerable, according to Jerome. [[6:13|hath not regarded thy law, nor the decree that thou hast made|Non curavit de lege tua, et de edicto quod constituisti]]. Law and edict here designate in reality the same thing, namely a precept or ordinance, which, inasmuch as it is promulgated in words or in writing, is called an edict.

paras.t: Quod verbum quum audisset rex, satis contristatus est, quod carissimum condemnaret ad mortem, et virum regno utilissimum perderet ; et pro Daniele apposuit cor ut liberaret eum, id est, variis modis quærens eum eripere, et usque ad solis occasum laborabat ut erueret eum. Viri autem illi intelligentes regem, id est, considerantes ejus intentum, quod scilicet quærebat modum vitandi seu differendi damnationem Danielis ; consideravit enim se illorum calliditate circumventum, et propria responsione arctatum, illos quoque ex invidia tetendisse insidias ; dixerunt ei : Scito, rex, quia lex Medorum est atque Persarum, ut omne decretum quod constituerit rex eorum, non liceat immutari, id est revocari aut violari. Ideo rex leges et consuetudines regni sui immutare non audens, regia potestate contra suos non utitur, sed ratione atque consilio. Quumque modum evasionis pro Daniele non cerneret, consensit petitioni suorum. Uno autem inconvenienti dato, multa sequuntur. Ideo qui constituit edictum blasphemum, et illud irrevocabiliter servandum putavit, alia quoque incidit vitia, ita quod innocentem rex humano timore damnavit.
paras.en: [[6:14|Now when the king had heard these words, he was very much grieved|Quod verbum quum audisset rex, satis contristatus est]], because he was condemning to death one most dear to him, and losing a man most useful to the kingdom; [[6:14|and in behalf of Daniel he set his heart to deliver him|et pro Daniele apposuit cor ut liberaret eum]], that is, seeking by various ways to rescue him, [[6:14|and even till sunset he laboured to save him|et usque ad solis occasum laborabat ut erueret eum]]. [[6:15|But those men perceiving the king's design|Viri autem illi intelligentes regem]], that is, considering his intent, namely that he was seeking a way to avoid or to put off the condemnation of Daniel (for he perceived that he had been circumvented by their cunning and bound by his own answer, and that they had laid snares out of envy), [[6:15|said to him|dixerunt ei]]: [[6:15|Know thou, O king, that the law of the Medes and Persians is, that no decree which the king hath made, may be altered|Scito, rex, quia lex Medorum est atque Persarum, ut omne decretum quod constituerit rex eorum, non liceat immutari]], that is, revoked or violated. Therefore the king, not daring to change the laws and customs of his kingdom, does not use his royal power against his own men, but reason and counsel. And when he saw no way of escape for Daniel, he consented to the petition of his men. Now when one unfitting thing is granted, many follow. Hence he who set up a blasphemous edict and thought it must be kept irrevocably fell into other vices as well, so that the king condemned an innocent man out of human fear.

paras.t: Tunc rex præcepit adduci Danielem de domo sua ; et adduxerunt Danielem, et miserunt eum in lacum leonum. Dixitque rex Danieli antequam in lacum descenderet : Deus tuus, quem tu colis semper, scilicet cultu latriæ, liberabit te. Quocirca scribit Hieronymus : Cedit rex multitudini, et consentientibus inter se adversariis, mortem amici non audet negare ; quodque ipse rex obtinere non potuit, scilicet Danielis liberationem, Dei tradit potentiæ. Nec ambigue loquitur, ut dicat, Si potuerit ; sed audacter et confidenter, Deus, inquit, tuus quem colis, liberabit te. Audierat enim tres pueros qui inferioris a Daniele meriti erant, flammas vicisse Babylonicas in fornace, et Danieli multa mysteria revelata. Unde et diligebat eum, hominemque captivum in maximo habebat honore.
paras.en: [[6:16|Then the king commanded|Tunc rex præcepit]] Daniel to be brought from his house, [[6:16|and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of the lions|et adduxerunt Danielem, et miserunt eum in lacum leonum]]. [[6:16|And the king said to Daniel|Dixitque rex Danieli]] before he went down into the den: [[6:16|Thy God, whom thou always servest|Deus tuus, quem tu colis semper]], namely with the worship of latria [that is, the worship due to God alone], [[6:16|he will deliver thee|liberabit te]]. On this Jerome writes: The king yields to the multitude, and, with his adversaries agreeing among themselves, he dares not refuse the death of his friend; and what the king himself could not obtain, namely the deliverance of Daniel, he hands over to the power of God. Nor does he speak doubtfully, so as to say, If he can; but boldly and confidently: [[6:16|Thy God|Deus]], he says, whom thou servest, [[6:16|he will deliver thee|liberabit te]]. For he had heard that the three youths, who were of lesser merit than Daniel, had overcome the Babylonian flames in the furnace[[Dan 3:23||]], and that many mysteries had been revealed to Daniel. Hence too he loved him, and held a captive man in the greatest honour.

paras.t: Allatusque est lapis unus, et positus super os laci, quem obsignavit rex annulo suo, et annulo optimatum suorum. Jussit ergo rex os foveæ lapide operiri, eumque signari, ne quis rege ignorante lapidem amoveret, aut Danieli nocumentum inferret. Ideo subditur : ne quid fieret contra Danielem ab adversariis ejus. Magis enim timuit rex sævitiam hominum quam leonum. Ideo Glossa sequens Hieronymum, dicit : Qui de leonibus securus est, homines pertimescit. Dicit quoque Hieronymus : Rex credit eum Dei potentiæ ; et signat lapidem etiam annulo optimatum suorum, ne quid suspicionis contra eos videatur habere.
paras.en: [[6:17|And a stone was brought, and laid upon the mouth of the den: which the king sealed with his own ring, and with the ring of his nobles|Allatusque est lapis unus, et positus super os laci, quem obsignavit rex annulo suo, et annulo optimatum suorum]]. So the king ordered the mouth of the pit to be covered with a stone and the stone to be sealed, so that no one might remove the stone without the king's knowledge or do harm to Daniel. Therefore it is added: [[6:17|that nothing should be done against Daniel|ne quid fieret contra Danielem]] by his adversaries. For the king feared the savagery of men more than that of the lions. Hence the Gloss, following Jerome, says: He who is without fear about the lions is afraid of men. Jerome also says: The king entrusts him to the power of God; and he seals the stone with the ring of his nobles as well, so as not to seem to hold any suspicion against them.

paras.t: Et abiit rex in domum suam, quia jam vespera fuit, et dormivit incœnatus. Quomodo verum est hoc ? quum sequatur, cibique non sunt allati coram eo a famulis suis, quia cibos sibi afferri prohibuit, insuper et somnus recessit ab eo. Et respondendum, quod forte parum dormivit, quum tristitia oculos gravet, et ad somnum inclinet. Nam et somnus est alleviativus tristitiæ. Hinc in Marco legitur : Erant oculi eorum, scilicet Apostolorum, gravati præ tristitia. Vel quod dicitur, Dormivit, exponendum est, Ad dormiendum se posuit, seu, in lecto quievit. Magnitudo autem tristitiæ, sicut et ceterarum passionum, tantam facit in corpore transmutationem ac dyscrasiam, ut somnum impediat ; similiter sollicitudo, et ingens consideratio rei, abstinentia quoque a cibo : quæ omnia in rege fuerunt. Circa hæc Hieronymus scribit et Glossa : Quanta benevolentia regis ! Nec die cibum capit, nec nocte dormit ; cum Propheta periclitante, quasi uno pendet affectu. Quanto magis nos pro peccatis propriis debemus Deum ad misericordiam flectere, quum rex Deum nesciens, formata scilicet notitia, hoc faciat pro eo quem vult de periculo liberare !
paras.en: [[6:18|And the king went away to his house|Et abiit rex in domum suam]], because it was already evening, [[6:18|and laid himself down without taking supper|et dormivit incœnatus]] [the Latin *dormivit* is literally "slept"; the Douay-Rheims follows the second answer below]. How is this true, since there follows: [[6:18|and meat was not set before him|cibique non sunt allati coram eo]] by his servants, because he forbade food to be brought to him, [[6:18|and even sleep departed from him|insuper et somnus recessit ab eo]]? It must be answered that perhaps he slept a little, since sorrow weighs down the eyes and inclines one to sleep. For sleep also relieves sorrow. Hence we read in Mark: [[Mark 14:40|their eyes|Erant oculi eorum]], namely the Apostles', [[Mark 14:40|were heavy|gravati]] for sorrow ["for sorrow" is in the parallel at Luke 22:45]. Or else what is said, *He slept*, is to be explained as: He laid himself down to sleep, or, he rested in his bed. Now the greatness of sorrow, as of the other passions, makes such a change and such a distemper [*dyscrasia*, an ill mixture of the bodily humours] in the body that it hinders sleep; and so too do anxiety, and intense thought about a matter, and abstinence from food: all of which were in the king. On this Jerome writes, and the Gloss: How great the good will of the king! He neither takes food by day nor sleeps by night; he hangs, as it were, on one and the same feeling with the Prophet in his danger. How much more ought we to bend God to mercy for our own sins, when a king who did not know God (that is, with a formed knowledge [knowledge given life by faith and charity, as the schoolmen speak of formed faith]) does this for one whom he wishes to deliver from danger!

paras.t: Sed quæritur, si rex firmam habuit confidentiam quod Deus eriperet Danielem, cur eatenus tristabatur. Et respondendum, quod confidentia ejus non fuit perfecta et pura, sed variis cogitationibus ac passionibus, plenæ confidentiæ contrariis, mixta. Sic quippe imperfecte sperantibus solet contingere, præsertim quia etsi de Dei potentia non dubitent, ejus tamen dispositionem et voluntatem non norunt : occulta namque sunt Dei judicia.
paras.en: But it is asked why, if the king had firm confidence that God would rescue Daniel, he was so sorrowful. It must be answered that his confidence was not perfect and pure, but mixed with various thoughts and passions contrary to full confidence. For so it usually happens to those who hope imperfectly, especially since, though they do not doubt the power of God, they do not know His disposition and will: for the judgments of God are hidden[[Rom 11:33||]].

paras.t: Tunc rex primo diluculo consurgens, festinus ad lacum leonum perrexit præ desiderio æstuanti. Appropinquansque lacui, Danielem voce lacrimabili inclamavit. Ex compassionis enim magnitudine lacrimas continere non potuit. Forsan lapidem jussit deponi, antequam sic clamavit. Daniel, serve Dei viventis. Deum Danielis vocat viventem, tanquam verum summumque Deum, et ad differentiam deorum qui manibus fiunt. Porro, secundum Hieronymum, rex iste oblitus regiæ dignitatis, victor ad captivum, et dominus cucurrit ad servum. Deus tuus cui tu servis semper, omni scilicet tempore opportuno, putasne valuit te liberare a leonibus ? Non quasi de Dei omnipotentia dubitans, ita rex loquitur ; sed secundum Hieronymum, in ambiguo sententiam temperat, ut quum Daniel incolumis apparuerit, quanto res incredibilior videbatur, tanto contra adversarios Danielis indignatio regis justior appareret.
paras.en: [[6:19|Then the king rising very early in the morning, went in haste to the lions' den|Tunc rex primo diluculo consurgens, festinus ad lacum leonum perrexit]], out of burning desire. [[6:20|And coming near to the den, cried with a lamentable voice to Daniel|Appropinquansque lacui, Danielem voce lacrimabili inclamavit]]. For from the greatness of his compassion he could not hold back his tears. Perhaps he ordered the stone to be taken away before he cried out so. [[6:20|Daniel, servant of the living God|Daniel, serve Dei viventis]]. He calls the God of Daniel living, as being the true and supreme God, and to distinguish Him from the gods that are made with hands. Further, according to Jerome, this king, forgetting his royal dignity, ran, the victor to the captive, the lord to the servant. [[6:20|hath thy God, whom thou servest always|Deus tuus cui tu servis semper]], that is, at every fitting time, [[6:20|been able, thinkest thou, to deliver thee from the lions|putasne valuit te liberare a leonibus]]? The king does not speak thus as though doubting the omnipotence of God; but, according to Jerome, he tempers his words with doubt, so that, when Daniel appeared unharmed, the more incredible the thing had seemed, the juster would the king's indignation against Daniel's adversaries appear.

paras.t: Et Daniel regi respondens, ait : Rex, in æternum vive. Honorantem se salutat, et afflictum ac blande loquentem, dulciter consolatur. Deus meus misit angelum suum et conclusit per angelum ora leonum, eorum feritatem, rictum rabiemque refrenans. Unde secundum Hieronymum, non est leonum feritas immutata, sed rabies refrenata. Et non nocuerunt mihi : quia coram eo justitia inventa est in me, id est, vere coram Deo justus apparui, non viribus meis, sed ope gratiæ ejus. Hoc ad gloriam Dei Propheta adjecit, ad satisfaciendum regi, quod ejus edictum prævaricando, non incidit culpam. Ideo subdit : Sed et coram te, rex, delictum non feci : quia jussio regis fuit vitiosa totaliter, ideo ejus transgressio fuit opus virtutis, non vitium.
paras.en: [[6:21|And Daniel answering the king, said: O king, live for ever|Et Daniel regi respondens, ait : Rex, in æternum vive]]. He greets the one who honours him, and sweetly consoles him in his distress and his gentle speech. [[6:22|My God hath sent his angel|Deus meus misit angelum suum]], [[6:22|and hath shut up|et conclusit]] by the angel [[6:22|the mouths of the lions|ora leonum]], curbing their fierceness, their gaping jaws and their rage. Hence, according to Jerome, the fierceness of the lions was not changed, but their rage was curbed. [[6:22|And they have not hurt me|Et non nocuerunt mihi]]: [[6:22|forasmuch as before him justice hath been found in me|quia coram eo justitia inventa est in me]], that is, I have truly appeared just before God, not by my own strength but by the help of His grace. The Prophet added this to the glory of God, to satisfy the king that by transgressing his edict he had not fallen into fault. Therefore he adds: [[6:22|yea, and before thee, O king, I have done no offence|Sed et coram te, rex, delictum non feci]]; for since the king's command was wholly vicious, the transgression of it was a work of virtue, not a vice.

paras.t: Tunc rex vehementer gavisus est super eum, videlicet quo eum magis amavit, et quo eum sibi ac suo imperio utiliorem agnovit ; et Danielem præcepit educi de lacu, et nulla læsio inventa est in eo, quia credidit Deo suo fide completa : de qua in prima sua epistola ait Joannes, Hæc est victoria quæ vincit mundum, fides nostra ; et Paulus ad Hebræos, Sancti per fidem vicerunt regna, obturaverunt ora leonum. Denique Salvator : Omnia, inquit, possibilia sunt credenti ; et rursus : Si habueritis fidem sicut granum sinapis, dicetis huic monti, Tollere, et jacta te in mare, et obediet vobis.
paras.en: [[6:23|Then was the king exceeding glad for him|Tunc rex vehementer gavisus est super eum]], namely the more because he loved him, and because he recognized him as more useful to himself and to his empire; [[6:23|and he commanded that Daniel should be taken out of the den|et Danielem præcepit educi de lacu]], [[6:23|and no hurt was found in him, because he believed in his God|et nulla læsio inventa est in eo, quia credidit Deo suo]], with a complete faith; of which John says in his first epistle: [[1 John 5:4|this is the victory which overcameth the world: Our faith|Hæc est victoria quæ vincit mundum, fides nostra]] [the Douay-Rheims text reads "overcameth"]; and Paul to the Hebrews: The saints [[Heb 11:33|by faith conquered kingdoms|per fidem vicerunt regna]], [[Heb 11:33|stopped the mouths of lions|obturaverunt ora leonum]]. Lastly the Saviour: [[Mark 9:22|all things|Omnia]], he says, [[Mark 9:22|are possible to him that believeth|possibilia sunt credenti]]; and again: [[Matt 17:19|if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you shall say to this mountain|Si habueritis fidem sicut granum sinapis, dicetis huic monti]]: Be thou removed, and cast thyself into the sea, [[Luke 17:6|And it would obey you|et obediet vobis]] [the margin gives Matt. xvii, 19 and Luke xvii, 6; the words "removed, and cast thyself into the sea" are as in Matt 21:21 and Mark 11:23].

paras.t: Jubente autem rege, adducti sunt viri illi, qui accusaverunt Danielem ; et in lacum leonum missi sunt, et filii eorum et uxores eorum, quos, secundum Albertum, incentores scelerum habuerunt, vel saltem fautores seu cooperatores. Rex autem viso tanto miraculo, sumpsit audaciam, et æmuli Danielis timore dejecti sunt. Et non pervenerunt usque ad pavimentum laci. Secundum aliquos, per gradus erat introitus foveæ, in fundo pavimentum habentis. Donec arriperent eos leones, et omnia ossa eorum comminuerunt ; forte quod angelus auxit tunc leonum ferociam, ut Danielis liberatio miraculosior monstraretur, et Deus per eam amplius glorificaretur. Et aliqui dicunt Josephum dicere, quod accusatores Danielis dixerunt leones fuisse carnibus saturatos, et ideo Danielem non devorassent ; tunc rex jussit, ut ipsi leonibus carnes darent : quod quum facere attentarent, a leonibus (sicut jam dictum est) sunt discerpti. Potius autem videtur juxta textum, quod rex in pœnam talionis jussit eos tradi his feris : quia hoc justum erat secundum pœnam talionis, quæ in æquales potissime locum habet. Præterea Glossa ait : Nulla lex æquior est, quam necis artificem sua arte perire. Propter quod ait Psalmista : Lacum aperuit et effodit eum, et incidit in foveam quam fecit. Et in Proverbiis : In insidiis suis capientur iniqui. Et Ecclesiasticus quoque ait : Facienti nequissimum consilium, super ipsum devolvetur, et non cognoscet unde illi adveniet illusio. Sic Aman fuit affixus patibulo quod paraverat Mardochæo.
paras.en: [[6:24|And by the king's commandment, those men were brought that had accused Daniel|Jubente autem rege, adducti sunt viri illi, qui accusaverunt Danielem]]: [[6:24|and they were cast into the lions' den|et in lacum leonum missi sunt]], [[6:24|and their children, and their wives|et filii eorum et uxores eorum]], whom, according to Albert, they had had as instigators of their crimes, or at least as abettors or helpers. Now the king, having seen so great a miracle, took courage, and Daniel's rivals were cast down by fear. [[6:24|And they did not reach the bottom of the den|Et non pervenerunt usque ad pavimentum laci]] [*pavimentum*: the floor or pavement]. According to some, the entrance to the pit was by steps, and it had a pavement at the bottom. [[6:24|before the lions caught them|Donec arriperent eos leones]], [[6:24|and broke all their bones in pieces|et omnia ossa eorum comminuerunt]]; perhaps because the angel then increased the ferocity of the lions, so that the deliverance of Daniel might be shown to be the more miraculous, and God be the more glorified by it. And some say that Josephus says that Daniel's accusers said that the lions had been sated with meat, and that this was why they had not devoured Daniel; then the king ordered that they themselves should give the lions meat, and when they tried to do so they were torn to pieces by the lions, as has been said. But it seems rather, according to the text, that the king ordered them to be handed over to these beasts as a punishment in kind [*pœna talionis*, the law of retaliation, like for like]: for this was just according to the punishment in kind, which has place chiefly among equals. Moreover the Gloss says: No law is juster than that the contriver of death should perish by his own contrivance. For which reason the Psalmist says: [[Ps 7:16|He hath opened a pit and dug it: and he is fallen into the hole he made|Lacum aperuit et effodit eum, et incidit in foveam quam fecit]]. And in the Proverbs: [[Prov 11:6|the unjust shall be caught in their own snares|In insidiis suis capientur iniqui]]. And Ecclesiasticus too says: [[Ecclus 27:30|A mischievous counsel shall be rolled back upon the author, and he shall not know from whence it cometh to him|Facienti nequissimum consilium, super ipsum devolvetur, et non cognoscet unde illi adveniet]] [Denis's text ends with *illusio*: "whence the mockery cometh to him"]. So Aman was fastened to [[Esth 7:10|the gibbet, which he had prepared for Mardochai|patibulo quod paraverat Mardochæo]].

paras.t: Tunc rex Darius scripsit universis populis, tribubus et linguis habitantibus in universa terra sui imperii : Pax vobis multiplicetur. Verba ista in epistola Nabuchodonosor regis supra exposita sunt. A me ergo constitutum est decretum, ut in universo imperio et regno meo. Per regnum, intelligi potest specialiter regio Medorum, quæ propria fuit Dario ; per imperium vero, omnis provincia sibi subjecta.
paras.en: [[6:25|Then king Darius wrote to all people, tribes, and languages, dwelling in the whole earth|Tunc rex Darius scripsit universis populis, tribubus et linguis habitantibus in universa terra]] of his empire: [[6:25|PEACE be multiplied unto you|Pax vobis multiplicetur]]. These words were explained above, in the letter of king Nabuchodonosor[[Dan 3:98||]]. [[6:26|It is decreed by me, that in all my empire and my kingdom|A me ergo constitutum est decretum, ut in universo imperio et regno meo]]. By the kingdom may be understood in particular the country of the Medes, which was Darius's own; and by the empire, every province subject to him.

paras.t: Tremiscant et paveant Deum Danielis, qui licet sit omnium Deus per creationem, Danielis tamen, per tam singularem ejus in omnibus gubernationem, et ob specialem cultum ei a Daniele exhibitum. Tremor autem ad corpus, pavor ad animum pertinet, quando tantus est timor internus, quod redundat in corpus usque ad ejus concussionem. Ipse enim est Deus vivens per essentiam, et ipsa actualissima, supersubstantialis, supervoluptuosissima vita, et æternus in sæcula, quum sit ens simpliciter primum, independens et incommutabile prorsus ; et regnum ejus non dissipabitur, quoniam congregatio electorum ac Beatorum (qui sunt regnum Dei) manet perpetuo. De horum expositione nunc transeo, quia supra verba hæc habita sunt ac diffuse exposita. Et potestas ejus usque in æternum. Ipse enim est sua potestas. De quo ait Psalmista : Qui dominatur in virtute sua in æternum.
paras.en: That [[6:26|all men dread and fear the God of Daniel|Tremiscant et paveant Deum Danielis]], who, though He is the God of all by creation, is yet Daniel's by His so singular governing of him in all things, and because of the special worship shown Him by Daniel. Now trembling [*tremor*] belongs to the body, dread [*pavor*] to the soul, when the inward fear is so great that it overflows into the body, even to the point of shaking it. [[6:26|For he is the living|Ipse enim est Deus vivens]] God by essence, and the very life, most actual, supersubstantial, supremely delightful, [[6:26|and eternal God for ever|et æternus in sæcula]], since He is simply the first being, independent and wholly unchangeable; [[6:26|and his kingdom shall not be destroyed|et regnum ejus non dissipabitur]], since the congregation of the elect and the Blessed (who are the kingdom of God) remains for ever. I pass over the exposition of these now, because these words came above and were expounded at length[[Dan 4:31||]]. [[6:26|and his power shall be for ever|Et potestas ejus usque in æternum]]. For He is His own power. Of which the Psalmist says: [[Ps 65:7|Who by his power ruleth for ever|Qui dominatur in virtute sua in æternum]].

paras.t: Ipse est liberator, ab adversitatibus eruendo, atque salvator, prospera beatitudinemque præstando, faciens signa et mirabilia : signa, in quantum sunt divinæ potentiæ supernaturaliter ostensiva ; et mirabilia, quia cernentes in admirationem convertunt ; in cælo et in terra : per quæ duo extrema, intelligenda est omnis creatura, quæ Creatori ad nutum obedit. Quomodo enim non plenum dominium super universa haberet, qui cuncta de nihilo fecit ? Qui liberavit Danielem de lacu leonum. Istam tam pulchram epistolam Darius rex, ut reor, Daniele eum plenius edocente de Deo, dictavit.
paras.en: [[6:27|He is the deliverer|Ipse est liberator]], by rescuing from adversities, [[6:27|and saviour|atque salvator]], by granting prosperity and beatitude, [[6:27|doing signs and wonders|faciens signa et mirabilia]]: signs, inasmuch as they supernaturally show forth the divine power; and wonders, because they turn those who see them to wonder; [[6:27|in heaven, and in earth|in cælo et in terra]]: by these two extremes every creature is to be understood, which obeys the Creator at His nod. For how should He not have full dominion over all things, who made all things out of nothing? [[6:27|who hath delivered Daniel out of the lions' den|Qui liberavit Danielem de lacu leonum]]. This so beautiful letter king Darius dictated, I think, with Daniel instructing him more fully about God.

paras.t: Porro Daniel perseveravit usque ad regnum Darii et regnum Cyri Persæ. Secundum Hieronymum, non est sensus quod solum vixit usque ad regnum Cyri, scilicet usque ad principium regni ejus super Medos et Persas : nam infra habetur, quod anno tertio Cyri regis Persarum verbum revelatum est Danieli. Sed sensus est quod usque ad primum annum monarchiæ atque imperii Darii regis, Daniel mansit in Chaldæa in potentia et honore, quousque scilicet Darius regnum Chaldæorum destruxit, et monarchiam adeptus est, qui tunc Danielem duxit in Mediam : quo defuncto, adhuc mansit Daniel sub Cyro rege per aliquot annos, qui Cyrus Dario successit in regno atque imperio.
paras.en: [[6:28|Now Daniel continued unto the reign of Darius, and the reign of Cyrus, the Persian|Porro Daniel perseveravit usque ad regnum Darii et regnum Cyri Persæ]]. According to Jerome, the sense is not that he lived only until the reign of Cyrus, that is, until the beginning of his reign over the Medes and Persians, for it is said further on that [[Dan 10:1|In the third year of Cyrus, king of the Persians, a word was revealed to Daniel|anno tertio Cyri regis Persarum verbum revelatum est Danieli]]. But the sense is that until the first year of the monarchy and empire of king Darius, Daniel remained in Chaldea in power and honour, that is, until Darius destroyed the kingdom of the Chaldeans and obtained the monarchy, who then took Daniel into Media; and after his death Daniel remained under king Cyrus for some years more, which Cyrus succeeded Darius in the kingdom and empire.

5.title: Expositio capituli quinti: Balthasar rex fecit grande convivium optimatibus
5.title_en: Exposition of the fifth chapter: Baltasar the king made a great feast for his nobles

paras.t: Balthasar rex fecit grande convivium. Quemadmodum in Scholastica historia edocetur, Daniel mutat hic historiæ ordinem, ita quod visio hic descripta, non contigit immediate post præcedentem, nec duas sequentes præcessit : imo licet sit quarta secundum ordinem libri, tamen secundum ordinem temporis, et juxta historiam, sexta est. Unde Hieronymus in prologo Habacuc prophetæ, sextam appellat eamdem. Porro secundum Albertum, in ista parte ostenditur ruina regni mundi per regnum Christi, in destructione Babylonici regni. Et ut aliqui dicunt, in hac visione ostenditur eminentia regni Christi et justorum, ad regnum Antichristi et malorum. Verumtamen in isto capitulo non est ad litteram sermo de Christo vel Antichristo. Ideo verba expositorum istorum intelligenda sunt quantum ad spiritualem ac mysticam designationem et interpretationem.
paras.en: [[5:1|Baltasar, the king, made a great feast|Balthasar rex fecit grande convivium]]. As is taught in the Scholastic History, Daniel here changes the order of the history, so that the vision described here did not happen immediately after the preceding one, nor did it come before the two that follow: indeed, though it is the fourth in the order of the book, yet in the order of time, and according to the history, it is the sixth. Hence Jerome, in the prologue to the prophet Habacuc, calls this same one the sixth. Further, according to Albert, in this part is shown the ruin of the kingdom of the world by the kingdom of Christ, in the destruction of the Babylonian kingdom. And, as some say, in this vision is shown the pre-eminence of the kingdom of Christ and of the just over the kingdom of Antichrist and of the wicked. Yet in this chapter there is no talk of Christ or of Antichrist according to the letter. Therefore the words of these expositors are to be understood of the spiritual and mystical signification and interpretation.

paras.t: Primo demum est inquirendum, quis sit Balthasar iste, qui infra in hoc ipso capitulo vocatur filius Nabuchodonosor regis, de quo præcedenti capitulo facta est mentio. Propter quod, ut refert Hieronymus, vulgo creditum fuit a pluribus, quod immediate fuisset filius ejus. Sed hujus oppositum certum est. Et B. Hieronymus cum aliis doctoribus tam Hebræis quam Latinis in hoc concordantibus, probat quod fuit filius Evilmerodach filii Nabuchodonosor regis.
paras.en: First, then, we must inquire who this Balthasar is, who further on in this very chapter is called the son of king Nabuchodonosor, of whom mention was made in the preceding chapter. For this reason, as Jerome relates, it was commonly believed by many that he had been his son in the first degree. But the opposite of this is certain. And blessed Jerome, with other doctors, Hebrew as well as Latin, who agree in this, proves that he was the son of Evilmerodach, the son of king Nabuchodonosor.

paras.t: Nihilo minus de catalogo regum Babylonis, et ordine successionis eorum, magna est inter exponentes distantia. Quidam enim, quos sequitur Lyra, affirmant quod Evilmerodach immediate regnavit post Nabuchodonosor, et quod post Evilmerodach immediate regnavit Balthasar filius ejus, de quo nunc sermo. Sed dictum istorum, ab Hieronymo quantum ad hoc reprobatur, quod dicunt Balthasar statim post Evilmerodach imperasse. Ait namque Hieronymus : Juxta Berosum qui Chaldæam scripsit historiam, et Josephum qui sequitur Berosum, post Nabuchodonosor qui regnavit annis quadraginta tribus, successit in regnum Evilmerodach, de quo scribit Jeremias quod primo anno regni sui eduxit Joachin regem Juda de carcere. Post Evilmerodach, secundum Josephum, regnavit filius ejus Neglisar, et post hunc filius ejus Labosardach, post quem regnavit filius ejus Balthasar. Hunc modum Albertus secutus est; sed in Scholastica historia longe aliter dicitur. Sic enim dicitur ibi : Et mortuus est Nabuchodonosor magnus, et regnavit pro eo Nabuchodonosor filius ejus, qui super lapides grandes instar montis evectos plantavit arbores, ac hortum qui suspensilis dicebatur, eo quod uxor ejus in finibus Mediæ nutrita, regionem suam a longe videre desideraret : quem Megasthenes historiographus asserit fortitudine et actuum magnitudine Herculem transcendisse. Quo mortuo, regnavit pro eo Evilmerodach frater ejus : qui Evilmerodach habuit tres filios, scilicet Neglisar et Labosardach jam præfatos, et Balthasar, ad quem, post regna fratrum, devolutum est regnum. — Quid horum sit verius, sapientiori committo. Constat tamen ex his, quod concordantia aliquorum, dicentium quod Evilmerodach et Balthasar fuerunt iidem numero cum Neglisar et Labosardach, eo quod ambo binomii fuerint, non procedat juxta prædicta, nec sit concordantia vera, quia secundum eam non diceretur quod quatuor isti sibi invicem per temporum intervalla successissent in regno.
paras.en: Nevertheless, about the list of the kings of Babylon and the order of their succession there is great disagreement among the expositors. For some, whom Lyra follows, affirm that Evilmerodach reigned immediately after Nabuchodonosor, and that immediately after Evilmerodach reigned Balthasar his son, of whom we are now speaking. But what these say is rejected by Jerome on this point, that they say Balthasar ruled straight after Evilmerodach. For Jerome says: According to Berosus, who wrote the history of Chaldea, and Josephus, who follows Berosus, after Nabuchodonosor, who reigned forty-three years, Evilmerodach succeeded to the kingdom, of whom Jeremias writes that in the first year of his reign he brought Joachin king of Juda out of prison[[Jer 52:31||]]. After Evilmerodach, according to Josephus, his son Neglisar reigned, and after him his son Labosardach, after whom his son Balthasar reigned. Albert has followed this account; but in the Scholastic History it is told very differently. For there it says: And Nabuchodonosor the Great died, and in his stead reigned Nabuchodonosor his son, who planted trees upon great stones raised up like a mountain, and a garden which was called the hanging garden, because his wife, who had been brought up in the borders of Media, longed to see her own country from afar: who, as the historian Megasthenes asserts, surpassed Hercules in strength and in the greatness of his deeds. When he died, Evilmerodach his brother reigned in his stead: and this Evilmerodach had three sons, namely Neglisar and Labosardach, already mentioned, and Balthasar, to whom, after the reigns of his brothers, the kingdom passed. Which of these is the truer I leave to one wiser. Yet it is clear from these that the harmonizing of some, who say that Evilmerodach and Balthasar were the same in number [that is, the very same persons] as Neglisar and Labosardach, because both had two names, does not hold good according to what has been said, nor is it a true harmony, since according to it it could not be said that these four succeeded one another in the kingdom over intervals of time.

paras.t: Itaque, Balthasar rex Babylonis fecit suis grande convivium. Sed mirum apparet quare hoc fecerit, quum tempore hujus convivii civitas sua fuerit a Persis ac Medis obsessa. Ad quod quidam respondent, quod quia Jeremias prædixit septuaginta annis evolutis finiendum regnum Babylonis, atque solvendam Judæorum captivitatem de Babylone, Balthasar putans annos illos fluxisse, nec tamen Judæos a sua jurisdictione solutos, æstimavit vaticinium Jeremiæ cassatum, atque exsultans, diis suis gratias egit; Judæorumque spei insultans, vasa templi Dei ad suam præcepit mensam portari, sicut dicetur inferius. Hoc dictum Hieronymus, Scholastica quoque historia, fabulam vocant. Imo illa testatur Historia : Sane illa annorum septuagena nondum fluxerat, sed septima decas jam currebat, id est septimus denarius. In septuaginta enim sunt septem denarii, et ultimus denarius illorum annorum tunc erat, secundum Historiam istam. Præterea Historia ista aliam hujus convivii rationem assignans, sic ait : Secundum Josephum, solennitas in Babylone fuerat instituta ob urbis defensionem : ad quam solennitatem majores convenerant. Denique in Judith historia legitur Ozias princeps plebis Israel, obsessa urbe sua Bethulia, fecisse cunctis presbyteris cœnam magnam.
paras.en: So then, [[5:1|Baltasar, the king|Balthasar rex]] of Babylon [[5:1|made a great feast|fecit suis grande convivium]] for his own. But it seems a wonder why he did this, since at the time of this feast his city was besieged by the Persians and the Medes. To this some answer that, because Jeremias foretold that when seventy years had run their course the kingdom of Babylon would be ended and the captivity of the Jews in Babylon loosed[[Jer 25:12||]][[Jer 29:10||]], Balthasar, thinking that those years had run out and yet that the Jews had not been freed from his jurisdiction, judged the prophecy of Jeremias to have come to nothing, and in his exultation gave thanks to his gods; and, mocking the hope of the Jews, ordered the vessels of the temple of God to be carried to his table, as will be said below. This saying Jerome, and the Scholastic History too, call a fable. Indeed that History bears witness: Truly the seventy of years had not yet run out, but the seventh decade was already running, that is, the seventh ten. For in seventy there are seven tens, and the last ten of those years was then running, according to that History. Moreover, that History, assigning another reason for this feast, says thus: According to Josephus, a solemn festival had been instituted in Babylon for the defence of the city, and the great men had come together for this festival. Lastly, in the history of Judith we read that Ozias, the prince of the people of Israel, when his city Bethulia was besieged, made a great supper for all the ancients[[Jdt 6:19||]][[Jdt 6:20||]].

paras.t: Porro quod ait, optimatibus suis mille, dupliciter intelligi potest : primo, ut ponatur ibi certus numerus optimatum ; secundo, ut per numerum determinatum insinuetur numerus indeterminatus, quod scilicet multi valde fuerunt. Dicuntque aliqui, omnes magnos Babylonici imperii principes convenisse in Babylonem, ut defenderent civitatem contra Cyrum et Darium reges eam tunc obsidentes. Et unusquisque secundum suam bibebat ætatem, id est secundum quod suæ congruebat ætati : ita quod non cogebatur bibere ultra vires, quemadmodum in convivio Assueri factum scribitur, quum dicitur : Non erat qui nolentes cogeret ad bibendum ; sed sic rex statuerat, ut sumeret unusquisque quod vellet. Secundo, et melius, ut apparet, exponitur secundum Glossam, quod ideo unusquisque secundum suam ætatem bibisse dicatur, quia secundum ætates suas erant in convivio collocati, videlicet seniores in altioribus locis. Et ut dicit Albertus, ætas intelligitur ibi non vitæ, sed dignitatis adeptæ, quia ex tunc honor eis debebatur : ita ut qui diutius fuerunt in dignitatibus atque officiis, seniores vocentur, sicut in religionibus qui prius venerunt, seniores dicuntur. In Actis quoque dicitur Jacobus Major, quia vocatione ad apostolatum fuit alio Jacobo prior.
paras.en: Further, what he says, [[5:1|for a thousand of his nobles|optimatibus suis mille]], can be understood in two ways: first, that a definite number of nobles is set down there; secondly, that by a determinate number an indeterminate number is suggested, namely that they were very many. And some say that all the great princes of the Babylonian empire had come together in Babylon, to defend the city against the kings Cyrus and Darius, who were then besieging it. [[5:1|and every one drank according to his age|Et unusquisque secundum suam bibebat ætatem]], that is, according to what suited his age: so that no one was compelled to drink beyond his strength, as is written to have been done at the feast of Assuerus, where it is said: [[Esth 1:8|Neither was there any one to compel them to drink that were not willing|Non erat qui nolentes cogeret ad bibendum]]; [[Esth 1:8|but as the king had appointed|sed sic rex statuerat]], [[Esth 1:8|that every man might take what he would|ut sumeret unusquisque quod vellet]]. Secondly, and better, as it seems, it is explained according to the Gloss that each is said to have drunk according to his age because they were placed at the feast according to their ages, that is, the elders in the higher places. And, as Albert says, age is understood there not of life but of dignity attained, because from that time honour was owed them: so that those who have been longer in dignities and offices are called elders, just as in religious orders those who came first are called seniors. In the Acts, too, James is called the Greater, because he was called to the apostleship before the other James.

paras.t: Præcepit autem jam temulentus rex, id est Balthasar ebrius factus : quum tamen ebrietas regi maxime disconveniat. Rex enim a regendo vocatur, et ebrietas regiminis impedit bonitatem. Ideo in Proverbiorum libro inducitur : Noli regibus dare vinum, quia nullum secretum ubi regnat ebrietas. Et Osee ait : Fornicatio et ebrietas et vinum auferunt cor. Et alibi : Væ terræ cujus rex puer est. Et mirum quod in tali obsidione sobrietatem reliquerit, quum tunc potissime consilio sano eguerit, nisi forte in fortitudine urbis confidens, putaverit eam inexpugnabilem esse. Ut afferrentur per suos ministros vasa cultus divini aurea et argentea quæ asportaverat Nabuchodonosor, pater ejus, non proximus, sed remotus. Est enim consuetudo Scripturæ, etiam avos, proavos et atavos, dicere patres, imo et remotiores, præsertim notabiles et famosos, sicut in libris Regum Asa et Ezechias filii David vocantur. De templo quod fuit in Jerusalem. Posuitque ea in templo dei sui in Babylone, ut in principio dictum est. Ut biberent in eis rex ipsemet, scilicet Balthasar, et optimates ejus, et uxores, et concubinæ. Quod prorsus sacrilegum fuit.
paras.en: [[5:2|And being now drunk, he commanded|Præcepit autem jam temulentus rex]], that is, Balthasar, having become drunk: though drunkenness is most unbecoming to a king. For a king (*rex*) is named from ruling (*regendo*), and drunkenness hinders the goodness of rule. Therefore it is set down in the book of Proverbs: [[Prov 31:4|give not wine to kings: because there is no secret where drunkenness reigneth|Noli regibus dare vinum, quia nullum secretum ubi regnat ebrietas]]. And Osee says: [[Osee 4:11|Fornication, and wine, and drunkenness, take away the understanding|Fornicatio et ebrietas et vinum auferunt cor]]. And elsewhere: [[Eccles 10:16|Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child|Væ terræ cujus rex puer est]]. And it is a wonder that in such a siege he abandoned sobriety, when he then most of all needed sound counsel; unless perhaps, trusting in the strength of the city, he thought it impregnable.
