[[5:2|that they should bring|Ut afferrentur]], by his servants, [[5:2|the vessels|vasa]] of divine worship, [[5:2|of gold and silver, which Nabuchodonosor, his father, had brought away|aurea et argentea quæ asportaverat Nabuchodonosor, pater ejus]]: not his nearest father, but a remote one. For it is the custom of Scripture to call grandfathers, great-grandfathers and great-great-grandfathers fathers, and even more remote ones, especially notable and famous ones, as in the books of Kings Asa and Ezechias are called sons of David[[3 Kings 15:11||]][[4 Kings 18:3||]]. [[5:2|out of the temple, that was in Jerusalem|De templo quod fuit in Jerusalem]]. And he put them in the temple of his god in Babylon, as was said at the beginning[[Dan 1:2||]]. [[5:2|might drink in them|Ut biberent in eis]]: [[5:2|the king|rex]] himself, namely Balthasar, [[5:2|and his nobles, and his wives, and his concubines|et optimates ejus, et uxores, et concubinæ]]. Which was utterly sacrilegious.

paras.t: Unde Nabuchodonosor vasa hæc aliqualiter secundum suam perfidiam honoravit, ea in domo dei sui ponendo ; iste vero totaliter ea contempsit, dum ea non solum usui applicavit humano, quantum ad se, sed et servis et conjugibus, imo et scortis ea apposuit ad utendum : ideo statim eum secuta est ultio Dei. Et tamen, ut dicit Albertus, istud quotidie fit, quando thesauri domus Dei et ecclesiastici reditus in scortorum convertuntur abusum. Quid autem hæc vasa mystice signent, dictum est primo capitulo.
paras.en: Thus Nabuchodonosor in some way honoured these vessels, after his own unbelief, by putting them in the house of his god; but this man despised them altogether, since he not only put them to human use as far as he himself was concerned, but also set them before servants and wives, and even harlots, to use: therefore the vengeance of God followed him at once. And yet, as Albert says, this is done every day, when the treasures of the house of God and the revenues of the Church are turned to the abuse of harlots. What these vessels signify mystically was said in the first chapter[[Dan 1:2||]].

paras.t: Bibebant vinum ex vasis his, et laudabant deos suos aureos et argenteos, æreos, ferreos, ligneos et lapideos. Quod dupliciter accipi potest. Primo, quod laudabant deos, quorum imagines erant de auro vel argento, ære, ferro, ligno aut saxis. Secundo, quod idola de his materiis facta laudaverint, putantes aliquid numinis esse in eis, prout Augustinus in libro octavo de Civitate Dei commemorat Trismegistum dixisse : Statuas dico animatas, sensu et spiritu plenas. Nempe, ut Valerius Maximus refert, quidam gentilium non idola templorum, sed deos per idola præsentatos, quidam vero idola ipsa colebant. De his diis ait in epistola Jeremias : Videbitis in Babylone deos aureos et argenteos, lapideos et ligneos portari in humeris. Secundum Hieronymum autem, laudant deos suos, insultantes Deo Judæorum, quod diis suis sibi victoriam tribuentibus, bibant in vasis Dei. Ad ostentationem quoque magnificentiæ suæ, Balthasar vasa Dei ita tractavit.
paras.en: [[5:4|They drank wine|Bibebant vinum]] from these vessels, [[5:4|and praised their gods of gold, and of silver, of brass, of iron, and of wood, and of stone|et laudabant deos suos aureos et argenteos, æreos, ferreos, ligneos et lapideos]]. This can be taken in two ways. First, that they praised the gods whose images were of gold or silver, brass, iron, wood or stone. Secondly, that they praised idols made of these materials, thinking that there was something of divinity in them, as Augustine, in the eighth book of the City of God, records that Trismegistus said: Statues, I say, animated, full of sense and spirit. Indeed, as Valerius Maximus relates, some of the Gentiles worshipped not the idols of the temples but the gods made present through the idols, while others worshipped the idols themselves. Of these gods Jeremias says in his epistle: [[Bar 6:3|you shall see in Babylon gods of gold, and of silver, and of stone, and of wood borne upon shoulders|Videbitis in Babylone deos aureos et argenteos, lapideos et ligneos portari in humeris]]. But according to Jerome, they praise their gods, mocking the God of the Jews, because, their gods having given them the victory, they drink from the vessels of God. Balthasar also treated the vessels of God in this way to make a show of his own magnificence.

paras.t: Insuper, secundum Hieronymum et Albertum, aurum sapientiam sæculi signat ; argentum, eloquentiam ; æs, carmina poetarum ; ferrum, ligamenta syllogismorum ; lignum et lapides, ineptas adinventiones ac faciles ad solvendum, duras tamen propter obstinationem errantium. Itaque qui ista immoderanter honorant, aut ista habentes propter ea, quasi adorant et laudant ac colunt aurum, argentum, æs, ferrum, ligna et saxa.
paras.en: Moreover, according to Jerome and Albert, gold signifies the wisdom of the world; silver, eloquence; brass, the songs of the poets; iron, the bonds of syllogisms; wood and stones, foolish inventions, easy to refute, yet hard because of the obstinacy of those who err. And so those who honour these things immoderately, or those who possess them, for their sake, as it were adore and praise and worship gold, silver, brass, iron, wood and stones.

paras.t: In eadem hora apparuerunt digiti, id est similitudines digitorum, quasi manus hominis. Non dicit, Manus, sed, Quasi manus : quia nec vere digiti, nec vere manus fuerunt, sed eorum effigies. Aliquid tamen reale apparuit in vigilia clare ad oculum, cujus materia ad formam digitorum ac manus hominis fuit redacta : quod totum angelico ministerio factum est. Et sicut præcedenti capitulo dicebatur, Quum adhuc sermo esset in ore regis, vox de cœlo ruit ; ita nunc dicitur, In eadem hora : ut utrobique intelligatur ob Dei blasphemiam illata vindicta, secundum Hieronymum. Tamen quia pœna Nabuchodonosor fuit terminanda, et ipse per pœnitentiam restituendus in regnum, idcirco in ejus pœnæ denuntiatione vox desuper ruit. Hic vero ob perpetuam rei memoriam scribitur, quia rex Balthasar fuit necandus, ejusque regnum irreparabiliter dissipandum, propter tantum Dei et vasorum ejus contemptum. Ex quo sequitur, quam temerarium sit, res Deo consecratas usibus applicare humanis, quum et Apostolus dicat : Si quis templum Dei violaverit, disperdet illum Deus. Scribentis contra candelabrum, id est ex opposito ejus, ut scriptura lumine candelæ directius tacta, clarius videretur a rege ac suis. Unde apparet, quod in cœna id accidit. In superficie parietis aulæ regiæ : ut rex adverteret scripturam pertinere ad se, quia et ex adverso ipsius est exarata.
paras.en: [[5:5|In the same hour there appeared fingers|In eadem hora apparuerunt digiti]], that is, likenesses of fingers, [[5:5|as it were of the hand of a man|quasi manus hominis]]. He does not say, *A hand*, but, *As it were a hand*: because they were neither truly fingers nor truly a hand, but their likeness. Yet something real appeared, clearly to the eye, to one awake, whose matter had been shaped into the form of the fingers and hand of a man: all of which was done by the ministry of angels. And as in the preceding chapter it was said, [[Dan 4:28|while the word was yet in the king's mouth, a voice came down from heaven|Quum adhuc sermo esset in ore regis, vox de cœlo ruit]], so now it is said, [[5:5|In the same hour|In eadem hora]]: so that in both places vengeance is understood to have been brought on for blasphemy against God, according to Jerome. Yet because the punishment of Nabuchodonosor was to have an end, and he was to be restored to his kingdom through penance, therefore at the announcing of his punishment a voice came down from above. But here it is written, for a perpetual memorial of the thing, because king Balthasar was to be slain, and his kingdom irreparably scattered, for so great a contempt of God and of His vessels. From this it follows how rash it is to put things consecrated to God to human uses, since the Apostle too says: [[1 Cor 3:17|if any man violate the temple of God, him shall God destroy|Si quis templum Dei violaverit, disperdet illum Deus]]. [[5:5|writing over against the candlestick|Scribentis contra candelabrum]], that is, opposite it, so that the writing, struck more directly by the light of the candle, might be seen more clearly by the king and his company. Hence it appears that this happened at supper. [[5:5|upon the surface of the wall of the king's palace|In superficie parietis aulæ regiæ]]: so that the king might perceive that the writing concerned himself, since it was traced right opposite him.

paras.t: Et rex adspiciebat articulos manus scribentis. Secundum Scholasticam historiam, incertum est an etiam adstantes viderint manum seu digitos. Et quidam super hæc verba ait : Hic non dicitur, quod alii viderint : ex quo videtur, quod non erat ibi manus scribentis secundum exsistentiam, quia talia communiter videntur ab omnibus adsistentibus ; sed erat ibi talis apparitio in oculis regis, et sententia in pariete scribebatur, ministerio tamen angelico. Oppositum autem istius jam dictum est : ideo magis credendum, quod ibi aliquid reale extra oculum fuit ac videbatur. Nec verum est, quod talia communiter a cunctis videntur : imo magis contrarium accidit, ut scilicet quæ angelico ministerio præsentantur per corpora ab eis assumpta sive formata, non æque ab omnibus videantur, sed ab eis dumtaxat propter quos talia specialiter exhibentur : nam et talia visum immutant, secundum angeli voluntatem. Frequenter etiam defuncti et spiritus mali aut boni, realiter vigilanti apparent in corpore quodam assumpto, nec tamen cunctis qui adsunt, apparent.
paras.en: [[5:5|and the king beheld the joints of the hand that wrote|Et rex adspiciebat articulos manus scribentis]]. According to the Scholastic History, it is uncertain whether those standing by also saw the hand or the fingers. And someone says on these words: It is not said here that others saw it; from which it seems that there was no hand writing there in real existence, since such things are commonly seen by all who are present; but there was such an appearance in the eyes of the king, and the sentence was written on the wall, though by the ministry of an angel. But the opposite of this has already been stated: and so it is rather to be believed that something real was there, outside the eye, and was seen. Nor is it true that such things are commonly seen by all: rather the contrary happens, namely that things presented by the ministry of angels through bodies assumed or formed by them are not seen equally by all, but only by those for whose sake they are especially shown: for such things also alter the sight, according to the angel's will. Often, too, the dead, and spirits evil or good, really appear to one who is awake in some assumed body, and yet do not appear to all who are present.

paras.t: Tunc facies regis commutata est, id est, in pallorem versa præ timore, ex quo sanguis amicus naturæ, decurrebat ad cor in ejus subsidium. Hinc in Ecclesiastico dicitur : Cor hominis immutat faciem ejus, sive in bono, sive in malo. Unde hujusmodi pallor quandoque timorem, quandoque dolorem cordis demonstrat. Siquidem secundo Machabæorum libro scribitur : Facies et color immutatus declarabant internum animi dolorem. Et cogitationes ejus conturbabant eum. Quadam enim ratiocinatione seu mentis discursu excogitare nitebatur, quid res tam inconsueta signaret, et cogitavit quod aliquid mali prætenderet : sicut et patri suo Nabuchodonosor contigit. At vero, secundum Albertum, cogitationes, quasi coagitationes dicuntur, quando mens hominis multa revolvit : quod naturale est homini conturbato, secundum illud in Job : Cogitationes meæ variæ succedunt sibi, et mens in diversa rapitur. Et compages renum ejus, ubi superiora inferioribus junguntur, solvebantur aliqualiter, non totaliter, ab invicem, utpote ab habitudine naturali, ita quod partim vires amisit. Passiones enim fiunt cum corporali transmutatione : et si fuerint multum intensæ præfatæ passiones timoris sive doloris, magnam valde improportionem harmoniæ in corpore pariunt, sicque compago renum dissolvitur. Et genua ejus ad se invicem collidebantur. Timor namque intensus in corde, facit tremorem in corpore. Sanguine etenim a membris fugiente ad cor, membra frigescunt ac tremunt.
paras.en: [[5:6|Then was the king's countenance changed|Tunc facies regis commutata est]], that is, turned pale for fear, because of which the blood, the friend of nature, ran down to the heart to help it. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 13:31|The heart of a man changeth his countenance, either for good, or for evil.|Cor hominis immutat faciem ejus, sive in bono, sive in malo]] Hence a pallor of this kind shows sometimes fear, sometimes sorrow of heart. For in the second book of Machabees it is written: [[2 Mach 3:16|his face, and the changing of his colour, declared the inward sorrow of his mind|Facies et color immutatus declarabant internum animi dolorem]]. [[5:6|and his thoughts troubled him|Et cogitationes ejus conturbabant eum]]. For by a kind of reasoning, or running to and fro of the mind, he strove to think out what so unaccustomed a thing might mean, and he thought that it foretold something evil: as happened also to his father Nabuchodonosor[[Dan 4:2||]]. But according to Albert, thoughts (*cogitationes*) are so called as being *coagitationes* [stirrings-together], when a man's mind turns many things over: which is natural to a man who is troubled, according to that in Job: [[Job 20:2|various thoughts succeed one another in me, and my mind is hurried away to different things|Cogitationes meæ variæ succedunt sibi, et mens in diversa rapitur]]. [[5:6|and the joints of his loins|Et compages renum ejus]], where the upper parts are joined to the lower, [[5:6|were loosed|solvebantur]] from one another in some measure, not wholly, that is, from their natural disposition, so that he partly lost his strength. For the passions come about with a bodily change: and if the aforesaid passions of fear or sorrow are very intense, they produce a very great disproportion of harmony in the body, and so the joint of the loins is loosed. [[5:6|and his knees struck one against the other|Et genua ejus ad se invicem collidebantur]]. For intense fear in the heart causes trembling in the body; since, as the blood flees from the limbs to the heart, the limbs grow cold and tremble.

paras.t: Exclamavit itaque rex fortiter ex ingenti affectu, ut magnitudo clamoris, magnitudinem interioris turbationis signaret. Naturale est enim homini angustiato ac territo, exclamare, juxta illud Baruch : Anima in angustiis et spiritus anxius clamat ad te, Domine. Ut introducerent ministri sui qui aderant, qui etiam scripturam viderunt, saltem postquam manus evanuit, secundum Scholasticam historiam, magos, Chaldæos et aruspices. Quid istis significetur nominibus, in expositione secundi capituli patet. Utque Glossa testatur, antiquum gentis suæ sectatur errorem, magos vocans, non Dei Prophetam. Et proloquens, id est procul ac publice loquens, rex, ait sapientibus Babylonis : Quicumque legerit scripturam hanc, et interpretationem ejus manifestam mihi fecerit, purpura vestietur, et torquem auream habebit in collo. Istud, secundum Glossam, summæ fuit dignitatis. Insuper Glossa dicit : Apud Judæos unctio fecit reges ; apud gentiles autem quatuor insignia, scilicet purpura, fibula, annulus, diadema ; unumque horum sine aliis concessum, non dabat honoris regii plenitudinem, sed participium. Simul enim accepta, regium designabant honorem perfecte ; singula autem per se accepta, vel quædam eorum simul, designabant aliquam regii honoris participationem. Ideo subditur : et tertius in regno meo erit. Quod dupliciter posse intelligi, breviter innuit Hieronymus, dicens : Vel tertius post me, vel unus de tribus principibus. Quidam sequuntur primum sensum, quod scilicet tertius a rege esset in honore. Scholastica historia et Albertus secuti sunt sensum secundum, dicendo : Unus erit trium principum præsidentium satrapis seu mille optimatibus.
paras.en: [[5:7|And the king cried out aloud|Exclamavit itaque rex fortiter]], from his great emotion, so that the greatness of the cry might show the greatness of the turmoil within. For it is natural for a man in anguish and terror to cry out, according to that of Baruch: [[Bar 3:1|the soul in anguish, and the troubled spirit crieth to thee|Anima in angustiis et spiritus anxius clamat ad te]], O Lord. [[5:7|to bring in|Ut introducerent]] (that is, that his servants who were there should bring them in; and these too saw the writing, at least after the hand had vanished, according to the Scholastic History) [[5:7|the wise men, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers|magos, Chaldæos et aruspices]]. What is signified by these names is plain from the exposition of the second chapter[[Dan 2:2||]] [the margin gives Dan. i, 2; the names are treated at Dan 2:2]. And, as the Gloss testifies, he follows the ancient error of his nation, calling the magi, not the Prophet of God. [[5:7|And the king spoke|Et proloquens]], that is, speaking out, far and wide and openly [Denis takes the *pro-* of *proloquens* as *procul*, "at a distance"], [[5:7|and said to the wise men of Babylon|rex, ait sapientibus Babylonis]]: [[5:7|Whosoever shall read this writing, and shall make known to me the interpretation thereof, shall be clothed with purple, and shall have a golden chain on his neck|Quicumque legerit scripturam hanc, et interpretationem ejus manifestam mihi fecerit, purpura vestietur, et torquem auream habebit in collo]]. This, according to the Gloss, was of the highest dignity. Moreover the Gloss says: Among the Jews anointing made kings; but among the Gentiles four insignia did, namely the purple, the brooch, the ring and the diadem; and one of these granted without the others did not give the fulness of royal honour, but a share in it. For taken together they signified royal honour perfectly; but taken one by one, or some of them together, they signified some share in royal honour. Therefore there is added: [[5:7|and shall be the third man in my kingdom|et tertius in regno meo erit]]. That this can be understood in two ways Jerome briefly suggests, saying: Either third after me, or one of three princes. Some follow the first sense, namely that he would be third from the king in honour. The Scholastic History and Albert followed the second sense, saying: He shall be one of the three princes set over the satraps, that is, over the thousand nobles.

paras.t: Porro torques dabatur in signum quod collum non erat solutum ad insipienter loquendum. Aurum enim sapientiam denotat, sicut in Proverbiis jubetur : Audi, fili mi, disciplinam patris tui, ut addatur gratia capiti tuo, et torques collo tuo. Purpura autem regia vestis est, qua uti non licuit nisi regibus, nisi de eorum licentia alii uterentur.
paras.en: Further, the chain was given as a sign that the neck was not loosed to speak foolishly. For gold denotes wisdom, as we are bidden in Proverbs: [[Prov 1:8|My son, hear the instruction of thy father|Audi, fili mi, disciplinam patris tui]], [[Prov 1:9|That grace may be added to thy head, and a chain of gold to thy neck|ut addatur gratia capiti tuo, et torques collo tuo]]. The purple, again, is a royal garment, which none but kings were allowed to wear, unless others wore it by their leave.

paras.t: Insuper illa scriptura sacram designat Scripturam, homines præmonentem de futuris suppliciis. Legit autem et interpretatur, qui de Scripturis monita profert salutis. Iste induitur purpura, id est devotionali animæ ornamento, in devotione passionis ac sanguinis Christi, de quo in Isaia habetur : Quare rubrum est indumentum tuum ? Accipit quoque et auream torquem, id est sapientialem discretionem loquendi. Hinc Ecclesiasticus ait : Injice pedem tuum in compedes illius, et in torques illius collum tuum.
paras.en: Moreover, that writing signifies holy Scripture, which forewarns men of punishments to come. And he reads and interprets it who brings forth from the Scriptures warnings of salvation. Such a one is clothed with purple, that is, with the devout adornment of the soul, in devotion to the passion and blood of Christ, of whom we have in Isaias: [[Is 63:2|Why then is thy apparel red|Quare rubrum est indumentum tuum]]? He receives also the golden chain, that is, a wise discretion in speaking. Hence Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 6:25|Put thy feet into her fetters, and thy neck into her chains|Injice pedem tuum in compedes illius, et in torques illius collum tuum]].

paras.t: Tunc ingressi omnes sapientes regis, non potuerunt scripturam legere. Scripta enim fuit Hebraice. Etiam quamvis verba legere potuissent, sensum tamen exponere sine revelatione non valuissent. Nam verba exarata ex humana institutione, sensum a Deo intentum non habuerunt. Nec interpretationem ejus indicare regi. Quo figuratur, quod sacra Scriptura nequit intelligi, nisi eodem spiritu quo est scripta, revelata seu edita.
paras.en: [[5:8|Then came in all the king's wise men|Tunc ingressi omnes sapientes regis]], [[5:8|but they could neither read the writing|non potuerunt scripturam legere]]. For it was written in Hebrew. And even if they could have read the words, they could not have expounded the sense without revelation. For the words, written down according to human convention, did not carry the sense intended by God. [[5:8|nor declare the interpretation to the king|Nec interpretationem ejus indicare regi]]. By this it is figured that holy Scripture cannot be understood except by the same Spirit by which it was written, revealed or put forth.

paras.t: Unde rex Balthasar satis conturbatus est præ sollicitudine, et vultus illius immutatus est præ pavore. Quocontra de justo loquitur Salomon, quod quasi leo confidens, absque terrore erit ; et item, Non contristabit justum quidquid ei acciderit. De Anna quoque matre Samuelis scriptum est : Vultus ejus non sunt amplius in diversa mutati. Ideo dicit Albertus, quod inconstantiæ signum sit, usque ad suffusionem vultus dejici in tristitia. Sed et optimates ejus turbabantur, regi compatiendo, et de suis simul periculis formidando.
paras.en: [[5:9|Wherewith king Baltasar was much troubled|Unde rex Balthasar satis conturbatus est]], for anxiety, [[5:9|and his countenance was changed|et vultus illius immutatus est]], for dread. Against this Solomon says of the just man: [[Prov 28:1|the just, bold as a lion, shall be without dread|quasi leo confidens, absque terrore erit]]; and again: [[Prov 12:21|Whatsoever shall befall the just man, shall not make him sad|Non contristabit justum quidquid ei acciderit]]. Of Anna, too, the mother of Samuel, it is written: [[1 Kings 1:18|her countenance was no more changed|Vultus ejus non sunt amplius in diversa mutati]]. Therefore Albert says that it is a sign of inconstancy to be cast down in sadness until the face changes colour. [[5:9|and his nobles also were troubled|Sed et optimates ejus turbabantur]], feeling for the king, and at the same time fearing for their own dangers.

paras.t: Regina autem : quam Porphyrius somniavit fuisse conjugem Balthasar, illudens eam viro sapientiorem, quasi non quotidie inveniantur uxores suis sapientiores maritis. Sed secundum Josephum, avia ejus fuit ; secundum Origenem, mater. Sicque ex senio recordabatur diu præteritorum. Pro re quæ acciderat regi et optimatibus ejus, sollicita, domum convivii ingressa est, in qua uxores concubinæque regis epulabantur simul cum rege. Nisi forte dicatur, quod mulieres seorsum resederint, sicut in convivio Assueri factum est : quod tamen ex superioribus non apparet. Unde regina ista propter senium suum videtur se a convivio absentasse. Et forte exemplo viri sui se aliqualiter emendavit : si tamen uxor Nabuchodonosor fuit. Et proloquens, ait : Rex, in æternum vive, nunc scilicet prospere, deinde in societate deorum, finita hac vita : sicut secundo capitulo magis expositum est. Et consolatorie ac magnanimiter loquitur regi, ut tristitiam temperet. Non te conturbent cogitationes tuæ, neque facies tua immutetur ; sed tumultuantes cogitationes has abjice, et esto securus.
paras.en: [[5:10|Then the queen|Regina autem]]: whom Porphyry dreamed to have been the wife of Balthasar, mocking her as wiser than her husband, as though wives wiser than their husbands were not found every day. But according to Josephus she was his grandmother; according to Origen, his mother. And so, being old, she remembered things long past. [[5:10|on occasion of what had happened to the king, and his nobles|Pro re quæ acciderat regi et optimatibus ejus]], being anxious, [[5:10|came into the banquet-house|domum convivii ingressa est]], in which the king's wives and concubines were feasting together with the king. Unless perhaps it be said that the women sat apart, as was done at the feast of Assuerus[[Esth 1:9||]]: which, however, does not appear from what goes before. Hence this queen seems to have kept away from the feast because of her age. And perhaps by the example of her husband she had amended herself in some measure: if indeed she was the wife of Nabuchodonosor. [[5:10|and she spoke, and said: O king, live for ever|Et proloquens, ait : Rex, in æternum vive]], that is, now in prosperity, and afterwards in the company of the gods, when this life is ended: as was explained more fully in the second chapter[[Dan 2:4||]]. And she speaks to the king consolingly and nobly, to temper his sadness. [[5:10|let not thy thoughts trouble thee, neither let thy countenance be changed|Non te conturbent cogitationes tuæ, neque facies tua immutetur]]; but cast away these tumultuous thoughts, and be secure.

paras.t: Est vir in regno tuo, qui spiritum deorum sanctorum habet in se. Quod præcedenti capitulo fuit expositum. Loquitur autem mulier more gentilium, et unius summi soliusque veri Dei donum gratuitum, putat esse donum deorum, secundum unam expositionem verborum istorum. Et in diebus patris tui, non proximi, sed remoti, scilicet Nabuchodonosor regis, ut in isto articulo dictum est plenius, scientia in humanis, et sapientia in divinis, inventæ sunt in eo abundantius quam in omnibus sapientibus Babylonis. Nam et rex Nabuchodonosor pater tuus principem magorum et incantatorum, Chaldæorum et aruspicum (quæ supra, præsertim primo et secundo capitulis, exstant exposita), posuit eum. Incantatores autem, secundum Albertum, dicuntur, qui carminibus in herbis aut animalibus divinant.
paras.en: [[5:11|There is a man in thy kingdom that hath the spirit of the holy gods in him|Est vir in regno tuo, qui spiritum deorum sanctorum habet in se]]. This was explained in the preceding chapter[[Dan 4:5||]]. But the woman speaks after the manner of the Gentiles, and thinks the free gift of the one supreme and only true God to be a gift of the gods, according to one exposition of these words. [[5:11|and in the days of thy father|Et in diebus patris tui]], not his nearest father but a remote one, namely king Nabuchodonosor, as was said more fully in this article, [[5:11|knowledge|scientia]] in human things [[5:11|and wisdom|et sapientia]] in divine things [[5:11|were found in him|inventæ sunt in eo]] more abundantly than in all the wise men of Babylon. [[5:11|for king Nabuchodonosor, thy father|Nam et rex Nabuchodonosor pater tuus]] [[5:11|appointed him|posuit eum]] [the margin notes the Vulgate's reading *constituit*, "appointed", for Denis's *posuit*, "set"] [[5:11|prince of the wise men, enchanters, Chaldeans, and soothsayers|principem magorum et incantatorum, Chaldæorum et aruspicum]] (which have been explained above, especially in the first and second chapters[[Dan 1:20||]][[Dan 2:2||]][[Dan 2:27||]][[Dan 2:48||]]). Now enchanters, according to Albert, are those who divine by spells over herbs or animals.

paras.t: Pater, inquam, tuus, o rex : quia spiritus amplior, id est copiosior illustratio spiritus superni, seu spiritus vel anima seu mens plura comprehendens, sicque amplior quoad multitudinem scitorum, et prudentia, id est clarior atque profundior, quoad agibilia, præsertim humana ; intelligentiaque, id est interna ac penetrativa cognitio per rationes cognitorum, et interpretatio, id est vocalis et evidens expositio, somniorum, mysticum aliquid continentium, ac prophetalium, aut naturaliter significativorum ; et ostensio secretorum, quæ ratione investigari non valent humana, seu intellectualium visionum, atque eorum quæ non in somniis nec imaginarie revelantur: talia namque ostensa sunt ei, et ipse talia aliis declaravit; et ligatorum, id est obscurorum quæ ænigmatibus, allegoriis atque metaphoris involuta sunt, qualia potissime sunt prophetica scripta, solutio ; inventæ sunt in eo a Nabuchodonosor rege, talia ab ipso quærente : noverat equidem rationes intricatorum. Sicque Philosophus loquitur, quod sicut nodum solvere nequit, qui ejus intricationem non novit; sic nec quæstionem dubitabilem, qui rationum ex utraque parte intricationes ignorat. Hoc est in Daniele, cui rex Nabuchodonosor imposuit per principem eunuchorum (ut patuit primo capitulo), nomen Balthasar. Circa quod scribit Hieronymus : Miranda viri et inter barbaros sancta conversatio, ut regina pro virtutum magnitudine tantis eum elevet laudibus. Ubique namque virtuti sua sunt præmia, dum et barbara femina virum Dei tantis extollit præconiis. Nunc itaque Daniel vocetur, etc.
paras.en: [[5:11|thy father, I say, O king|Pater, inquam, tuus, o rex]]: [[5:12|Because a greater spirit|quia spiritus amplior]], that is, a more abundant enlightening by the Spirit from on high; or a spirit, or soul, or mind that takes in more things, and so greater as regards the number of things known; [[5:12|and knowledge|et prudentia]] [Latin *prudentia*, prudence, the knowledge of what is to be done], that is, clearer and deeper as regards things to be done, especially human ones; [[5:12|and understanding|intelligentiaque]], that is, an inward and penetrating knowledge through the reasons of the things known; [[5:12|and interpretation|et interpretatio]], that is, a spoken and plain exposition, [[5:12|of dreams|somniorum]] containing something mystical, prophetic ones, or ones that signify by nature; [[5:12|and shewing of secrets|et ostensio secretorum]], which cannot be searched out by human reason, or of intellectual visions, and of the things revealed neither in dreams nor in images: for such things were shown to him, and he made such things known to others; [[5:12|and resolving|solutio]] [[5:12|of difficult things|et ligatorum]] [*ligatorum*, literally "of things bound"; hence the knot below], that is, of obscure things wrapped in enigmas, allegories and metaphors, such as above all are the writings of the prophets; [[5:12|were found in him|inventæ sunt in eo]] by king Nabuchodonosor, who sought such things of him: for he knew the reasons of tangled things. And so the Philosopher says that, as he cannot undo a knot who does not know how it is tangled, so neither can he resolve a doubtful question who does not know the tangles of the arguments on either side. [[5:12|that is, in Daniel|Hoc est in Daniele]]: [[5:12|whom the king|cui rex]] Nabuchodonosor, through the master of the eunuchs (as appeared in the first chapter[[Dan 1:7||]]), [[5:12|named Baltassar|nomen Balthasar]]. On this Jerome writes: Wonderful is the holy manner of life of the man, even among barbarians, that the queen should raise him with such praises for the greatness of his virtues. For everywhere virtue has its rewards, when even a barbarian woman extols the man of God with such commendations. [[5:12|Now, therefore, let Daniel be called for|Nunc itaque Daniel vocetur]], etc.

paras.t: Igitur introductus est Daniel coram rege. Ad quem rex ait. Ecce quod contemnendus non est sexus. Unde si mulier loquatur viriliter ac prudenter, non abjiciendum ejus eloquium, nec parvi pendendum consilium. Tu es Daniel de filiis captivitatis Judæ, id est tribus Juda seu Judæorum, quem adduxit pater meus rex Nabuchodonosor de Judæa cum Joakim rege Juda? Mirum quod virum tam famosum, sapientem ac sanctum, rex iste non novit. Unde videtur totus fuisse sacrilegus et carnalis, nec quidquam de virtuosis curasse hominibus. Audivi de te, quoniam spiritum deorum habeas in te ; et scientia humanorum, intelligentiaque secretorum, ac sapientia divinorum, ampliores quam in aliis, inventæ sint in te, etc. Si ergo vales scripturam hanc in pariete apparentem legere, et interpretationem ejus indicare mihi, purpura vestieris, etc. Quæ transiliuntur, nulla difficultate teguntur : imo et si quam habent, supra jam patuerunt.
paras.en: [[5:13|Then Daniel was brought in before the king|Igitur introductus est Daniel coram rege]]. [[5:13|And the king spoke, and said to him|Ad quem rex ait]]. See how that sex [that is, the female sex: the queen's counsel is followed] is not to be despised. Hence if a woman speaks manfully and prudently, her words are not to be cast aside, nor her counsel held cheap. [[5:13|Art thou Daniel, of the children of the captivity of Juda|Tu es Daniel de filiis captivitatis Judæ]], that is, of the tribe of Juda, or of the Jews, [[5:13|whom my father, the king|quem adduxit pater meus rex]], Nabuchodonosor, [[5:13|brought out of Judea|de Judæa]] with Joakim king of Juda[[Dan 1:2||]]? It is a wonder that this king did not know a man so famous, wise and holy. Hence he seems to have been wholly sacrilegious and carnal, and to have cared nothing for virtuous men. [[5:14|I have heard of thee, that thou hast the spirit of the gods|Audivi de te, quoniam spiritum deorum habeas]] in thee; and that knowledge of human things, and understanding of secret things, and wisdom of divine things, greater than in others, [[5:14|are found in thee|inventæ sint in te]], etc. [[5:16|now if thou art able|Si ergo vales]] to read this writing appearing on the wall, [[5:16|and to shew me the interpretation thereof, thou shalt be clothed with purple|et interpretationem ejus indicare mihi, purpura vestieris]], etc. What is passed over is hidden by no difficulty: indeed, if it has any, that has already been made plain above.

paras.t: Ad quæ respondens Daniel ait coram rege : Munera tua quæ promittis, sint tibi, id est, remaneant tui juris, et dona domus tuæ alteri da. In quo constantia, justitia atque perfectio Danielis emicuit, quia nil veritus est, nec pro spirituali temporale accipere voluit, atque in omnibus ordinate processit. Denique, sicut et Lyra dicit : Ex pacto non est aliquid accipiendum pro revelatione divini secreti, sed post factum potest aliquid accipi ex liberalitate dantis. Et ut Seneca ait, Liber non est qui munus accipit. Hieronymus hic loquitur : Æmulemur Danielem, regiam dignitatem et munera contemnentem, qui absque pretio proferens veritatem, jam ipse legis præceptum evangelicum sequebatur : Gratis accepistis, gratis date. Alioqui, et tristia nuntiantem, indecens erat libenter munera accipere. Scripturam autem legam tibi, rex, et interpretationem ejus ostendam tibi. Videtur quod jam omnia ista revelata fuerint Danieli, quomodo, cur, et quid scriptum esset, quid item scripta significarent, quamvis in ipsa scripturæ inspectione quiverit Deus Danieli expositionem ostendere.
paras.en: [[5:17|To which Daniel made answer, and said before the king|Ad quæ respondens Daniel ait coram rege]]: [[5:17|thy rewards|Munera tua]] which thou promisest, [[5:17|be to thyself|sint tibi]], that is, let them remain in thy own right, [[5:17|and the gifts of thy house give to another|et dona domus tuæ alteri da]]. In this the constancy, justice and perfection of Daniel shone forth, for he feared nothing, and would not take a temporal thing for a spiritual one, and in everything he proceeded in due order. Further, as Lyra too says: Nothing is to be taken by bargain for the revealing of a divine secret, but after the deed something may be accepted from the liberality of the giver. And as Seneca says, He who accepts a gift is not free. Jerome says here: Let us imitate Daniel, who despised the royal dignity and gifts, and who, uttering the truth without price, already under the Law followed the precept of the Gospel: [[Matt 10:8|freely have you received, freely give|Gratis accepistis, gratis date]]. Besides, for one who brought sad tidings it was unseemly to accept gifts gladly. [[5:17|but the writing I will read to thee, O king, and shew thee the interpretation thereof|Scripturam autem legam tibi, rex, et interpretationem ejus ostendam tibi]]. It seems that all these things had already been revealed to Daniel: how, why and what had been written, and also what the writing signified; although God could have shown Daniel the explanation in the very looking at the writing.

paras.t: O rex Balthasar. Exclamationem præmittit, ut dicenda seriosius advertantur, atque ut notabilia prorsus et magna esse pandantur. Deus altissimus, a cujus majestate omnia distant in infinitum in perfectione et gloria, regnum, imo et orientis monarchiam ac grande imperium, magnificentiam, gloriam et honorem (ista præcedenti capitulo prolixe exposita sunt), dedit Nabuchodonosor patri tuo. Omnis enim potestas a Deo est, et omne bonum naturæ atque fortunæ datur ac dispensatur ab ipso : qui bonis et malis, gratis et ingratis ista communicat, occulto quidem judicio, diversisque modis.
paras.en: [[5:18|O king|O rex]] Balthasar. He sets an exclamation first, so that what is to be said may be heeded more earnestly, and so that it may be shown to be altogether notable and great: [[5:18|the most high God|Deus altissimus]], from whose majesty all things stand infinitely distant in perfection and glory, [[5:18|gave to Nabuchodonosor, thy father|dedit Nabuchodonosor patri tuo]] [[5:18|a kingdom|regnum]], nay, the monarchy of the East and a great empire, [[5:18|and greatness, and glory, and honour|magnificentiam, gloriam et honorem]] (these were set out at length in the preceding chapter). For all power is from God[[Rom 13:1||]], and every good of nature and of fortune is given and dispensed by him: who bestows these things on good and bad, on the grateful and the ungrateful[[Matt 5:45||]], by a hidden judgment indeed, and in divers ways.

paras.t: Et propter magnificentiam quam dederat ei, universi populi, tribus et linguæ : quorum differentia capitulo tertio fuit exposita ; tremebant et metuebant eum, ita quod præ magnitudine pavoris cordis, etiam corpora contremebant. Estque distributio ista accommoda et pro generibus singulorum. Atque de his potissime sermo est qui regi huic subjecti fuerunt, vel ab ipso impugnari verebantur. Præcipue quippe timenda est iracundia regum, juxta illud Proverbiorum : Sicut fremitus leonis, ita et ira regis ; sicut ros super herbam, ita et hilaritas ejus.
paras.en: [[5:19|And for the greatness that he gave to him, all people, tribes, and languages|Et propter magnificentiam quam dederat ei, universi populi, tribus et linguæ]]: the difference between these was explained in the third chapter[[Dan 3:4||]]; [[5:19|trembled, and were afraid of him|tremebant et metuebant eum]], so that from the greatness of the dread in their hearts their bodies too trembled. And this distribution is an accommodated one, taken for the kinds of individuals [a term of the logicians: *all* here means people of every kind, not every single person]. And the speech is chiefly of those who were subject to this king, or feared to be attacked by him. For the wrath of kings is above all to be feared, according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 19:12|As the roaring of a lion, so also is the anger of a king|Sicut fremitus leonis, ita et ira regis]]; [[Prov 19:12|and his cheerfulness as the dew upon the grass|sicut ros super herbam, ita et hilaritas ejus]].

paras.t: Quos volebat, interficiebat ; et quos volebat, percutiebat lædendo seu mutilando. Quos volebat, exaltabat ; et quos volebat, humiliabat opprimendo. Deus enim permittit præsidentes potestate sibi collata abuti, et frequenter ob hominum pravitatem dat reges principesque crudeles, sicut per Osee protestatur : Dabo tibi regem in furore meo, et principes in indignatione mea. Verumtamen impii hi dominatores nil agunt in subditos, nisi Deo volente aut juste permittente : sub cujus providentia omnia cadunt ; et qui per sapientiam atque justitiam suam judicialiter ordinat, et præsertim in die generalis judicii, rectissime ordinabit, quidquid interim obliquum impiumque videtur. Sed et feroces ac impii præsidentes, sæpe sunt instrumentum æquitatis divinæ contra iniquos, quorum Deus punit excessus per illos. Hanc regis tyrannidem sequuntur tyranni crudelesque domini, illud Sapientiæ dicentes, Sit fortitudo nostra lex justitiæ : voluntatem, non rationem, sequentes. Denique istud agebat Nabuchodonosor ante suam amentiam, multum injuste et irrationabili voluntate. Ad mentem vero reversus, quando et major virtus ac gloria datæ sunt ei, similia quidem egit quoad substantiam facti, sed rationabiliter, judicialiter, ac juste, cum Dei timore, Danielis utens doctrinis.
paras.en: [[5:19|whom he would, he slew|Quos volebat, interficiebat]]: [[5:19|and whom he would, he destroyed|et quos volebat, percutiebat]], by wounding or maiming them. [[5:19|whom he would, he set up|Quos volebat, exaltabat]]: [[5:19|and whom he would, he brought down|et quos volebat, humiliabat]], by oppressing them. For God permits those who preside to abuse the power conferred on them, and often, because of the wickedness of men, gives cruel kings and princes, as he declares by Osee: [[Osee 13:11|I will give thee a king in my wrath|Dabo tibi regem in furore meo]], and princes in my indignation [so Denis; the Vulgate goes on: and will take him away in my indignation]. Yet these wicked lords do nothing against their subjects except as God wills or justly permits: under whose providence all things fall; and he who orders things judicially by his wisdom and justice will, above all in the day of the general judgment, set most rightly in order whatever meanwhile seems crooked and wicked. Moreover fierce and wicked rulers are often the instrument of the divine equity against the wicked, whose excesses God punishes through them. This tyranny of the king is followed by tyrants and cruel lords, who say that of Wisdom, [[Wis 2:11|let our strength be the law of justice|Sit fortitudo nostra lex justitiæ]]: following will, not reason. Finally, Nabuchodonosor did this before his madness, most unjustly and with an unreasonable will. But when he had come back to his mind, when greater power and glory too were given him, he did the like as to the substance of the deed, but reasonably, judicially and justly, with the fear of God, making use of the teachings of Daniel.

paras.t: Quando vero elevatum est cor ejus elationis tumore : juxta illud in Job, Cucurrit impius adversus Deum erecto collo ; et spiritus ejus, id est anima, quoad superiorem ejus partem et voluntatem, obfirmatus est ad superbiam, id est induratus in ea, in tantum ut se in statua aurea quam erexit, faceret adorari, et diceret, Nonne hæc est Babylon civitas magna? prout præcedenti dicebatur capitulo ; depositus est de solio regni sui, etc. Deo enim sibi usum rationis abstrahente, pulsus est regno ut vere insanus, juxta modum præcedenti scriptum capitulo, in quo, quæ nunc transilio, clare tractata sunt.
paras.en: [[5:20|But when his heart was lifted up|Quando vero elevatum est cor ejus]] with the swelling of elation: according to that in Job, [[Job 15:26|He hath run against him with his neck raised up|Cucurrit impius adversus Deum erecto collo]] [Denis reads: The wicked man hath run against God with his neck raised up]; [[5:20|and his spirit|et spiritus ejus]], that is, his soul, as to its higher part and the will, [[5:20|hardened unto pride|obfirmatus est ad superbiam]], that is, was hardened in it, so far that he had himself adored in the golden statue which he set up[[Dan 3:1||]], and said, [[Dan 4:27|Is not this the great Babylon|Nonne hæc est Babylon civitas magna]]? as was said in the preceding chapter; [[5:20|he was put down from the throne of his kingdom|depositus est de solio regni sui]], etc. For God took from him the use of reason, and he was driven from his kingdom as one truly mad, in the manner written in the preceding chapter[[Dan 4:30||]], in which the things I now pass over have been clearly treated.

paras.t: Tu quoque filius ejus, Balthasar, non humiliasti cor tuum, quum scires hæc omnia : forte ex aliquorum relatu, et quia hujusmodi facta regum scribi solebant ; nec istud fuit tam diu præteritum, quin in memoriis plurimorum recenter permanserit, quia et multi qui istud viderunt, adhuc vivebant, ut Daniel. Et in hoc aggravabatur impietas Balthasar, quod patris sui exemplo se non correxit, quum in Proverbiis scriptum sit : Pestilente flagellato, stultus sapientior erit. Et Ptolemæus disserit : Qui exemplo alterius non corrigitur, alii corrigentur ab ipso. Præterea, felix quem faciunt aliena damna peritum ; qui istud Ecclesiastici sapienter advertit : Memor esto judicii mei, sic enim erit et tuum ; mihi heri, et tibi hodie. Innotescit demum ex his, quod superiorum ac præsidentium vitia non sunt palpanda, sed juste reprehendenda, quando locus, tempus, causa, caritas, discretioque requirunt. Quod tamen discrete agendum est, ne exacerbentur.
paras.en: [[5:22|Thou also, his son, O Baltasar, hast not humbled thy heart, whereas thou knewest all these things|Tu quoque filius ejus, Balthasar, non humiliasti cor tuum, quum scires hæc omnia]]: perhaps from the account of some, and because such deeds of kings were customarily written down; nor was it so long past that it did not remain fresh in the memories of very many, for many who had seen it were still alive, as Daniel was. And the impiety of Balthasar was aggravated in this, that he did not correct himself by his father's example, since it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 19:25|The wicked man being scourged, the fool shall be wiser|Pestilente flagellato, stultus sapientior erit]]. And Ptolemy teaches: He who is not corrected by another's example, others will be corrected by him. Moreover, happy is he whom other men's harms make wise; who wisely heeds this of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 38:23|Remember my judgment: for thine also shall be so: yesterday for me, and to day for thee|Memor esto judicii mei, sic enim erit et tuum ; mihi heri, et tibi hodie]]. Finally it becomes known from these things that the vices of superiors and rulers are not to be stroked [that is, smoothed over with flattery], but justly rebuked, when place, time, cause, charity and discretion require it. Which yet is to be done with discretion, lest they be exasperated.

paras.t: Sed adversus Dominatorem cæli elevatus es, id est, obtenebrata pompositate opposuisti te Deo. Superbus autem præcipue opponit se Deo, juxta illud in Job : Quid tumet contra Deum spiritus tuus? Superbus quippe gloriam et honorem, quæ Deo debentur, usurpat inique. Et vasa domus ejus allata sunt coram te : sicut in principio hujus capituli dictum est atque expositum. Deos quoque argenteos et aureos, etc., laudasti, cultum soli Deo vero debitum, vilissimis impendendo. Idola autem, ut dicitur, de diversis fiebant metallis, secundum proprietatem illorum quibus fiebant : ut idolum Martis de ferro, similiter aliorum deorum quos in bellis potestatem habere credebant ; idolum solis, de auro ; lunæ, de argento. Vel etiam opinandum, quod idola de materiis pretiosis aut vilioribus fabricabantur, secundum facultatem majorem aut minorem facientium fieri ea.
paras.en: [[5:23|But hast lifted thyself up against the Lord of heaven|Sed adversus Dominatorem cæli elevatus es]], that is, in darkened pomp thou hast set thyself against God. Now the proud man above all sets himself against God, according to that in Job: [[Job 15:13|Why doth thy spirit swell against God|Quid tumet contra Deum spiritus tuus]]? For the proud man wickedly usurps the glory and honour which are due to God. [[5:23|and the vessels of his house have been brought before thee|Et vasa domus ejus allata sunt coram te]]: as was said and explained at the beginning of this chapter[[5:3||]]. [[5:23|and thou hast praised the gods of silver, and of gold|Deos quoque argenteos et aureos, etc., laudasti]], etc., paying to the vilest things the worship due to the true God alone. Now idols, as is said, were made of divers metals according to the property of those for whom they were made: as the idol of Mars of iron, and likewise those of the other gods who were believed to have power in wars; the idol of the sun, of gold; that of the moon, of silver. Or it may also be supposed that idols were fashioned of precious or of cheaper materials according to the greater or lesser means of those who had them made.

paras.t: Porro Deum qui habet flatum tuum, id est spiritum seu animam vel respirandi virtutem, qua vita servatur, in manu, id est in potestate sua, ita ut quum ei placuerit, tollat eum a te. Potest quoque eum damnare, et gratiam salvationis potest præstare. Sic enim accipitur flatus, quum per Isaiam Dominus loquitur : Ego Dominus dans flatum populo qui est super terram, et spiritum calcantibus eam. Et ideo anima flatus vocatur, quoniam scriptum est : Inspiravit Dominus in faciem ejus (scilicet hominis) spiraculum vitæ, et factus est homo in animam viventem. Unde per Isaiam Dominus contestatur : Flatus ego faciam. Et omnes vias tuas, id est cogitatus, affectiones et actus, ita ut possit eas per lineas æquitatis clementer dirigere, et in abruptis vitiorum juste deserere, easque ad libitum condemnare. Flatus quoque et via regum fertur esse in manu Dei, quia ad nutum inclinat ea quocumque voluerit, prout Salomon dicit : Cor regis in manu Dei ; quocumque voluerit, vertet illud. Non glorificasti, nec verbis nec operibus, imo utroque modo blasphemasti : quod est pessima apostasia. Atque infelicissima calamitas creaturæ rationalis hæc est, quod Creatorem suum relinquit, et vana ac vilia ei præponit. Propter quod in Ecclesiastico legitur : Initium superbiæ hominis est, apostatare a Deo ; quoniam ab illo qui fecit eum, recessit cor ejus.
paras.en: [[5:23|but the God who hath thy breath|Porro Deum qui habet flatum tuum]], that is, thy spirit or soul, or the power of breathing by which life is kept, [[5:23|in his hand|in manu]], that is, in his power, so that when it pleases him he may take it from thee. He can also condemn it, and he can bestow the grace of salvation. For so is *breath* taken when the Lord speaks by Isaias: I the Lord, [[Is 42:5|that giveth breath to the people upon it, and spirit to them that tread thereon|dans flatum populo qui est super terram, et spiritum calcantibus eam]]. And therefore the soul is called breath, since it is written: The Lord [[Gen 2:7|breathed into his face|Inspiravit Dominus in faciem ejus]] (that is, man's) [[Gen 2:7|the breath of life, and man became a living soul|spiraculum vitæ, et factus est homo in animam viventem]]. Hence by Isaias the Lord declares: [[Is 57:16|breathings I will make|Flatus ego faciam]]. [[5:23|and all thy ways|Et omnes vias tuas]], that is, thy thoughts, affections and acts, so that he can mercifully direct them along the lines of equity, and justly forsake them on the precipices of vice, and condemn them at his pleasure. The breath and the way of kings, too, are said to be in the hand of God, because he inclines them at his nod whithersoever he will, as Solomon says: [[Prov 21:1|the heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord: whithersoever he will, he shall turn it|Cor regis in manu Dei ; quocumque voluerit, vertet illud]]. [[5:23|thou hast not glorified|Non glorificasti]], neither by words nor by works; nay, in both ways thou hast blasphemed: which is the worst apostasy. And this is the unhappiest calamity of a rational creature, that it forsakes its Creator and sets vain and vile things before him. Wherefore we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:14|The beginning of the pride of man, is to fall off from God|Initium superbiæ hominis est, apostatare a Deo]]; [[Ecclus 10:15|Because his heart is departed from him that made him|quoniam ab illo qui fecit eum, recessit cor ejus]].

paras.t: Idcirco, id est pro tantis demeritis, missus est ab eo articulus manus : Deo enim jubente, angelus effigiem hanc formavit ; quæ scripsit hoc quod exaratum est. Ex quo, secundum Albertum, videtur quod non colore, sed in lapide scriptum fuit.
paras.en: [[5:24|Wherefore|Idcirco]], that is, for such great demerits, [[5:24|he hath sent the part of the hand|missus est ab eo articulus manus]]: for at God's command an angel formed this likeness; [[5:24|which hath written this that is set down|quæ scripsit hoc quod exaratum est]] [*exaratum*, 'set down', properly means 'ploughed', that is, cut in]. From this, according to Albert, it seems that it was written not in colour but in the stone.

paras.t: Hæc est autem scriptura quæ digesta est verbis Hebraicis, ut aliqui dicunt : Mane, Thecel, Phares, id est, numerus, appensio, divisio. Ad quod partim applicari potest illud Sapientiæ : Omnia in numero, pondere ac mensura constituisti.
paras.en: [[5:25|And this is the writing that is written|Hæc est autem scriptura quæ digesta est]] in Hebrew words, as some say: [[5:25|MANE, THECEL, PHARES|Mane, Thecel, Phares]], that is, number, weighing, division. To which may in part be applied that of Wisdom: [[Wis 11:21|thou hast ordered all things in measure, and number, and weight|Omnia in numero, pondere ac mensura constituisti]] [Denis's order is number, weight and measure].

paras.t: Et hæc est interpretatio sermonis, id est expositio horum trium verborum : quorum quodlibet ex divina institutione integrum sensum significavit, qui non nisi per revelationem poterat sciri. Mane significat : numeravit Deus regnum tuum, id est, tempus durationis Babylonici imperii in certo posuit numero, ut (juxta oraculum Jeremiæ, imo Dei per eum) omnes gentes septuaginta annis servirent regibus Babylonis. Vel, secundum Albertum, Numeravit Deus regnum tuum, id est omnes actus et verba quæ habuisti in regno : secundum illud Job, Nonne Deus considerat vias meas, et omnes gressus meos dinumerat? Et complevit illud, id est, jam in te illud terminabit, ita quod te occiso, regnum Babyloniæ transferetur ad alios.
paras.en: [[5:26|And this is the interpretation of the word|Et hæc est interpretatio sermonis]], that is, the explanation of these three words: each of which, by divine institution, signified a whole sense, which could not be known except by revelation. [[5:26|MANE|Mane]] signifies: [[5:26|God hath numbered thy kingdom|numeravit Deus regnum tuum]], that is, he set the time of the duration of the Babylonian empire at a fixed number, so that (according to the oracle of Jeremias, or rather of God through him) all the nations should serve the kings of Babylon seventy years[[Jer 25:11||]][[Jer 29:10||]]. Or, according to Albert, [[5:26|God hath numbered thy kingdom|Numeravit Deus regnum tuum]], that is, all the acts and words that thou hast had in thy reign: according to that of Job, [[Job 31:4|Doth not he consider my ways, and number all my steps|Nonne Deus considerat vias meas, et omnes gressus meos dinumerat]]? [[5:26|and hath finished it|Et complevit illud]], that is, he will now end it in thee, so that, thou being slain, the kingdom of Babylon will be transferred to others.

paras.t: Thecel significat : appensum est regnum tuum, vel, appensus es tu, in statera, id est in æquitate seu examine divini judicii, et inventum est, vel, inventus es, a Deo infallibili judice omnia intuente, minus habens de justitia quam merito haberet, vel haberes ; vel, minus habens bonitatis, quam tu ipse putabas. De hac statera loquitur Job : Si ambulavi in vanitate, appendat me in statera. Et in Proverbiis : Pondus et statera judicia Domini sunt.
paras.en: [[5:27|THECEL|Thecel]] signifies: thy kingdom is weighed, or, [[5:27|thou art weighed in the balance|appensus es tu, in statera]], that is, in the equity or examination of the divine judgment, and it is found, or, [[5:27|and art found|inventus es]], by God, the infallible judge who beholds all things, [[5:27|wanting|minus habens]] in justice, having less than it ought by right to have, or than thou oughtest; or, having less goodness than thou thyself didst think. Of this balance Job speaks: [[Job 31:5|If I have walked in vanity|Si ambulavi in vanitate]], [[Job 31:6|let him weigh me in a just balance|appendat me in statera]]. And in Proverbs: [[Prov 16:11|Weight and balance are judgments of the Lord|Pondus et statera judicia Domini sunt]].

paras.t: Phares significat : divisum est regnum tuum, et datum est Medis et Persis, id est, jam statim separabitur et tolletur a te ac tua progenie, et ad Medos transferetur ac Persas : juxta illud Isaiæ, Non est solium ultra filiæ Chaldæorum ; et rursus, Ecce ego suscitabo super eos Medos et Persas, etc.
paras.en: [[5:28|PHARES|Phares]] signifies: [[5:28|thy kingdom is divided, and is given to the Medes and Persians|divisum est regnum tuum, et datum est Medis et Persis]], that is, it will now at once be severed and taken away from thee and thy offspring, and transferred to the Medes and Persians: according to that of Isaias, [[Is 47:1|there is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans|Non est solium ultra filiæ Chaldæorum]]; and again, [[Is 13:17|Behold I will stir up the Medes against them|Ecce ego suscitabo super eos Medos]], and the Persians, etc. [the words 'and the Persians' are Denis's; Isaias names only the Medes here].

paras.t: Tunc jubente rege, indutus est Daniel purpura, et circumdata est torques aurea collo ejus ; et prædicatum est de eo, quod haberet potestatem tertius in regno suo, scilicet Balthasar regis, id est, quod unus esset trium principalium principum, vel tertius in potestate post regem. Et secundum Albertum, forte unus istorum trium principum præfuit curiæ, alter exercitui, tertius terræ. Omnia ista exhibuit Balthasar Danieli, ut promissionem suam impleret, qua interpretanti scripturam ista promisit ; et ut Glossa Hieronymum sequens tangit, quatenus Dei hominem venerando, veniam mereretur : quam idcirco non meruit, quia gravius fuit sacrilegium ejus in Deum, quam veneratio in servum ipsius ; vel, quia non putavit interpretationem Danielis tam cito implendam. Daniel quoque, secundum Hieronymum, ista ornamenta accepit, ut per ea Dario in regnum mox successuro fieret notior, et per notitiam honoratior.
paras.en: [[5:29|Then by the king's command, Daniel was clothed with purple, and a chain of gold was put about his neck|Tunc jubente rege, indutus est Daniel purpura, et circumdata est torques aurea collo ejus]]: [[5:29|and it was proclaimed of him that he had power as the third man in the kingdom|et prædicatum est de eo, quod haberet potestatem tertius in regno suo]], that is, in the kingdom of King Balthasar; that is, that he was one of three chief princes, or third in power after the king. And according to Albert, perhaps one of these three princes was over the court, another over the army, the third over the land. All these things Balthasar bestowed on Daniel to fulfil his promise, by which he had promised them to whoever should interpret the writing; and, as the Gloss touches on, following Jerome, so that by honouring the man of God he might win pardon: which he did not win, because his sacrilege against God was graver than his honour paid to God's servant; or because he did not think that Daniel's interpretation would be fulfilled so soon. Daniel too, according to Jerome, accepted these ornaments so that by them he might become better known to Darius, who was soon to succeed to the kingdom, and, being known, more honoured.

paras.t: Eadem nocte interfectus est Balthasar rex Chaldæus. Circa quod scribit Hieronymus : Refert Josephus decimo Antiquitatis Judaicæ libro, quod Babylone a Medis et Persis obsessa, Balthasar in tantam venit sui oblivionem seu negligentiam, ut celeberrimum iniret convivium, et vasis templi Dei allatis, vacaret epulis. Unde potest stare historia, quod eadem nocte sit captus et jugulatus, omnibus interpretatione somnii territis aut ebrietate sopitis, aut convivio ac celebritati intentis. Aliqui dicunt Balthasar regem a cubiculariis suis occisum, et proditione eorum urbem hostibus traditam. Secundum Glossam vero, a Medis ac Persis occisus est. Dicuntque aliqui, quod Persæ ac Medi, audita visione atque divina sententia contra Balthasar per exploratores suos, fecerunt contra civitatem audacter insultum ; bellatoresque urbis nequibant resistere, quoniam ex prædicta visione et Danielis interpretatione attoniti erant, et in stuporem conversi, et quoniam vino atque convivio fuerant fatigati. Sed mirum apparet, quomodo tam cito percipere poterant Persæ ac Medi, quæ in aula regia intra urbem acciderant, quum ista visio ac interpretatio in cœna aut post eam contigerint, ut ex præhabitis liquet, eademque nocte occisus est Balthasar, et capta est Babylon. Denique, dato quod ea tam celeriter percepissent, nequaquam videtur quod tam subito urbem cepissent, cujus muri, ut statim dicetur, ducentorum cubitorum in altitudine erant. Imo, secundum Hieronymum, incredibilius videbatur eam posse capi et destrui, quam ædificari.
paras.en: [[5:30|The same night Baltasar, the Chaldean king, was slain|Eadem nocte interfectus est Balthasar rex Chaldæus]]. On this Jerome writes: Josephus relates in the tenth book of the Jewish Antiquities that when Babylon was besieged by the Medes and Persians, Balthasar came to such forgetfulness or neglect of himself that he held a most famous banquet and, having had the vessels of the temple of God brought, gave himself up to feasting. Hence the history can stand, that he was taken and slain that same night, when all were terrified by the interpretation of the dream [so the Latin, *somnii*, though it was a writing], or sunk in drunkenness, or intent on the banquet and the festivity. Some say that King Balthasar was killed by his chamberlains, and that by their treachery the city was handed over to the enemy. But according to the Gloss he was killed by the Medes and Persians. And some say that the Persians and Medes, having heard through their scouts of the vision and of the divine sentence against Balthasar, boldly made an assault on the city; and the warriors of the city could not resist, because they were astounded and turned to stupor by the said vision and Daniel's interpretation, and because they were wearied with wine and feasting. But it seems a wonder how the Persians and Medes could learn so quickly what had happened in the royal hall within the city, since this vision and interpretation took place at supper or after it, as is clear from what was said before, and that same night Balthasar was slain and Babylon taken. Moreover, granting that they learned these things so quickly, it in no way seems that they could so suddenly have taken a city whose walls, as will be said presently, were two hundred cubits in height. Nay, according to Jerome, it seemed more incredible that it could be taken and destroyed than that it could be built.

paras.t: Rationabilius ergo existimo quod de hac re in Scholastica historia atque in Chronica Martini scriptum est. Sic quippe in Scholastica fertur historia : Cyrus divisit Euphraten longe a civitate per alveos plures, ut alveum qui influebat in civitatem, vadabilem faceret ; et per ipsum ingressi sunt hostes in civitatem sub muro. De qua re in Chronica Martini plenius ita narratur : Quum Cyrus orientem sibi pro magna parte subjecisset, ad Babylonem, quæ aliis civitatibus opulentior fuit, accessit. Sed Euphrates magnus fluvius obstitit. Quumque unus de suis militibus audacior et forma elegantior transitum attentaret, et fluvii rapacitate absorptus fuisset, rex Cyrus dolens pro milite, iratus protestatus est, quod fluvium qui tam præclarum militem voravit, adeo meabilem faceret, ut genua feminarum transeuntium non tangeret. Quod et factum est. Nam per campi amplitudinem in quadringentos sexaginta alveos fluvium divisit. Sicque Euphraten validissimum fluvium per mediam Babylonem fluentem, a civitate avertit ; et sic per alveum in luto aquarum multarum, sicut prophetavit Habacuc, civitatem hostiliter introivit. Cepitque urbem, quam (ut dicit Orosius) vel humano opere exstrui, vel humana virtute destrui potuisse, pene incredibile apud mortales erat. Nam civitas in amplitudine latissimi atque planissimi campi sita, undique conspicua, natura loci lætissima, per quadrum fuit disposita, scilicet quadrangularis, non rotunda. Murorum ejus latitudo fuit quinquaginta cubitorum, et in altitudine quater tantum, scilicet ducentorum. Murus ejus ex cocto latere atque interfuso bitumine fuit compactus. A fronte murorum centum portas æreas habuit. Porro, secundum Hieronymum super Isaiam, quodlibet latus muri quadrati civitatis hujus, sedecim milliaria, id est octo leucas, in longitudine habuit. Nec incredibile est hoc, quia (ut aliqui asserunt) tunc sic ædificabantur civitates, saltem aliquæ, quod quilibet secundum statum suum habebat juxta domum suam hortum et vineam, ubi crescebant terræ nascentia, de quibus tempore obsidionis diu simul cum sua familia vivere posset. Capitolium vero seu fortalitium urbis istius, fuit turris Babel, post diluvium a filiis Noe ædificata, ut in Genesi legitur, in altitudine quatuor millia passuum habens. In hac civitate erant templa marmorea, ac aureæ statuæ, atque plateæ auro lapidibusque fulgentes. Nunc vero infra mœnia, vastissima solitudo est et bestiarum tumultus. Et sicut Hieronymus sibi testatur relatum, sunt ibi venationes regales. Unde et muri coctiles subinde instaurantur propter bestias includendas, ut facilius capiantur.
paras.en: I therefore think more reasonable what is written on this matter in the Scholastic History and in the Chronicle of Martin. For thus it is told in the Scholastic History: Cyrus divided the Euphrates, far from the city, into many channels, so as to make the channel that flowed into the city fordable; and through it the enemy entered the city under the wall. Of which the Chronicle of Martin tells more fully thus: When Cyrus had subjected the East to himself for the most part, he came to Babylon, which was wealthier than the other cities. But the Euphrates, a great river, stood in the way. And when one of his soldiers, bolder than the rest and handsomer in form, attempted the crossing and was swallowed up by the violence of the river, King Cyrus, grieving for the soldier, declared in anger that he would make the river that had devoured so splendid a soldier so passable that it would not touch the knees of women crossing it. And this was done. For across the breadth of the plain he divided the river into four hundred and sixty channels. And so he turned away from the city the Euphrates, a most mighty river that flowed through the midst of Babylon; and so through the channel, [[Hab 3:15|in the mud of many waters|in luto aquarum multarum]], as Habacuc prophesied, he entered the city as an enemy. And he took the city of which (as Orosius says) it was almost incredible among mortals that it could either have been built by human work or destroyed by human strength. For the city, set in the breadth of a very wide and very level plain, visible on every side, most delightful by the nature of the place, was laid out in a square, that is, four-cornered, not round. The breadth of its walls was fifty cubits, and their height four times as much, that is, two hundred. Its wall was built of baked brick with bitumen poured between. In the face of the walls it had a hundred gates of brass. Further, according to Jerome on Isaias, each side of the square wall of this city was sixteen miles, that is, eight leagues, in length. Nor is this incredible, because (as some assert) cities were then so built, some at least, that each man according to his station had beside his house a garden and a vineyard, where the fruits of the earth grew, on which he could live a long time with his household in time of siege. The capitol or stronghold of this city was the tower of Babel, built after the flood by the sons of Noe, as we read in Genesis[[Gen 11:4||]], having a height of four thousand paces. In this city were temples of marble, and golden statues, and streets shining with gold and precious stones. But now within the walls there is a vast wilderness and the din of beasts. And, as Jerome testifies was told him, there are royal hunting grounds there. Hence the brick walls are also repaired from time to time to shut in the beasts, so that they may be caught more easily.

paras.t: De hac destructione Babylonis, Isaias in diversis libri sui capitulis plura prædixit. Siquidem inter alia quamplurima de ea legitur vaticinatus : Et erit Babylon illa gloriosa in regnis, inclyta, subversa sicut subvertit Deus Sodomam et Gomorrham. Non habitabitur usque in finem ; sed requiescent ibi bestiæ, et replebuntur domus eorum draconibus, et habitabunt ibi struthiones, et pilosi saltabunt ibi ; et respondebunt ibi ululæ in ædibus ejus, et sirenes in delubris voluptatis. Quod vero exsistente convivio protinus caperetur, ita prædixit : Pone mensam, contemplare in specula ; comedentes et bibentes, surgite, principes, arripite clypeum. Tanquam dicat, Tempus præliandi est, non epulandi. De qua etiam re Jeremias ille præclarus tam lucide vaticinatur, ut ipsam videatur historiam recitare.
paras.en: Of this destruction of Babylon Isaias foretold many things in divers chapters of his book. For among very many other things he is read to have prophesied of it: [[Is 13:19|And that Babylon, glorious among kingdoms|Et erit Babylon illa gloriosa in regnis]], renowned, shall be overthrown [[Is 13:19|even as the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrha|sicut subvertit Deus Sodomam et Gomorrham]]. [[Is 13:20|It shall no more be inhabited for ever|Non habitabitur usque in finem]]; [[Is 13:21|But wild beasts shall rest there, and their houses shall be filled with serpents, and ostriches shall dwell there, and the hairy ones shall dance there|sed requiescent ibi bestiæ, et replebuntur domus eorum draconibus, et habitabunt ibi struthiones, et pilosi saltabunt ibi]]; [[Is 13:22|And owls shall answer one another there, in the houses thereof, and sirens in the temples of pleasure|et respondebunt ibi ululæ in ædibus ejus, et sirenes in delubris voluptatis]]. And that it would be taken at once while the banquet was going on, he foretold thus: [[Is 21:5|Prepare the table, behold in the watchtower them that eat and drink: arise, ye princes, take up the shield|Pone mensam, contemplare in specula ; comedentes et bibentes, surgite, principes, arripite clypeum]]. As if to say, It is the time for fighting, not for feasting. Of this too that illustrious Jeremias prophesies so clearly that he seems to be reciting the very history[[Jer 50:1||]][[Jer 51:1||]] [the margin reads Jer. i, li, evidently Jer. l, li: the prophecy against Babylon in chapters 50 and 51; on the feast, see 51:39].

paras.t: Et Darius Medus, id est rex Medorum, successit in regnum Balthasar regis, ita quod illud suo adjecit imperio, non quod Babylonem reparaverit atque possederit, annos natus sexaginta duos, ita quod sexaginta duorum tunc erat annorum. Ideo Cyrus rex cum eo obsidens Babylonem, cessit ei in regni sui successione, videlicet ratione ætatis ; et quia Darius avunculus Cyri fuit ; et rursus, quoniam usque ad illud tempus, regnum Mediæ majus fuit regno Persarum. Has tres rationes tangit breviter Hieronymus. Postremo de hoc Dario scribit Josephus, quod fuit filius Astyagis, qui alio nomine dictus est Assuerus, et quod ætate et moribus regno fuerat dignus.
paras.en: [[5:31|And Darius, the Mede|Et Darius Medus]], that is, the king of the Medes, [[5:31|succeeded to the kingdom|successit in regnum]] of King Balthasar, in the sense that he added it to his own empire, not that he rebuilt Babylon and held it, [[5:31|being threescore and two years old|annos natus sexaginta duos]], that is, he was then sixty-two years of age. Therefore King Cyrus, who was besieging Babylon with him, yielded to him in the succession to that kingdom, namely by reason of age; and because Darius was Cyrus's uncle; and again, because up to that time the kingdom of Media was greater than the kingdom of the Persians. These three reasons Jerome touches on briefly. Lastly, Josephus writes of this Darius that he was the son of Astyages, who by another name was called Assuerus, and that by age and character he had been worthy of the kingdom.
